title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium
subtitle: What sound is: longitudinal wave, s(x,t), λ = v/f, wave vs particle speed.
takeaway: Sound is a longitudinal wave: s(x,t), lambda = v/f; the wave moves at v, the gas jiggles in place.

cards.title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium
items: Sound needs a medium: it is a disturbance that travels through a material by pushing and pulling along the travel direction. Gas molecules oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions while the pattern — the wave — moves at the speed of sound; no bulk gas flows along the pipe. Sound in a fluid is purely longitudinal (transverse waves need shear); in a solid rod, longitudinal and transverse modes can coexist (Oly 10).
The wave pattern of a pure tone is sinusoidal, so everything follows from the displacement field $s(x,t) = s_0\sin(kx - \omega t)$:

cards.title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium (cont.)
items: $s$ is the small displacement of a fluid element from its equilibrium position, amplitude $s_0$ is microscopic (audible sounds give $s_0 \sim 10^{-8}$ to $10^{-4}$ m), $k = 2\pi/\lambda$, $\omega = 2\pi f$, and the wave speed is $v = \omega/k = f\lambda$ in the medium — only the pattern moves at $v$.

Compressions (pressure maxima) and rarefactions (minima) sit half a wavelength apart. The distance between two consecutive compressions is exactly $\lambda$. If a source vibrates with frequency $f$, it launches $f$ wavefronts per second, and the wavelength in the medium is $\lambda = v/f$ — the medium fixes $v$, the source fixes $f$, the medium and source together give $\lambda$.

cards.title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium (cont.)
items: A wave with frequency 340 Hz in air at 20 C has $\lambda = 343/340 = 1.009$ m. Direction convention: $s = s_0\sin(kx - \omega t)$ travels toward $+x$ because a phase point $kx - \omega t = $ const has $dx/dt = \omega/k = v > 0$.

Speed is a bulk property: $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ for a fluid (Section JEE-04), so it does not depend on frequency — a bass drum and a piccolo travel together (non-dispersive medium), and the tone reaching a listener is undistorted. Loudness relates to amplitude $s_0$ or pressure amplitude $\Delta P_0$ (JEE-02/12); pitch relates to $f$.

cards.title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium (cont.)
items: In vacuum $B = 0$, there is no sound, which is itself proof that sound is a pressure-elastic wave. For exam problems the working chain is: given $f$ and $v$, get $\lambda$; given $s(x,t)$, read $s_0, k, \omega, v = \omega/k$ and the travel direction from the sign of the $kx - \omega t$ combination.

longitudinal means the oscillation of each gas element is along the wave travel direction: layers alternately pile up (compression, higher pressure) and spread out (rarefaction, lower pressure), and this pattern advances at $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ — the elements themselves only jiggle about their mean positions.

title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium (cont.)
subtitle: What sound is: longitudinal wave, s(x,t), λ = v/f, wave vs particle speed.
takeaway: Sound is a longitudinal wave: s(x,t), lambda = v/f; the wave moves at v, the gas jiggles in place.

cards.title: Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave in a medium (cont.)
items: given $s = 2\times 10^{-6}\sin(1000x - 3.43\times 10^{5}t)$: $k = 1000$ rad/m so $\lambda = 2\pi/1000 = 6.28$ mm; $\omega = 3.43\times 10^{5}$ rad/s so $f = 54.6$ kHz; $v = \omega/k = 343$ m/s — air at room temperature; the $-\omega t$ sign means travel toward $+x$.

$v_{\mathrm{wave}} = \omega/k$ is the speed of the pattern; the gas element itself oscillates with velocity $u = ds/dt = -s_0\omega\cos(kx - \omega t)$, whose amplitude $s_0\omega$ is tiny (for $s_0 = 10^{-6}$ m at 340 Hz: $u_{\max} = 2.1\times 10^{-3}$ m/s against $v = 343$ m/s). The wave transports energy and momentum; the medium transports neither over long distances.

cards.title: Particle velocity vs wave speed — the classic confusion (cont.)
items: Two waves can pass through the same region and superpose (JEE-13) because the governing equation is linear for small $s$.

One full oscillation of the source emits exactly one wavelength of sound. The period $T = 1/f$ is the time in which the wave advances by $\lambda$: $v = \lambda/T = f\lambda$. When a wave crosses into another medium (sound from air into water), $f$ is fixed by the source, $v$ changes with the medium, so $\lambda$ changes: $\lambda_{\mathrm{water}} = 1480/340 = 4.35$ times longer for the same tone.

the wave equation for $s$ is $\partial^2 s/\partial t^2 = v^2 \partial^2 s/\partial x^2$ (JEE-04) — linear and second order, so sinusoidal solutions of any $f$ travel at the same $v$ (no dispersion), and the superposition principle holds.

cards.title: Particle velocity vs wave speed — the classic confusion (cont.)
items: a 200 Hz tuning fork is held in air at 20 C ($v = 343$ m/s): $\lambda = 1.72$ m; the same fork under water ($v = 1480$ m/s): $\lambda = 7.4$ m — same $f$, same pitch, different wavelength and different speed.

Sources are all vibrating bodies: strings, air columns, membranes, vocal cords. The vibrating surface alternately compresses and rarefies the adjacent air, launching the wave. Receivers are resonant systems too: the ear canal (~2.5 cm closed pipe, fundamental ~3.4 kHz — the ear is most sensitive near 3 kHz), microphone diaphragms, plates.

cards.title: How sound is produced and detected (practical frame) (cont.)
items: Resonance (JEE-16/17) amplifies sound both at the source and at the receiver, which is why Helmholtz resonators sing at one pitch and why a room has preferred frequencies (room modes = open/closed pipe problem in 3D).

A pure tone (single $f$) is a sine wave; real sounds are sums of harmonics + noise. The phase velocity of the fundamental defines $v$; timbre lives in the harmonic content. Ultrasound ($f > 20$ kHz) and infrasound ($f < 20$ Hz) obey exactly the same equations — the audible band is a biological, not physical, boundary. In air at 20 C the audible range spans $\lambda = 17$ m (20 Hz) to 17 mm (20 kHz).

items: in a duct filled with flowing gas of speed $w$ the observed frequency is Doppler-shifted (JEE-25): stationary listener in moving medium hears $f$ unchanged if both source and listener are carried by the same wind; wind matters only for relative motion along the line of sight.

(a) Find $v$ for a wave $s = s_0\sin(2.4x - 1.1\times 10^{3}t)$ in a metal: $v = \omega/k = 1100/2.4 = 458$ m/s, $\lambda = 2.62$ m, $f = 175$ Hz. (b) A sound wave has $\lambda = 1.62$ m in air at 20 C: $f = 343/1.62 = 212$ Hz. (c) Two speakers 1 m apart vibrate in phase at 340 Hz — the wavelength 1 m sets the fringe spacing (JEE-13). (d) A stone dropped in a well:
sound travels down, water splash returns — combines wave travel time with kinematics (paper Section D style).

cards.title: Worked micro-examples (cont.)
items: Linearity check: doubling $s_0$ doubles both $\Delta P_0$ and intensity (JEE-10), and raises the level by 6.02 dB in pressure terms (3.01 dB in intensity terms for doubling power). The wave speed stays exactly the same — amplitude never changes $v$ in linear acoustics (nonlinear acoustics, shocks, are outside the syllabus).
if $v$ depended on amplitude, a loud note would arrive later than a soft one and music would smear — linear acoustics ($s_0 \ll \lambda$) rules this out for everyday sound.
for $f = 1$ kHz, $s_0 = 10^{-5}$ m: $s_0/\lambda = 3\times 10^{-8}$ — infinitesimal strain, so the linear wave equation is superbly accurate for ordinary sound.

cards.title: Strain and acoustic pressure: dP = -B ds/dx
items: Sound is a small-amplitude compression wave: when a gas element is squeezed (negative $\partial s/\partial x$) its pressure rises. The extra pressure above ambient, $\Delta P = P - P_{0}$, is the acoustic (excess) pressure. Bulk modulus of the fluid is $B = -V\,dP/dV$ (positive), and for a displaced column the fractional volume change is exactly the strain $\partial s/\partial x$ (displacement gradient).
Linearizing gives the fundamental relation $\Delta P = -B\,\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial x}$ — the minus sign is essential: where displacement decreases with $x$ (elements pile up), pressure rises.

cards.title: Strain and acoustic pressure: dP = -B ds/dx (cont.)
items: Insert $s = s_0\sin(kx - \omega t)$: $\partial s/\partial x = k s_0\cos(kx - \omega t)$, so $\Delta P = -B k s_0\cos(kx - \omega t)$, i.e. pressure amplitude $\Delta P_0 = B k s_0$. Using $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$, $B = \rho v^2$ and $k = \omega/v$, this becomes the exam workhorse $\Delta P_0 = B k s_0 = \rho v \omega s_0$. In air at 20 C: $\rho = 1.2$ kg/m$^3$, $v = 343$ m/s, so $\Delta P_0 \approx 412\,\omega s_0$ (SI).
Example: $s_0 = 2\times 10^{-6}$ m at $f = 340$ Hz gives $\Delta P_0 = 1.2\times 343\times 2136\times 2\times 10^{-6} = 1.76$ Pa.

title: Strain and the acoustic pressure Delta P = -B,partial s/partial x
subtitle: Strain, acoustic pressure, $\Delta$P = −B $\partial$s/$\partial$x, $\Delta$P$_0$ = $\rho$v$\omega$s$_0$, bulk modulus frame.
takeaway: Pressure is the slope of displacement: dP = -B ds/dx and dP0 = rho v omega s0 bridge the two amplitudes.

cards.title: Strain and acoustic pressure: dP = -B ds/dx (cont.)
items: Physical sizes: atmospheric pressure $P_0 = 1.013\times 10^{5}$ Pa, while audible acoustic pressures run $2\times 10^{-5}$ Pa (threshold) to ~20 Pa (threshold of pain) — $\Delta P \ll P_0$ always, which is why the linear treatment works and why air density barely changes. Threshold of hearing:
$s_0 = \Delta P_0/(\rho v\omega) \approx 2.87\times 10^{-5}/(412\cdot 2\pi\cdot 1000) \approx 1.1\times 10^{-11}$ m at 1 kHz — a nuclear-scale displacement, yet the ear detects it.

the sign in $\Delta P = -B\partial s/\partial x$ is Hooke-type restoring physics: stretch the element (positive strain) and pressure drops below ambient — the fluid pulls back; squeeze and pressure rises — exactly like a spring $F = -kx$ with $B$ playing the stiffness role.

cards.title: Strain and acoustic pressure: dP = -B ds/dx (cont.)
items: where $s$ is at a maximum ($s = s_0$ at $kx - \omega t = \pi/2$), $\partial s/\partial x = 0$, so $\Delta P = 0$: displacement antinodes are pressure nodes. A microphone placed at a displacement node of a standing wave registers maximum pressure fluctuation (JEE-16).

Master formula: $\Delta P_0 = \rho v \omega s_0$. In air $\rho v \approx 412$ kg m$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ (often quoted as $Z = 412$ rayl, conventionally rounded to 400 — Oly 01). Three worked numbers from the source: (i) $f = 340$ Hz, $s_0 = 2\times 10^{-6}$ m $\Rightarrow \Delta P_0 = 1.76$ Pa; (ii) at threshold of hearing ($\Delta P_0 = 2\times 10^{-5}$ Pa at 1 kHz) $s_0 = 1.1\times 10^{-11}$ m;

cards.title: Pressure amplitude from displacement amplitude (cont.)
items: (iii) a loud rock concert ($\Delta P_0 = 20$ Pa) has $s_0 = 20/(412\cdot 6283) = 7.8\times 10^{-6}$ m at 1 kHz — still microscopic.

Frequency dependence at fixed $s_0$: $\Delta P_0 \propto \omega$ — high frequencies carry more pressure for the same displacement. At fixed pressure (same loudness) $s_0 \propto 1/\omega$ — bass drivers must swing much farther than tweeters for equal acoustic pressure, which is why woofers are large-excursion and tweeters tiny. Membrane displacement of a loudspeaker at 20 Hz and 120 Pa: $s_0 = 120/(412\cdot 126) = 2.3$ mm — visible shaking.
the $\omega$ factor is calculus, not physics: pressure is a gradient of displacement, and a fixed-amplitude pattern with shorter wavelength (higher $f$) has steeper slope $k s_0 = (\omega/v) s_0$.

cards.title: Pressure amplitude from displacement amplitude (cont.)
items: consistency with JEE-10: intensity $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$: for 1.76 Pa, $I = 3.1/824 = 3.7\times 10^{-3}$ W/m$^2$ — plausible loud speech-to-shout level, $\beta = 95.7$ dB.

The strain in a sound wave is $\partial s/\partial x = k s_0\cos(\cdot)$, of order $k s_0 = 2\pi s_0/\lambda$: for $s_0 = 10^{-6}$ m, $\lambda = 1$ m, strain $\sim 6\times 10^{-6}$ — the medium is compressed by parts per million. Bulk modulus of air at 1 atm, with adiabatic assumption (JEE-07): $B = \gamma P_0 = 1.4\times 1.013\times 10^{5} = 1.42\times 10^{5}$ Pa.

title: Strain and the acoustic pressure Delta P = -B,partial s/partial x (cont.)
subtitle: Strain, acoustic pressure, $\Delta$P = −B $\partial$s/$\partial$x, $\Delta$P$_0$ = $\rho$v$\omega$s$_0$, bulk modulus frame.
takeaway: Pressure is the slope of displacement: dP = -B ds/dx and dP0 = rho v omega s0 bridge the two amplitudes.

cards.title: Strain, bulk modulus, and where the speed comes from (cont.)
items: Then $v = \sqrt{B/\rho} = \sqrt{1.42\times 10^{5}/1.2} = 344$ m/s ok. For water $B = 2.2$ GPa, $\rho = 1000$: $v = 1483$ m/s ok; for steel $Y = 2\times 10^{11}$ Pa, $\rho = 7800$: $v = 5.06\times 10^{3}$ m/s (rod) ok.

Stiffness vs inertia: $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ says speed grows with restoring stiffness and falls with inertia. That is why sound is fast in diamond and slow in heavy gases, and why the isothermal vs adiabatic question (JEE-06/07) decides $B$ for gases: $B_{\mathrm{iso}} = P$, $B_{\mathrm{ad}} = \gamma P$ — a factor 1.18 in speed.

cards.title: Strain, bulk modulus, and where the speed comes from (cont.)
items: the speed of sound cannot exceed the bulk sound-speed limit of the material and never depends on $s_0$ or $f$ in the linear regime — two constraints every formula must respect.
at very high intensity (shock waves) the linear law breaks: the crests steepen because the compressed gas is locally faster. Sonic booms (JEE-28) are the built-up edge of this nonlinearity.

(a) $s(x,t) = 5\times 10^{-6}\cos(800x - 2.75\times 10^{5}t)$ in air: $\omega = 2.75\times 10^{5}$, $f = 43.8$ kHz (ultrasound), $v = 344$ m/s, $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0 = 1.2\times 344\times 2.75\times 10^{5}\times 5\times 10^{-6} = 568$ Pa — strong ultrasound. (b) Given $\Delta P_0 = 0.3$ Pa at 250 Hz in air:

cards.title: Micro-worked set (pressure–displacement round trip) (cont.)
items: $s_0 = 0.3/(412\cdot 1571) = 4.6\times 10^{-7}$ m. (c) In a Kundt tube dust heaps sit at pressure nodes... (d) The ear canal closed at one end has displacement node at the eardrum — maximum pressure on the eardrum (why it is sensitive).

Round-trip conversions examiners love: given $s_0$ and $f$ in a medium of known $\rho, v$: $\Delta P_0 = \rho v 2\pi f s_0$; given $\Delta P_0$: $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(2\pi f \rho v)$; given both: $v = \Delta P_0/(2\pi f \rho s_0)$, $\rho = \Delta P_0/(2\pi f v s_0)$. Dimension check: $\rho v\omega s_0 = $ kg m$^{-3}$ m s$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ m = kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ = Pa ok.

acoustic pressure is the quantity microphones and ears respond to; displacement is what optics-based methods (Laser Doppler Vibrometry) measure — exams give one, physics often wants the other, and $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$ is the bridge.

cards.title: Micro-worked set (pressure–displacement round trip) (cont.)
items: in water ($\rho v = 1.48\times 10^{6}$) the same $s_0$ at same $f$ gives $\Delta P_0$ 3600 times larger than in air — same displacement, hugely different pressure because water is far stiffer.

For a travelling wave $s = s_0\sin(kx - \omega t)$ the acoustic pressure is $\Delta P = -B\partial s/\partial x = -B k s_0\cos(kx - \omega t) = \Delta P_0\sin(kx - \omega t - \pi/2)$: pressure lags displacement by 90 degrees (is in quadrature). Graphically:

at points where gas has maximum displacement from equilibrium, the local density is unmodified (slope of $s$ is zero), so pressure is ambient; where the slope of $s$ is steepest (elements pile up most), displacement itself is zero and pressure is extremal. Compressions therefore sit a quarter wavelength from displacement maxima.

cards.title: Displacement vs pressure phase: the quadrature structure of sound.
items: Energy picture: in a sound wave, energy sloshes between ordered motion of elements (kinetic, max where elements move fastest = displacement-phase crossings) and elastic compression energy (max where $\Delta P$ is extremal). The two are in quadrature, exactly like a mass-spring oscillator being driven through equilibrium. Mean energy density $\bar u = \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 (k s_0)^2\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2$... cleanly:

$\bar u = \frac{1}{2}\rho\omega^2 s_0^2$ (equal mean kinetic and potential share $\frac{1}{4}\rho\omega^2 s_0^2$ each; equivalently $\bar u = \Delta P_0^2/(4B)\cdot 2 = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v^2)$ since $B = \rho v^2$).

cards.title: Displacement vs pressure phase: the quadrature structure of sound.
items: For a standing wave the roles exchange spatially instead: nodes of $s$ are antinodes of $\Delta P$ and vice versa, and standing-wave energy density is maximum at both node types at different phases. The quadrature relation $\Delta P = -B\partial s/\partial x$ is the safest way to get the relative phase right in any geometry — more reliable than memorising "pressure leads/lags".

pressure measures the local slope (spatial derivative) of the displacement pattern; for a sinusoid, derivative = phase shift by $\pi/2$. The minus sign adds $\pi$, giving $\Delta P$ in antiphase with $\partial s/\partial x$, quadrature with $s$ itself.

displacement node in a pipe closed at the rigid end: the end forces $s = 0$ there, slope is maximal, pressure is maximum — consistent with $\Delta P = -B\partial s/\partial x$ and with the physics that a wall bears the full pressure swing.

cards.title: Energy density and the travelling-wave energy flux
items: Mean energy density of a travelling sound wave: $\bar u = \frac{1}{2}\rho\omega^2 s_0^2 = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2\rho v^2} = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2B}$. Numerically at 1 kHz, $\Delta P_0 = 1$ Pa in air: $\bar u = 1/(2\cdot 1.42\times 10^{5}) = 3.5\times 10^{-6}$ J/m$^3$ — tiny energy densities carrying audible sound across rooms.
The energy flux (intensity) is energy density times speed: $I = \bar u v = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2\rho v} = \frac{1}{2}\rho v\omega^2 s_0^2$ (JEE-10 keeps the full intensity toolkit).

cards.title: Energy density and the travelling-wave energy flux (cont.)
items: Compare EM waves: there $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are in phase and energy flux is peak-crossing; in sound the kinetic and compressive energies are in quadrature but their SUM is what travels, and $I = \bar u v$ still holds cycle-averaged. Peak instantaneous energy density doubles the mean: $u_{\max} = \rho\omega^2 s_0^2 = 2\bar u$.

units: $\rho\omega^2 s_0^2 = $ kg m$^{-3}$ s$^{-2}$ m$^2$ = J m$^{-3}$ ok; $I = \bar u v$ = J m$^{-3}$ m s$^{-1}$ = W m$^{-2}$ ok; both expressions for $\bar u$ agree through $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$: $\Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v^2) = \rho^2 v^2\omega^2 s_0^2/(2\rho v^2) = \frac{1}{2}\rho\omega^2 s_0^2$ ok.

title: Displacement vs pressure phase: the quadrature structure of sound (cont.)
subtitle: s–$\Delta$P quadrature, energy density ½$\rho$$\omega$²s$_0$², phase map of one wavelength.
takeaway: Pressure lags displacement by 90 degrees; energy density averages 1/2 rho omega^2 s0^2.

cards.title: Energy density and the travelling-wave energy flux (cont.)
items: the 1/2 factors come from time-averaging $\sin^2$ and $\cos^2$ over a cycle (both give 1/2); the two energies peak alternately, so the total energy density actually oscillates at $2\omega$ around $\bar u$ — a detail Olympiad problems exploit (Oly 05).

At $kx - \omega t = 0$: $s = 0$ (elements crossing equilibrium), $\Delta P = -\Delta P_0$ (rarefaction trough, slope of $s$ maximal positive... careful: $\partial s/\partial x = k s_0\cos 0 = +k s_0 > 0$ gives $\Delta P = -Bk s_0$, a rarefaction). At $kx - \omega t = \pi/2$: $s = +s_0$ (max displacement), $\Delta P = 0$ (undisturbed density). At $\pi$: $s = 0$, $\Delta P = +\Delta P_0$ (compression).

cards.title: Phase map of one wavelength (memorise the picture) (cont.)
items: At $3\pi/2$: $s = -s_0$, $\Delta P = 0$. So moving along $x$ at fixed time: compression (P max) sits at $s$ rising through zero; rarefaction at $s$ falling through zero; $\Delta P$ extrema are $\lambda/4$ from $s$ extrema and in sign alternation every $\lambda/2$.

Auditory perspective: the eardrum is a pressure sensor; what we "hear" is the $\Delta P(t)$ sequence at our location. If you could see the air, you would watch elements sloshing back and forth by $s_0$ while crests of density stream past at $v$. The displacement field is the more fundamental variable (it obeys the wave equation directly), the pressure field its derivative partner.

cards.title: Phase map of one wavelength (memorise the picture) (cont.)
items: the pair ($s$, $\Delta P$) forms a two-component wave state analogous to ($x$, $p$) in mechanics; characteristic acoustic impedance $Z = \Delta P/u = \rho v$ is the ratio (Oly 01), constant for a travelling wave, imaginary/position-dependent for standing waves.

(a) Write $\Delta P(x,t)$ for $s = s_0\sin(kx - \omega t + \phi)$: always $\Delta P = -B k s_0\cos(kx - \omega t + \phi) = \Delta P_0\sin(kx - \omega t + \phi - \pi/2)$. The phase shift is universal: pressure lags displacement by $\pi/2$ regardless of $\phi$. (b) Standing wave $s = 2s_0\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$:

cards.title: Worked check set on phase and energy (cont.)
items: $\Delta P = -2Bk s_0\cos(kx)\cos(\omega t)$ — node of $s$ at $kx = 0$ is antinode of $\Delta P$ ok. (c) Energy: $\bar u = \frac{1}{2}\rho\omega^2 s_0^2$ for $f = 340$ Hz, $s_0 = 2\times 10^{-6}$: $\bar u = 0.5\cdot 1.2\cdot (2136)^2\cdot(2\times 10^{-6})^2 = 1.1\times 10^{-5}$ J/m$^3$; intensity $I = \bar u v = 3.7$ mW/m$^2$ ok consistent with SN-02.

Traps: (i) writing $\Delta P = \Delta P_0\sin(kx - \omega t)$ "in phase with $s$" — wrong, off by $\pi/2$; (ii) treating $\Delta P_0 = B k s_0$ as $B s_0/\lambda$ — missing $2\pi$; (iii) using $I = \Delta P_0 v$ instead of the time-averaged $\Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$ — factor $\sqrt 2$ bookkeeping (RMS vs peak: $I = \Delta P_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/(\rho v)$ with $\Delta P_{\mathrm{rms}} = \Delta P_0/\sqrt 2$).

takeaway: Pressure lags displacement by 90 degrees; energy density averages 1/2 rho omega^2 s0^2.

cards.title: Worked check set on phase and energy (cont.)
items: the factor-2 in $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$ vs $\Delta P_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/(\rho v)$ is the peak-vs-RMS convention; state which amplitude you use before writing the intensity.

cross-check every amplitude formula with two routes: $I = \frac{1}{2}\rho v\omega^2 s_0^2$ and $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$ must agree through $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$ — if not, a $\sqrt 2$ or $2\pi$ is missing.

Derivation from two laws. (1) Newton 2nd law for a slice of fluid of thickness $\Delta x$, area $A$: net force $-A\,\partial(\Delta P)/\partial x\,\Delta x$ equals mass $\rho A\Delta x$ times acceleration $\partial^2 s/\partial t^2$: $\rho\,\dfrac{\partial^2 s}{\partial t^2} = -\dfrac{\partial(\Delta P)}{\partial x}$. (2) The medium law $\Delta P = -B\,\partial s/\partial x$. Differentiate (2) in $x$ and insert: $\rho\,\partial^2 s/\partial t^2 = B\,\partial^2 s/\partial x^2$, i.e.

cards.title: The sound wave equation and v = sqrtB/rho (cont.)
items: the wave equation $\dfrac{\partial^2 s}{\partial t^2} = v^2\dfrac{\partial^2 s}{\partial x^2}$ with $\mathbf{v = \sqrt{B/\rho}}$.

Everything follows from that box: for a gas with adiabatic bulk modulus $B = \gamma P$ (JEE-07) $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} = \sqrt{\gamma R T/M}$; for a rod $B \to Y$ (JEE-05); for a liquid $B = $ bulk modulus. The wave equation is linear and second order, so sinusoids of every frequency travel at the same $v$ (no dispersion in this regime) and superposition holds. General solutions:
$s = f(x - vt) + g(x + vt)$ — any shape travels undistorted at $\pm v$.

cards.title: The sound wave equation and v = sqrtB/rho (cont.)
items: Velocity of the medium is not $v$: energy propagates at phase speed $v = \omega/k$ for these non-dispersive waves (group speed $d\omega/dk = v$ too). The two constants of the wave equation, $\rho$ (inertia) and $B$ (elasticity), fully determine speed — frequency and amplitude do not enter. Compressibility $\kappa = 1/B$: $v = 1/\sqrt{\rho\kappa}$ — a form worth recognising since some data give $\kappa$.

the derivation is exactly the spring-mass continuum: $\rho$ is the inertia density, $B$ the stiffness against compression; $\sqrt{stiffness/inertia}$ has units m/s and is the only combination that can be a speed — dimensional analysis alone already shows $v \propto \sqrt{B/\rho}$.

cards.title: The sound wave equation and v = sqrtB/rho (cont.)

(i) $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ when bulk modulus/density given. (ii) $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$ for gases when $P, \rho$ known (careful: use adiabatic $\gamma$). cards.title: What the wave equation does NOT say (scope guard)
items: It assumes: small amplitude ($s_0 \ll \lambda$, $\Delta P \ll P_0$), no viscosity/thermal conduction (no attenuation), linear $B$, homogeneous medium. Shock waves (sonic boom edges) need nonlinear theory. All exam formulas are the linear limit.

The equation also holds in moving media if you transform to the medium frame (JEE-25 wind), and in 3D as $\partial^2 s/\partial t^2 = v^2\nabla^2 s$ with solutions like $s = (A/r)\sin(kr - \omega t)$ for a point source (JEE-11).

title: Newton's isothermal estimate: 280 m/s — and why it fails
subtitle: Newton isothermal 280 m/s, time-scale argument, √$\gamma$ correction physics.
takeaway: Newton isothermal gives 280 m/s because B = P; sound is far too fast for heat to flow.

cards.title: Newton's isothermal estimate: 280 m/s — and why it fails (cont.)
items: $v = \sqrt{1.013\times 10^{5}/1.293} = 2.80\times 10^{2}$ m/s — about 15% below the measured 331.5 m/s at 0 C. Newton noticed the discrepancy and fudged the density; the real fix is the thermodynamics (JEE-07).

Why isothermal is wrong: a compression cycle at 340 Hz is far too fast for heat to flow. Compression time scale $\sim 1/f \approx 3$ ms; thermal diffusion time across a half wavelength ($\lambda/2 \sim 0.5$ m) is $t_{\mathrm{th}} \sim x^2/\alpha$ with $\alpha = 2.2\times 10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s for air: $t_{\mathrm{th}} \sim 10^{4}$ s — ten million periods. The compression is therefore adiabatic:
no heat exchange, temperature rises slightly in compressions ($\Delta T = T\Delta P/(\gamma P) \sim 10^{-2}$ K at 1 Pa), and the gas is stiffer: $B_{\mathrm{ad}} = \gamma P$.

cards.title: Newton's isothermal estimate: 280 m/s — and why it fails (cont.)
items: The measured number at 0 C is 331.5 m/s; $\sqrt{\gamma} = \sqrt{1.4} = 1.183$; $280\times 1.183 = 331.3$ m/s — the Laplace factor is exactly what is needed. Thermodynamic check: sound speed equals $\sqrt{(\partial P/\partial \rho)_s}$ (entropy constant) not $(\partial P/\partial \rho)_T$; for an ideal gas these differ by exactly $\gamma$.

the medium is stiffer when it cannot thermally relax: adiabatic compression raises $T$, which raises pressure further (extra $\gamma - 1 = 0.4$ of push), so the restoring force and hence speed rise by $\sqrt\gamma = 1.183$ — the 18.3% correction turns 280 into 331.

cards.title: Newton's isothermal estimate: 280 m/s — and why it fails (cont.)
items: ratio measured/Newton $= 331.5/279.9 = 1.184 = \sqrt{1.4}$ ok to three digits — the discrepancy is 100% of the error and 0% mystery.

General principle: a gas process is isothermal if the period is much longer than the thermal diffusion time ($f \ll \alpha/\lambda^2$-type condition), adiabatic if much shorter. Sound frequencies 20 Hz – 20 kHz give periods 0.05 – 50 ms; thermal equilibration across $\lambda/2$ takes seconds to hours. So ALL audible sound is adiabatic.
The isothermal assumption would only hold for extremely slow, quasi-static compressions (e.g. 0.01 Hz in a small chamber — infrasonic creep, not sound propagation).

cards.title: Why heat cannot flow: time-scale argument (the physics core) (con.
items: At very high frequencies in rarefied gases (mean free path comparable to $\lambda$, MHz in low-pressure chambers) the regime changes again (relaxation, Knudsen) — speed can deviate; outside syllabus, but flag the validity domain: $\lambda \gg$ mean free path ($\sim 70$ nm in air at STP, so up to THz acoustics it holds).

the thermal diffusion time grows as $\lambda^2$ while the period grows only as $1/f$: for any fixed medium there is always a frequency above which the process is adiabatic, and ordinary sound sits many orders above it.
numerically: at $f = 1$ kHz, $\lambda = 0.34$ m, $t_{\mathrm{th}} \sim (0.17)^2/2.2\times 10^{-5} = 1.3\times 10^{3}$ s vs period 1 ms — ratio $10^{6}$: adiabatic by a factor of a million.

cards.title: What Newton got right, and the exam framing
items: Newton correctly: (i) identified sound with a compressional wave in air; (ii) derived $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ (in modern form); (iii) computed the isothermal $B = P$ rigorously; (iv) saw temperature and molar-mass dependence in $P/\rho = RT/M$. He lacked the first law of thermodynamics (Carnot-Clausius came later), so the adiabatic exponent was unavailable.

Laplace supplied it in 1816. Exam questions often ask "explain the discrepancy and derive the corrected speed" — full marks need: isothermal value 280, measured 331, ratio $\sqrt\gamma$, time-scale argument, and the corrected formula $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$.

cards.title: What Newton got right, and the exam framing (cont.)
items: Traps: (i) using $B = P$ "because it is a gas" — must ask isothermal or adiabatic; always adiabatic for sound. (ii) writing $v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$ from the ideal gas law as if it were the final answer — that form is Newton speed; multiply by $\sqrt\gamma$. (iii) confusing $\gamma = C_p/C_v = 1.4$ (diatomic) with $5/3$ (monatomic) — He, Ar: $\gamma = 5/3$, $\sqrt\gamma = 1.29$.

monatomic gas check: at STP with $\gamma = 5/3$, $M = 4$ g (He): $v = \sqrt{(5/3)\cdot 1.013\times 10^{5}/0.179} = 971$ m/s at 0 C ($\rho_{\mathrm{He}} = 0.179$); formula route $\sqrt{\gamma R T/M} = 969$ m/s ok consistent.

cards.title: Mini-worked: isothermal vs adiabatic side by side
items: Given an unknown gas at $P = 1$ atm, $\rho = 1.6$ kg/m$^3$, measured $v = 450$ m/s. Isothermal prediction $\sqrt{1.013\times 10^{5}/1.6} = 252$ m/s; ratio $450/252 = 1.79 = \sqrt{\gamma} \Rightarrow \gamma = 3.2$?? Non-physical — so either the measurement or the density is off: real gases have $1 < \gamma \leqslant 1.67$.
Reverse-engineering traps like this train consistency checks: $v\sqrt{\rho/P} = \sqrt\gamma \in [1, 1.29]$ always.

cards.title: Mini-worked: isothermal vs adiabatic side by side (cont.)
items: Another: at what temperature does Newton predict the CORRECT 331 m/s? $T = M v^2/(\gamma R)$... Newton form $v = \sqrt{RT/M}$: $T = Mv^2/R = 0.029\cdot 331^2/8.314 = 378$ K = 105 C — an isothermal gas at 105 C would carry sound like an adiabatic gas at 0 C. Cute but never physical for propagation.

the entire 280-vs-331 story is a single exponent: $v_{\mathrm{ad}} = \sqrt\gamma v_{\mathrm{iso}}$, and every sound speed in a gas can be written $v = \sqrt\gamma\, v_{\mathrm{Newton}}$ with $v_{\mathrm{Newton}} = \sqrt{RT/M}$ at temperature $T$.

cards.title: Laplace correction: B = gamma P, v = sqrtgamma P/rho = sqrtga.
items: Derivation of $B_{\mathrm{ad}} = \gamma P$: $PV^{\gamma} = C \Rightarrow P\gamma V^{\gamma-1}dV + V^{\gamma}dP = 0 \Rightarrow dP/dV = -\gamma P/V \Rightarrow B = -V dP/dV = \gamma P$ ok. Microscopic meaning of $\gamma = C_p/C_v$: in adiabatic compression no heat escapes, so the temperature rise adds thermal pressure on top of the compression pressure; $C_p - C_v = R$ (per mole) quantifies the extra push;

cards.title: Laplace correction: B = gamma P, v = sqrtgamma P/rho = sqrtga.
items: Consequences to memorise: (i) $v \propto \sqrt T$ (absolute temperature!); (ii) $v$ independent of $P$ at fixed $T$ (double $P$, $\rho$ doubles too, ratio $P/\rho = RT/M$ fixed); (iii) $v \propto 1/\sqrt M$ at fixed $T, \gamma$; (iv) humid air faster than dry (effective $M$ drops); (v) $\gamma$ from sound speed: $\gamma = v^2 M/(RT)$ — the classic "measure $\gamma$ by sound" experiment.

the correction factor is exactly $\sqrt\gamma$ because $B_{\mathrm{ad}}/B_{\mathrm{iso}} = \gamma P/P = \gamma$ and $v \propto \sqrt B$; the measured/Newton ratio 331/280 = 1.183 = $\sqrt{1.4}$ is the quantitative proof.

Near the ground this makes sound refract upward during the day (hot ground) and downward at night (temperature inversion) — why sound carries over lakes at night.
