cards.title: Laplace-era consistency drills (cont.)
items: Cross-check anchors: air 0 C 331, 20 C 343, He 20 C 1007, H2 0 C 1260, CO2 0 C 259, water 20 C 1482, steel rod 5064 — keep this handful in memory for sanity checks of every computation.

the speed formula $\sqrt{(\partial P/\partial\rho)_s}$ is general: for a van der Waals gas or a liquid with thermal expansion corrections the sound speed measures the adiabatic stiffness — acoustic measurements probe the equation of state directly (Oly 12).

cards.title: Temperature law: v = 331.3 sqrt(T/273) m/s
items: From $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$: at fixed gas, $v \propto \sqrt T$ with $T$ in kelvin. Anchored at 0 C: $v(T) = 331.3\sqrt{T/273.15}$ m/s. Linear form for everyday range: $v \approx 331.3 + 0.60\,t$ C (exact slope at 20 C: $dv/dT = v/2T = 343/(2\cdot 293) = 0.585$ m/s/K; the "0.6" is a rounded staple). Values: $-40$ C: 306; 0 C: 331; 20 C: 343; 37 C: 350; 100 C: 386 m/s.
The $\sqrt T$ law is exact for ideal gases; the linear law is its first-order expansion: $v = 331.3(1 + t/273.15)^{1/2} \approx 331.3(1 + t/546)$ — slope 0.605 m/s/K at 0 C.

cards.title: Temperature law: v = 331.3 sqrt(T/273) m/s
items: Physics: heating a gas at constant pressure lowers its density ($\rho = PM/RT$) while $B = \gamma P$ stays put — lighter medium, same stiffness, faster wave. At constant volume, heating raises $P$ and $B$ with $\rho$ fixed — also faster. In both cases only $T$ matters: $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$ carries no $P$ or $\rho$ separately.

Micro-physical picture (kinetic theory): $v_{\mathrm{sound}} \sim 0.68\,\bar c$ for $\gamma = 1.4$ where $\bar c = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$ is the mean molecular speed — sound is a coherent disturbance propagated by molecular collisions at roughly the thermal speed. $\bar c$ at 293 K in air $= 464$ m/s; $0.68\times 464 = 316$... order of magnitude; exact $v/\bar c = \sqrt{\gamma\pi/8} = 0.74$.

title: Temperature dependence: v = 331.3sqrtT/273 m/s, approx 331 + 0.6t
subtitle: v $\propto$ √T, linear 331+0.6t, lapse-rate refraction, sound horizon formula.
takeaway: v = 331.3 sqrt(T/273) m/s, about 0.6 m/s per degree; kelvin only inside the root.

cards.title: Temperature dependence: v = 331.3sqrtT/273 m/s, approx 331 + 0..
items: the $\sqrt T$ law is the same $\sqrt{stiffness/inertia}$ as always, with $B = \gamma PM/RT$ after eliminating $\rho$ — the gas constant $R$ is what ties mechanics to thermodynamics here.
halving absolute temperature drops speed by $\sqrt 2$ only: 300 K $\to$ 347; 150 K $\to$ 245 m/s. Speed is a SLOW function of $T$ — temperature errors of 10 K move $v$ by 1.7%.

Temperature lapse rate $dT/dz = -6.5$ K/km (troposphere): $dv/dz = (v/2T)(dT/dz) = 0.585\times(-6.5) = -3.8$ m/s per km near the surface. Consequence: sound rays curve toward the cold region. Day: ground hot, air cooler aloft $\to$ rays bend up $\to$ sound shadows near ground. Night:

cards.title: Sound horizon, lapse rate, and the bonus gravity formula (cont.)
items: temperature inversion (warm aloft) $\to$ rays bend down $\to$ sound hugs the ground and carries far — the "lake at night" effect. Acoustic shadow zones behind warm columns.
Isothermal-atmosphere bonus (source §2.5): $v(h) = v_0\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{2Mgh}{\gamma R T_0}}$ with constant $g$;

setting $v = 0$ gives atmosphere height $h_{\max} = \dfrac{\gamma R T_0}{Mg} = \dfrac{1.4\cdot 8.314\cdot 288}{0.029\cdot 9.8} = 11.9$ km — the thermosphere-scale estimate for an isothermal troposphere. Beyond it there is no medium, no sound.

cards.title: Sound horizon, lapse rate, and the bonus gravity formula (cont.)
items: Refraction quantitative: the ray curvature radius $R_c = v/|dv/dz|$... for the standard treatment $R_c = v/(dv/dz)$; with $dv/dz = -3.8$ m/s/km and $v = 343$: $R_c = 343/0.0038 = 90$ km — rays over long distances curve gently on a 90 km radius arc. Over 1 km, the ray drops $\approx L^2/(2R_c) = 5.5$ m — enough to matter for precise ranging.

speed at 5 km altitude with lapse rate: $T = 288 - 32.5 = 255.5$ K, $v = 331.3\sqrt{255.5/273.15} = 320$ m/s — 7% slower than sea level; aircraft sound takes longer to arrive from above than naive $h/v_{0}$ estimates.

cards.title: Temperature-based problem patterns
items: (a) "At what temperature is the speed 350 m/s?" $T = 273.15(350/331.3)^2 = 305$ K = 32 C. (b) "By how much does speed change from 20 C to 25 C?" $\Delta v = 0.585\cdot 5 = 2.9$ m/s (or exact $346.1 - 343.2 = 2.9$ ok). (c) "A pipe closed at one end resonates at 300 Hz at 20 C; find its length" then "at what T does it resonate at 306 Hz?" — $f \propto v \propto \sqrt T$:
$T_2 = T_1(306/300)^2 = 293.15\cdot 1.0404 = 305$ K = 32 C ok pattern: frequency of fixed-length modes scales as $\sqrt T$.

title: Temperature dependence: v = 331.3sqrtT/273 m/s, approx 331 + 0.6t (cont.)
subtitle: v $\propto$ √T, linear 331+0.6t, lapse-rate refraction, sound horizon formula.
takeaway: v = 331.3 sqrt(T/273) m/s, about 0.6 m/s per degree; kelvin only inside the root.

cards.title: Temperature-based problem patterns (cont.)
items: Humidity angle (JEE-09): speed at fixed $T$ rises with water-vapour fraction — at 20 C saturated air ($p_{\mathrm{vap}} = 2.3$ kPa) has $v$ about 0.2% (0.7 m/s) above dry — small but the same order as 1 C! Exam problems often say "dry air" implicitly.

modes of any resonator scale with $v$: pipe, Kundt, resonance tube — frequency ratios at two temperatures collapse to $\sqrt{T_2/T_1}$ regardless of geometry. That ratio trick shortens many problems to one line.
compute twice with the exact and linear laws at 37 C: exact $331.3\sqrt{310.15/273.15} = 353.0$; linear $331.3 + 0.6\cdot 37 = 353.5$ — agree to 0.5 m/s; either is fine in exams if you state which.

cards.title: Traps and consistency checks for the v(T) family
items: Trap list: (i) Celsius in the square root — always kelvin. (ii) $v \propto \sqrt T$ vs "0.6 m/s per C" — the linear law is a local approximation (fails far from 0 C: at 300 C, linear gives 511, exact gives 587). (iii) Forgetting $\gamma$ changes between gases when comparing (He vs air needs both $M$ and $\gamma$). (iv) Assuming pressure changes matter — they do not (at fixed T). (v) Applying the gas law to solids or liquids.

Consistency loop for any $v$ computation: compute with $\sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$ in SI; compare against the anchor table (air 331/343, He ~1000, H2 ~1260, water ~1480, steel ~5000); check $T$ in kelvin and $M$ in kg/mol; the answer should land within a few percent of anchors for known media.

cards.title: Traps and consistency checks for the v(T) family (cont.)
items: for a hard vacuum, $\rho \to 0$ and $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$ stays formally finite while the wave amplitude interpretation changes — no molecules, no sound; the formula survives only as a limit of a thinning gas with vanishing mean free path conditions.

From $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$: (i) $v \propto 1/\sqrt M$ at fixed $\gamma, T$ — light gases sound fast: He 972 m/s at 0 C, H2 1260 m/s at 0 C vs air 331. (ii) $\gamma$ matters too: He has $\gamma = 5/3$ vs air 1.4 — comparing gases needs both factors: $v_2/v_1 = \sqrt{\gamma_2 M_1/(\gamma_1 M_2)}$. (iii) Pressure: none — the ideal-gas speed has no $P$ in it. Double the pressure of a sealed air sample at fixed T:

cards.title: Molar mass, humidity, and the pressure-independence of sound spee.
items: $\rho$ doubles, $B = \gamma P$ doubles, $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ unchanged ok. Sound inside a high-pressure scuba tank (200 atm) still travels 343 m/s at room temperature (density is 200x, stiffness 200x).

Humidity: water vapour ($M = 18$) replaces N2/O2 ($M_{\mathrm{dry}} = 29$): effective molar mass $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = 0.622 M_d + 0.378 M_v$... precisely with mole fraction $x$ of vapour: $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = (1-x)\cdot 29 + x\cdot 18$. At 30 C saturated, vapour pressure 4.2 kPa, $x = 0.042$: $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = 28.5$, $v$ up 0.9% (3 m/s). But humid air is ALSO less dense... consistent:
$v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M_{\mathrm{eff}}}$ grows as $M_{\mathrm{eff}}$ falls. Rule: humid air sounds faster; the effect peaks in hot humid weather.

title: Molar mass, humidity, and the pressure-independence of sound speed
subtitle: Molar mass, humidity, pressure independence, gas identity problems.
takeaway: Light gases sound fast (1/sqrt(M)); humidity helps a little; pressure is irrelevant at fixed T.

cards.title: Molar mass, humidity, and the pressure-independence of sound spee.
items: Gas mixtures: $\gamma_{\mathrm{eff}}$ for a mixture is not the average of $\gamma$; use $C_p, C_v$ averaging: $C_{v,\mathrm{mix}} = \sum x_i C_{v,i}$, $\gamma = (C_v + R)/C_v$. For air-like N2/O2 this is automatic ($\gamma = 1.4$). For a 50-50 He-N2 mix: $C_v = 12.5 + 20.8 = 33.3$ J/mol-K... ($C_{v,\mathrm{He}} = 3R/2 = 12.5$, $C_{v,\mathrm{N2}} = 5R/2 = 20.8$), $\gamma = 35.8/33.3 = 1.075$, $M = 16.5$ g:

pressure independence: $P$ and $\rho$ both live in $P/\rho = RT/M$; any process that changes $P$ at fixed $T$ (pumping, sealing) moves them together. Only $T$, $M$, $\gamma$ are free parameters of gas sound speed.

cards.title: Molar mass, humidity, and the pressure-independence of sound spee.
items: scuba-tank paradox: same $v$ at 200 atm, but intensity for a given $s_0$ rises with $\rho v$: a speaker driven at the same displacement is much louder (higher $Z = \rho v$) in dense gas — Oly 01 impedance thinking.

cards.title: Numbers table (gas speeds at 0 C unless noted) (cont.)
items: Sound in CO2 is slower than air — deep voices from helium-free "heavy" mixtures... the party trick: He raises formant frequencies (sound speed in He is 2.9x, resonant cavities of the vocal tract scale up in pitch); SF6 ($M = 146$ g) drops it to 134 m/s... roughly $\sqrt{1.0\cdot 8.314\cdot 273/0.146} = 125$ m/s — deep voice effect.

Humidity worked: 25 C, 60% RH: vapour pressure 1.9 kPa, $x = 0.019$, $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = 28.8$, $v = 346.3$ vs dry 346.1 — 0.2 m/s only at moderate humidity; saturated 35 C: 1.5 m/s effect. Small — often neglected, but state "dry air" or "neglect humidity" explicitly.

cards.title: Numbers table (gas speeds at 0 C unless noted) (cont.)
items: independence stress-test: at 20 C, air at 0.1 atm (density 0.12 kg/m$^3$): $v = \sqrt{1.4\cdot 10^{4}/0.12} = 342$ ok ~343; at 50 atm: same. Only temperature moves it.

gas sound speed in a stellar interior ($T = 10^{7}$ K, ionised H, $\gamma = 5/3$): $v = \sqrt{(5/3)\cdot 8.314\cdot 10^{7}/0.001} = 3.7\times 10^{5}$ m/s = 370 km/s — same formula, all the way to stars (acoustic asteroseismology).

title: Molar mass, humidity, and the pressure-independence of sound speed (cont.)
subtitle: Molar mass, humidity, pressure independence, gas identity problems.
takeaway: Light gases sound fast (1/sqrt(M)); humidity helps a little; pressure is irrelevant at fixed T.

cards.title: Problem patterns on gas identity
items: (a) Identify a gas: $v = 263$ m/s at 0 C: $M = \gamma R T/v^2 = 1.4\cdot 8.314\cdot 273/263^2 = 0.046$ kg/mol $\approx$ CO2 (44 g) with $\gamma = 1.3$ gives 259 ok. (b) A gas mixture of unknown proportion: use $M_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from measured $v$: $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = \gamma R T/v^2$, then mole fraction from $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = 29(1-x) + 2x$ (He-air: $x = (29 - M_{\mathrm{eff}})/27$).
(c) "A sound pulse takes 2.92 s to travel 1 km in a gas at 27 C; identify": $v = 342.5$, $T = 300$: $M = \gamma R T/v^2 = 0.0285$ kg/mol — nitrogen-dominated air ok.

cards.title: Problem patterns on gas identity (cont.)
items: Comparison traps: "Sound is faster in warm air because molecules move faster" — TRUE but the exam formula is $\sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$; "sound is faster at higher pressure" — FALSE; "sound is faster in denser media" — FALSE as a general rule (steel beats mercury? steel 5000 vs Hg 1440: stiffness dominates; lead is dense yet slow: 1190).
density alone never sets speed; the ratio $B/\rho$ does. Heavy gases are slow only when stiffness does not compensate — in ideal gases $B/\rho = \gamma RT/M$ is density-free at fixed T.
round-trip: given $v = 1260$ m/s at 0 C, $M = 2$ g, find $\gamma$: $\gamma = v^2 M/(RT) = 1260^2\cdot 0.002/(8.314\cdot 273) = 1.40$ ok diatomic hydrogen.

cards.title: Consolidation: the gas-speed parameter space
items: Free parameters of $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = \sqrt{\gamma R T/M}$: just ($\gamma$, $T$, $M$). Pressure, density, volume, container size, amplitude, frequency: none of them enter. For a closed container being heated, $v$ rises as $\sqrt T$ regardless of pressure rise. For a weather front, $v$ changes with T (and slightly with humidity) — standard correction in precise acoustic ranging:
0.6 m/s per C, so a 5 C error in assumed temperature gives 1.7% error in distance measured by time of flight (3.4 m per km).

cards.title: Consolidation: the gas-speed parameter space (cont.)
items: Sonic boom geometry (JEE-28) and Doppler (JEE-22-27) all need the LOCAL $v$; atmospheric sound-speed profile $v(T(z))$ is the refractive index of acoustics: $n_{\mathrm{ac}} = v_{0}/v(z) > 1$ aloft... rays bend toward lower speed (colder air) — exactly like light in a gradient index.

meteorological "acoustic sounding" (SODAR) inverts Doppler + refraction of sound to measure wind and temperature profiles — the exam toolkit ($v(T)$, Doppler, refraction) is literally the working method.

title: Intensity of sound: I = frac12rho vomega2 s 02 = dfracDelta P 022rho v
subtitle: I = ½$\rho$v$\omega$²s$_0$² = $\Delta$P$_0$²/2$\rho$v, energy budget, amplitude scaling table.
takeaway: I = dP0^2/(2 rho v) = 1/2 rho v omega^2 s0^2; two forms must always agree.

cards.title: Sound intensity: I = (1/2) rho v omega^2 s_0^2
items: Intensity = average power per area = $\bar u v$ with $\bar u = \frac{1}{2}\rho\omega^2 s_0^2$ (SN-03): $I = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v\omega^2 s_0^2$. Since $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$, equally $I = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2\rho v} = \dfrac{\Delta P_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{\rho v} = \dfrac{1}{2}u_{\max}\omega s_0\cdot$...

keep the two boxed forms only. Third useful form: $I = \frac{1}{2} Z \omega^2 s_0^2$ with impedance $Z = \rho v$ (Oly 01). Worked (source Q3): $P = 0.1$ W isotropic at $r = 100$ m: $I = P/(4\pi r^2) = 7.96\times 10^{-5}$ W/m$^2$; $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I} = 0.256$ Pa; $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0) = 79.0$ dB;

cards.title: Sound intensity: I = (1/2) rho v omega^2 s_0^2
items: $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(\rho v\omega)$ — the full round trip.

Power of a source: $P = \oint I\,dA$; isotropic: $P = 4\pi r^2 I$; line source (infinite line): $P/L = 2\pi r I$. The wave equation alone does not set $I$ — amplitude does; energy conservation sets the geometry scaling: $I \propto 1/r^2$ point, $\propto 1/r$ line (JEE-11). Loudness perception is roughly logarithmic in $I$ (Weber-Fechner) which is why decibels (JEE-12) are the scale of hearing.

cards.title: Sound intensity: I = (1/2) rho v omega^2 s_0^2
items: Amplitude conversions (exam currency): $s_0 = \dfrac{\Delta P_0}{\rho v \omega} = \dfrac{\Delta P_0}{2\pi f \rho v}$; $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I}$; $I = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2\rho v}$. In air $\rho v = 412$: $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{824\,I}$, $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(2\pi f \cdot 412)$.

the factor 2 in $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$ is the time-average of $\cos^2$ — peak squared over twice; if data give RMS quantities use $I = \Delta P_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/(\rho v)$ with no 2. State the convention every time.

cards.title: Sound intensity: I = (1/2) rho v omega^2 s_0^2
items: units: $\rho v\omega^2 s_0^2$ = kg m$^{-3}$ m s$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ m$^2$ = kg s$^{-3}$ = W m$^{-2}$ ok. Sanity: 1 mW/m$^2$ is loud speech at 1 m; 1 W/m$^2$ is on the edge of pain (120 dB).

A source of power $P$ spreads its energy on expanding wavefronts. Point source: $I(r) = P/(4\pi r^2)$ — doubling distance drops $I$ 4x, pressure $\Delta P_0 \propto 1/r$, displacement $s_0 \propto 1/r$ (same $1/r$: both amplitudes share the geometric dilution; $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$ keeps them proportional). Line source: $I(r) = (P/L)/(2\pi r)$ — halving rate. Near a large vibrating surface (plane wave):

title: Intensity of sound: I = frac12rho vomega2 s 02 = dfracDelta P 022rho v (cont.)
subtitle: I = ½$\rho$v$\omega$²s$_0$² = $\Delta$P$_0$²/2$\rho$v, energy budget, amplitude scaling table.
takeaway: I = dP0^2/(2 rho v) = 1/2 rho v omega^2 s0^2; two forms must always agree.

cards.title: Energy budget: where the power goes (cont.)
items: $I$ constant with distance until diffraction/fringing takes over.

Energy density vs intensity at 1 kHz, 1 Pa amplitude: $\bar u = 3.5\times 10^{-6}$ J/m$^3$, $I = 1.2$ mW/m$^2$; total energy in a 10 m room playing at that level: $3.5\times 10^{-5}$ J — less than the kinetic energy of a mosquito... yet hours of music are carried because the source continuously supplies power; the room just transmits.

Efficiency of real sources: loudspeakers 1–5% (most power heats the voice coil); the human voice ~0.01–0.1 W acoustic of ~50 W metabolic... spoken voice 1 m: ~10 $\mu$W; shouting: ~1 mW; jet engine 100 kW acoustic — most of 100 MW shaft power becomes heat.

cards.title: Energy budget: where the power goes (cont.)
items: source Q3 chain once more, symbolically: $I = P/4\pi r^2$; $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I} = \sqrt{\rho v P/(2\pi r^2)}$; $\beta = 10\log_{10}(P/(4\pi r^2 I_0))$; $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(\rho v \omega) = \sqrt{P/(2\pi r^2 \rho v)}/\omega$ — five answers from two data, one chain.
energy conservation + spherical spreading alone gives $\Delta P_0 \propto 1/r$ — no wave mechanics needed beyond $I = \Delta P_0^2/2\rho v$; a favourite derivation-shortcut for exams.

cards.title: Amplitude scaling reference card (memorise the column)
items: Given: $I$. Then $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I}$; $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(\rho v\omega)$; $\beta = 10\log(I/I_0)$. Given: $\Delta P_0$. Then $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$; $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(\rho v\omega)$. Given: $s_0$. Then $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$; $I = \frac{1}{2}\rho v\omega^2 s_0^2$. Given: $P$, $r$ (point). Then $I = P/(4\pi r^2)$ + above. Given: $P/L$, $r$ (line). Then $I = (P/L)/(2\pi r)$ + above.

Ratios: double $s_0$ at fixed $f$: $\Delta P_0$ doubles, $I$ quadruples, $\beta$ rises 6.02 dB. Double $f$ at fixed $s_0$: $\Delta P_0$ doubles, $I$ quadruples — "same displacement, twice as loud" is FALSE perception-wise... dB up 6, phon loudness curves (equal-loudness) complicate perception — physically 6 dB up. Double distance from a point source: $I/4$, $\Delta P_0/2$, $\beta$ drops 6.02 dB.

cards.title: Amplitude scaling reference card (memorise the column) (cont.)
items: near-field vs far-field: within about $\lambda$ of a real radiator the $1/r$ law misbehaves (evanescent/reactive fields); exam problems implicitly assume far field $r \gg \lambda$... and for sound $\lambda \sim 1$ m so room-scale problems are fine.

(a) $s_0 = 2\times 10^{-6}$ m at 340 Hz in air: $\Delta P_0 = 412\cdot 2136\cdot 2\times 10^{-6} = 1.76$ Pa; $I = 1.76^2/824 = 3.76$ mW/m$^2$; $\beta = 95.8$ dB; $P$ on 1 m$^2$ panel $= 3.76$ mW. (b) Threshold of pain $I = 1$ W/m$^2$: $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{824} = 28.7$ Pa;

$s_0 = 28.7/(412\cdot 6283) = 1.1\times 10^{-5}$ m at 1 kHz. (c) Two identical speakers in phase at one point: amplitudes add $\to$ $\Delta P_0$ doubles $\to$ $I$ quadruples (6 dB) at antinodes; out of phase: silence.

title: Intensity of sound: I = frac12rho vomega2 s 02 = dfracDelta P 022rho v (cont.)
subtitle: I = ½$\rho$v$\omega$²s$_0$² = $\Delta$P$_0$²/2$\rho$v, energy budget, amplitude scaling table.
takeaway: I = dP0^2/(2 rho v) = 1/2 rho v omega^2 s0^2; two forms must always agree.

cards.title: Worked intensity drills (cont.)
items: Inverse drill (source-style): "Find the distance at which a 50 W siren falls to 80 dB": $I = 10^{8}\cdot 10^{-12} = 10^{-4}$ W/m$^2$; $r = \sqrt{P/(4\pi I)} = \sqrt{50/(1.257\times 10^{-3})} = 199$ m. "Find $s_0$ there at 600 Hz": $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{824\cdot 10^{-4}} = 0.091$ Pa; $s_0 = 0.091/(412\cdot 3770) = 5.9\times 10^{-8}$ m.

every intensity answer should pass the loudness sniff test: whisper $10^{-10}$ W/m$^2$, conversation $10^{-6}$, shout $10^{-3}$, rock concert front row $10^{-1}$, pain 1. If your number is 10 W/m$^2$ for a tuning fork, an exponent slipped.

cards.title: Worked intensity drills (cont.)
items: intensity is the perceptually and physically central quantity: it is what the inverse square law, the decibel scale, and the Doppler energy shifts (Oly 05) all manipulate; pressure and displacement amplitudes are bookkeeping devices for the same $I$.
Isotropic point source of power $P$: energy crosses any sphere of radius $r$ at total rate $P$, so $I(r) = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}$.

Consequently $\Delta P_0(r) = \sqrt{2\rho v I} = \dfrac{A}{r}$ and $s_0(r) = \dfrac{\Delta P_0}{\rho v\omega} = \dfrac{B}{r}$ — both amplitudes fall as $1/r$; intensity as $1/r^2$. In dB: each distance doubling costs 6.02 dB.

cards.title: Point and line sources: 1/r2, 1/r, and the amplitude laws (cont.)
items: The wave solution matching this is the spherical wave $s = \dfrac{\mathcal{A}}{r}\sin(kr - \omega t)$: the $1/r$ in amplitude is forced by energy conservation (the wave equation in 3D admits it: $\nabla^2(1/r \cdot e^{ikr}) \approx -k^2/r\cdot e^{ikr}$ for $kr \gg 1$).

Infinite line source (line of speakers, traffic on a straight road): cylindrical spreading, area $2\pi r L$: $I(r) = \dfrac{P/L}{2\pi r}$ — intensity $\propto 1/r$, amplitudes $\propto 1/\sqrt r$. Distance doubling: 3.01 dB drop only. Semi-infinite/other geometries: plane wave (large wall): $I$ constant. Practical: near a motorway the noise falls off slowly (line); near a single machine quickly (point).

cards.title: Point and line sources: 1/r2, 1/r, and the amplitude laws (cont.)
items: Superposition of two point sources (JEE-13): interference pattern with $\Delta P_{\mathrm{tot}} = \Delta P_1 + \Delta P_2$ as waves; near-field geometry corrections $1/r_i$ matter only within a wavelength or so; exam interference uses equal-$r$ approximation unless stated.

the $1/r$ amplitude law is dimensional bookkeeping of energy: $I \propto (amplitude)^2 \propto 1/(area)$; area $= 4\pi r^2$ (point) or $2\pi r$ per length (line). The wave equation carries the phase; conservation carries the amplitude.

spherical wave consistency: $I = \frac{1}{2}\rho v\omega^2 s_0^2$ with $s_0 = \mathcal{A}/r$ gives $I \propto 1/r^2$ ok. Line: $s_0 \propto 1/\sqrt r$ gives $I \propto 1/r$ ok. Any other power law breaks energy conservation.

title: Point and line sources: 1/r2, 1/r, and the amplitude laws
subtitle: Point/line spreading, 1/r amplitude law, absorption and diffraction.
takeaway: Point sources fall as 1/r in amplitude, 1/r^2 in intensity; line sources as 1/sqrt(r).

cards.title: Decay laws in practice (attenuation on top of spreading)
items: Real air adds absorption: $I(r) = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}e^{-\alpha r}$, $\alpha$ growing roughly $f^2$ (classical: $\alpha \propto f^2$ from viscosity + thermal conduction; ~0.1 dB/m at 20 kHz, 0.001 dB/m at 1 kHz in dry air — humidity adds relaxation peaks). Consequences:

high frequencies die first — distant thunder is a rumble, distant speech muffled, ultrasonic imaging range limited to cm–m in tissue. Fog horns are low pitch (hundreds of Hz) to beat both absorption and diffraction over 10 km of sea.

cards.title: Decay laws in practice (attenuation on top of spreading) (cont.)
items: Diffraction: sound with $\lambda \sim 1$ m bends around corners and doorways freely (open door: you hear the whole room) — no sharp shadows for speech; ultrasound ($\lambda \sim 1$ mm) shadows like light. The doorway diffraction angle $\theta \sim \lambda/w$ for opening width $w$: 1 m sound through a 1 m door: strong spreading; 20 kHz ($\lambda = 17$ mm) through the same door: narrow beam.

combine laws carefully: "level falls by how much from 5 m to 50 m with $\alpha = 0.05$ dB/m?" — spreading: $20\log(10) = 20$ dB; absorption: $0.05\cdot 45 = 2.25$ dB; total 22.3 dB. Two effects add in dB.
inverse-square fitting of data: plot $10\log I$ vs $\log r$; slope $-20$ dB/decade = point source; $-10$ dB/decade = line source — a data-analysis question format used in Olympiad papers.

cards.title: Worked geometry problems
items: (a) Two point sources of the same power 4 m apart, incoherent: level at midpoint: each gives $I_1 = P/(4\pi 4)$; sum doubles: +3 dB over one. (b) A listener moving from 10 m to 3 m from a point source: $\Delta\beta = 20\log(10/3) = 10.5$ dB louder. (c) "Find $r$ where a 2 W source is at threshold of hearing": $I_0 = 10^{-12}$:

$r = \sqrt{2/(4\pi\cdot 10^{-12})} = 4\times 10^{5}$ m = 400 km — theoretical vacuum-free geometry with zero absorption; with $\alpha = 0.01$ dB/m absorption limit: $10\log(2/4\pi r^2/10^{-12}) - 0.01 r = 0$ cuts this to a few km in practice.

cards.title: Worked geometry problems (cont.)
items: Line-source drill: highway with equivalent $P/L = 0.05$ W/m: $I$ at 20 m: $0.05/(2\pi\cdot 20) = 4\times 10^{-4}$ W/m$^2$ = 86 dB — plausible traffic roar; at 200 m: 76 dB — only 10 dB down (vs 20 dB for a point source) ok line law.
matching the geometry to the decay law is half the marks in such problems: write the law first ($4\pi r^2$ vs $2\pi r L$), then the numbers.
cross-check with dB slopes: point source distance x10 = 20 dB; line source x10 = 10 dB; plane = 0 dB. Your computed dB difference must fit one of these unless absorption is in play.

title: Point and line sources: 1/r2, 1/r, and the amplitude laws (cont.)
subtitle: Point/line spreading, 1/r amplitude law, absorption and diffraction.
takeaway: Point sources fall as 1/r in amplitude, 1/r^2 in intensity; line sources as 1/sqrt(r).

cards.title: Spherical wave phasor picture (bridge to Oly)
items: A spherical wave $s = (\mathcal{A}/r)\sin(kr - \omega t)$ has local plane-wave character when $r \gg \lambda$: locally $\Delta P \approx \rho v u$ where $u = -\partial s/\partial t$... more precisely for $kr \gg 1$, $\Delta P \approx \rho v \,\partial s/\partial t\,/v = \rho v u$ — the travelling-wave impedance $Z = \rho v$ holds locally (Oly 01).
The exact spherical solution has a reactive (quadrature) component near the source, decaying as $(kr)^2$ — the near-field correction.

Beam patterns of real sources: a circular piston of radius $a$ beams when $\lambda < 2a$ (directivity $D = I(0)/I_{\mathrm{iso}}$; megaphone: $D \sim 10$, +10 dB forward). Loudspeaker arrays: interference of $N$ elements gives $I \propto N^2$ on axis (coherent) vs $N$ (incoherent) — exam contrast question.

cards.title: Spherical wave phasor picture (bridge to Oly) (cont.)
items: sound intensity level of a point source of known power at distance r: $\beta = 10\log_{10}\dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2 I_0}$; solve for any variable — the standard closed-form exam answer.

Sound intensity spans $10^{-12}$ to $1$ W/m$^2$ — twelve decades. The decibel compresses it: $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ with reference $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m$^2$ (roughly the 1 kHz hearing threshold; formally $2\times 10^{-5}$ Pa pressure threshold). Purely a scale: 0 dB $= I_0$; 10 dB $= 10 I_0$; 20 dB $= 100 I_0$; 120 dB $= 1$ W/m$^2$ (threshold of pain). Key derived relation:

cards.title: Decibel scale: beta = 10log 10(I/I 0), I 0 = 10-12 W/m2 (cont.)
items: $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I}$: at $I_0$ in air, $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\cdot 412\cdot 10^{-12}} = 2.87\times 10^{-5}$ Pa — the standard threshold pressure.

Addition rules (must-know): doubling $I$ = +3.01 dB; doubling $\Delta P_0$ (or $s_0$) = +6.02 dB; distance doubling from a point source = $-6.02$ dB; ten sources of equal incoherent level = +10 dB; two identical coherent speakers at an antinode = +6.02 dB (amplitudes add). Adding two different levels: $100$ dB + $90$ dB $= 100.4$ dB — the louder dominates (10 dB difference = 1.04x total).

cards.title: Decibel scale: beta = 10log 10(I/I 0), I 0 = 10-12 W/m2 (cont.)
items: Never add dB arithmetically: convert to intensity, add, convert back: $I_{\mathrm{tot}} = I_0\sum 10^{\beta_i/10}$.

Loudness perception: phon scale matches dB at 1 kHz only; at 100 Hz the ear is ~40 dB less sensitive (equal-loudness curves, Fletcher-Munson) — bass needs more power. Pain 120 dB; conversation 60 dB at 1 m; whisper 30 dB; rock concert 110–120. Damage threshold ~85 dB prolonged.

the ear responds roughly logarithmically (Weber-Fechner), and physics ranges over decades — decibels make multiplication of gains (each stage in dB adds) into addition: total gain of loudspeaker chain $= 10\log\prod G_i = \sum 10\log G_i$.

title: Decibel scale: beta = 10log 10(I/I 0), I 0 = 10-12 W/m2
subtitle: dB scale, 10 vs 20 log rules, addition of levels, perception notes.
takeaway: beta = 10 log(I/I0) with I0 = 1e-12 W/m2; doubling intensity is 3 dB, doubling amplitude 6 dB.

cards.title: Decibel scale: beta = 10log 10(I/I 0), I 0 = 10-12 W/m2 (cont.)
items: convert back and forth: $\beta = 80$ dB $\Rightarrow I = 10^{8}\cdot 10^{-12} = 10^{-4}$ W/m$^2$; $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I} = 0.091$ Pa. Sanity: engine room 80–100 dB corresponds to 0.1–1 Pa pressure swings — tiny vs 1 atm, but destructive to hearing.

Since $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2\rho v)$, and $\Delta P_0 = \rho v\omega s_0$: $\beta = 20\log_{10}\dfrac{\Delta P_0}{\Delta P_{\mathrm{ref}}} = 20\log_{10}\dfrac{s_0}{s_{\mathrm{ref}}}$ with same-medium references ($\Delta P_{\mathrm{ref}} = 2.87\times 10^{-5}$ Pa; $s_{\mathrm{ref}}$ = threshold displacement at the SAME frequency). The 20 = 2x10 because amplitude squared is intensity.

cards.title: Pressure and displacement forms of the level (cont.)
items: Same-number rule: level differences computed from pressure amplitudes use $20\log$; from intensities $10\log$; both give identical dB.

Frequency weighting in engineering: dBA filters (mimic ear), dBC (flat-ish); exam problems use plain dB. For two tones of equal level but different f, the perceived loudness differs — physics dB equal, phon not.

Worked: (a) pressure amplitude doubles: $20\log 2 = 6.02$ dB ok matches intensity route (I quadruples, $10\log 4 = 6.02$). (b) $s_0$ from 10 nm to 1 $\mu$m at 1 kHz: ratio 100: $+40$ dB. (c) A microphone sees $\Delta P_0 = 1$ Pa:

cards.title: Pressure and displacement forms of the level (cont.)
items: the two conventions (10 vs 20) are the same law wearing intensity or amplitude clothing; mixing them (writing $10\log(\Delta P_0/\Delta P_{\mathrm{ref}})$) halves every answer — the single most common dB error.
always cross-check one number both ways: pick $I$, find $\beta$; find $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2\rho v I}$; recompute $20\log(\Delta P_0/\Delta P_{\mathrm{ref}})$ — must agree exactly.

cards.title: dB algebra drills
items: (a) Speaker efficiency: electrical 20 W, acoustic 2%: $P_{\mathrm{ac}} = 0.4$ W; at 3 m: $I = 0.4/(4\pi\cdot 9) = 3.5\times 10^{-3}$; $\beta = 95.5$ dB. (b) Two machines 85 and 88 dB: $I_1 = 3.16\times 10^{-4}$, $I_2 = 6.3\times 10^{-4}$; sum $= 9.5\times 10^{-4}$: $\beta = 89.8$ dB. (c) "How many identical sources to raise the level by 10 dB?" 10 (incoherent).
(d) "Level falls how much from 2 m to 7 m?" $20\log(7/2) = 10.9$ dB.
Combining with attenuation: $\beta(r) = \beta_1 + 20\log(r_1/r) - 0.05(r - r_1)$ (dB, r in m, $\alpha = 0.05$ dB/m): monotone fall with both terms negative — model fitting format.

title: Decibel scale: beta = 10log 10(I/I 0), I 0 = 10-12 W/m2 (cont.)
subtitle: dB scale, 10 vs 20 log rules, addition of levels, perception notes.
takeaway: beta = 10 log(I/I0) with I0 = 1e-12 W/m2; doubling intensity is 3 dB, doubling amplitude 6 dB.

cards.title: dB algebra drills (cont.)
items: sound exposure level (SEL) and time-weighted average (85 dB / 8 h) are workplace regulations on the same algebra — doubling time halves allowed intensity: 88 dB / 4 h etc. — pure dB arithmetic.

The phon scale: loudness in phons equals dB SPL at 1 kHz; at 100 Hz a 40 dB tone sounds like a 10 dB 1 kHz tone — the ear curve dives at low and high frequencies. So "bass boost" on speakers raises low-frequency dB to match perceived loudness. The physical reason: middle-ear mechanics + cochlear resonance (ear canal closed pipe resonance ~3.4 kHz gives free gain there — JEE-01).

cards.title: Perception vs physics (why equal dB does not mean equal loudness).
items: Pain and damage: 130 dB ruptures eardrums; 150 dB+ sonic boom overpressure is a pressure transient, not a tone (JEE-28): typical boom 50–500 Pa $\Delta P$ transient = 128–138 dB if it were a tone — but it is a N-wave, broadband.

convert a boom overpressure to "equivalent dB" only as an order-of-magnitude: 100 Pa: $20\log(100/2.87\times 10^{-5}) = 131$ dB — consistent with boom descriptions; state it as an intensity-equivalent, not a tone level.

cards.title: Superposition and interference of sound waves
items: Linear wave equation $\Rightarrow$ superposition: if $s_1$ and $s_2$ are solutions, $s_1 + s_2$ is too. For two harmonic waves of the same $f$ at a point: $s = s_0\sin(\omega t - \phi_1) + s_0\sin(\omega t - \phi_2) = 2s_0\cos(\Delta\phi/2)\sin(\omega t - \bar\phi)$ with $\Delta\phi = \phi_2 - \phi_1$: the resultant is same frequency, amplitude $2s_0|\cos(\Delta\phi/2)|$, phase $\bar\phi$. Constructive: $\Delta\phi = 2n\pi$ (path difference $\delta = n\lambda$); destructive:
$\Delta\phi = (2n+1)\pi$ ($\delta = (n+\frac{1}{2})\lambda$). Max intensity $4I_0$, min 0, for equal sources.

cards.title: Superposition and interference of sound waves (cont.)
items: Path-difference working rule: $\delta = |r_2 - r_1|$ plus any extra inversion (phase changes on reflection — closed end of pipe adds $\pi$ to pressure wave... reflection at rigid wall inverts the PRESSURE wave, i.e. pressure phase jump $\pi$, displacement phase jump 0 — a classic trap). Then $\Delta\phi = 2\pi\delta/\lambda + \Delta\phi_{\mathrm{inv}}$.

Standing waves (JEE-16) are the structured superposition of counter-propagating waves: $s = 2s_0\sin kx\cos\omega t$; beats (JEE-15) are slow superposition of slightly different frequencies; interference of many sources gives diffraction patterns. Everything in this chapter family is the same addition formula.

title: Superposition and interference of sound waves
subtitle: Superposition principle, coherent/incoherent, addition formula toolkit.
takeaway: Superpose pressures, not intensities, for coherent sources; the amplitude sum decides everything.

cards.title: Superposition and interference of sound waves (cont.)
items: sound from two speakers adds as pressures at the eardrum: $\Delta P = \Delta P_1 + \Delta P_2$; intensities do NOT add where waves are coherent (fixed phase relation) — only the amplitude sum, then $I = (\Delta P_{\mathrm{tot}})^2/2\rho v$; for incoherent sources (random phases) intensities add.

equal speakers in phase at equal distance: $\Delta P_0$ doubles, $I$ quadruples = +6 dB; two equal-power INCOHERENT speakers at the same place: +3 dB only. Which one the problem means is often the whole question.

cards.title: Coherent vs incoherent, and the interference visibility
items: Coherent: sources with constant phase difference (same source split, two loudspeakers driven by one amplifier, forks struck in sync). Interference: static pattern of maxima/minima; visibility $\mathcal{V} = (I_{\max} - I_{\min})/(I_{\max} + I_{\min}) = 2s_{1}s_{2}/(s_1^2 + s_2^2)$ for amplitudes $s_1, s_2$ — full contrast when equal amplitudes. Incoherent: two independent forks: intensities add everywhere, no pattern — "two lamps" case.

Partial coherence (real rooms): phase drifts slowly; at points of near-equal path the listener hears slow "wandering" of level — room modes and flutter echo are semi-coherent phenomena. Exam idealisation: always coherent unless stated.

cards.title: Coherent vs incoherent, and the interference visibility (cont.)
items: Interference at fixed frequency, moving one source: pattern sweeps past the listener at rate $f\,d\delta/dt$... the intensity at a point modulates as the path difference changes — principle of the acoustic interferometer (Quincke tube is the 1D version, JEE-14).
coherence decides whether amplitudes or intensities add; every "two speakers" problem must first ask: same signal (amplitudes) or independent (intensities)?

extremes: $s_1 = 3s_2$ (in phase): $I = (4s_2)^2/(s_2^2$-scale$) = 16/10 = 1.6\times$ single-sum-of-intensities... precisely: $I_{\mathrm{coh}} = (3+1)^2 I_0 = 16I_0$ vs $I_{\mathrm{incoh}} = 9 + 1 = 10I_0$: +2 dB difference — quantifying "almost incoherent".

cards.title: The addition formula toolkit (memorise)
items: Two waves same frequency, phases $\phi_1, \phi_2$, amplitudes $a_1, a_2$: resultant amplitude $a = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + 2a_1a_2\cos\Delta\phi}$; phase $\tan\bar\phi = \dfrac{a_1\sin\phi_1 + a_2\sin\phi_2}{a_1\cos\phi_1 + a_2\cos\phi_2}$. Max $= a_1 + a_2$, min $= |a_1 - a_2|$. For $N$ equal in-phase sources:
$a = N a_0$ (on-axis), $I = N^2 I_0$; $N$ equal random: $a \approx \sqrt{N}a_0$, $I = N I_0$ (Oly 04 phasor treatment).

Different frequencies: $\sin\omega_1 t + \sin\omega_2 t = 2\sin\bar\omega t\cos(\Delta\omega t/2)$ — the beats structure (JEE-15) — amplitude envelope $2s_0|\cos(\Delta\omega t/2)|$ at beat frequency $|f_1 - f_2|$.

title: Superposition and interference of sound waves (cont.)
subtitle: Superposition principle, coherent/incoherent, addition formula toolkit.
takeaway: Superpose pressures, not intensities, for coherent sources; the amplitude sum decides everything.

cards.title: The addition formula toolkit (memorise) (cont.)
items: three-source interference: adding $N$ phasors geometrically (polygon) — partial cancellation when $\delta = \lambda/N$-type settings; the "N-slit" pattern logic carries directly from light to sound.

(a) Two speakers 1.5 m apart, in phase, $f = 340$ Hz ($\lambda = 1$ m) on the perpendicular bisector 2 m away: path difference 0  $\to$  max. Move listener 0.5 m toward one speaker: $\delta = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2} - \sqrt{2^2 + 1^2}$... set coordinates; first minimum when $\delta = 0.5$ m $= \lambda/2$: solve $\sqrt{x^2 + 2^2} - \sqrt{(1.5-x)^2 + 2^2} = 0.5$ numerically — exam answer form.

cards.title: Worked superposition examples (cont.)
items: (b) Pressure amplitudes 0.3 Pa and 0.3 Pa with $\Delta\phi = 60°$: $a = \sqrt{0.09+0.09+2\cdot 0.09\cdot 0.5} = 0.52$ Pa; $I/I_{\mathrm{one}} = (0.52/0.3)^2 = 3$... three times ONE source intensity; vs incoherent sum 2x.

(c) A wall reflects: incident + reflected standing wave; pressure node at distance $\lambda/4$ from wall (pressure antinode AT rigid wall): microphone sweeps detect maxima spaced $\lambda/2$ — measure $\lambda$ = the acoustic standing-wave interferometer.
the phasor diagram (Oly 04) turns all of this into vector addition: same formula, geometric intuition, and the fastest route to $N$-source results.

cards.title: Quincke's tube: interference with a controllable path difference
items: Construction (source fig. 17): a sound wave from S splits at junction A into two U-shaped arms of different length and recombines at junction B toward the detector (listener/microphone). Sliding one U-tube changes its length continuously. Path difference $\delta = 2\Delta L$ when the adjustable arm is lengthened by $\Delta L$ (the wave traverses the changed section twice — out and back). Source worked example:

frequencies 340–512 Hz ("standards 500 Hz ish"), $\lambda = v/f$; minima spacing when sliding by $\lambda/2$... precisely: intensity minima occur when $\delta = (2n+1)\lambda/2$, i.e. sliding the U-tube by $\Delta L = \lambda/2$ takes you from one minimum to the next.

cards.title: Quincke's tube: interference with a controllable path difference (co.
items: Formulas: distance between consecutive minima (as a function of U-tube displacement): $\Delta L_{\min-min} = \lambda/2$; the wavelength from the measurement: $\lambda = 2\times$ (displacement between minima); $v = f\lambda = 2f\,\Delta L_{\min-min}$. Source numbers: $f = 340$ Hz, minima every 0.50 m: $\lambda = 1.0$ m, $v = 340$ m/s ok. Quincke half-lens: open end reflection is weak (pressure node-ish), so contrast is modest but measurable.

Uses: (i) measure $\lambda$ and $v$ precisely (minima are sharp nulls); (ii) demonstration of superposition; (iii) subtracting path for acoustic interferometry (Oly 08); (iv) measuring speed in different gases by filling the tube.

title: Quincke's tube: interference with a controllable path difference
subtitle: Quincke tube, double-pass λ/2 rule, discrimination of interference methods.
takeaway: Quincke: the sliding U-tube changes the path by 2 dL; nulls every lambda/2 of slider travel.

cards.title: Quincke's tube: interference with a controllable path difference (co.
items: the double-pass factor 2 is the trap: the adjustable segment lies in one arm that the wave covers twice (the U goes out and back), so tube displacement $\Delta L$ changes $\delta$ by $2\Delta L$ — every Quincke formula carries that 2.
source consistency: minima spacing $\lambda/2 = 0.5$ m at 340 Hz $\Rightarrow \lambda = 1$ m ok $v = f\lambda = 340$ ok. If a formula gives spacing $\lambda$, the factor 2 is missing.

At recombination B, the two waves have amplitudes $a$ each (losses neglected) and phase difference $\Delta\phi = k\delta = 2\pi\delta/\lambda$ (plus a possible $\pi$ if one path inverts... in the gas-filled U-tube both paths are gas-gas, no inversion). Resultant amplitude $2a|\cos(\Delta\phi/2)|$, intensity $4I_0\cos^2(\Delta\phi/2)$. Minima at $\delta = (2n+1)\lambda/2$; maxima at $\delta = n\lambda$.

cards.title: The interference geometry in detail (cont.)
items: With the source covering $f = 340$–512 Hz range and tube path difference swept, the listener hears the level pulsing as the slider moves; counting nulls over a slider range $x$ gives $\delta_{\mathrm{span}} = 2x = N\lambda/2$... $N$ nulls in displacement $x$: $\lambda = 4x/N$... precisely: consecutive nulls at $\lambda/2$ displacement: $\lambda = 2\cdot(2x/N)$? Let: displacement between two nulls $= d$: $\lambda = 2d$ always — safest formula.

Amplitude at detector with unequal arms (loss $\alpha$ per pass): contrast ratio $C = (\sqrt{I_{\max}} - \sqrt{I_{\min}})/(\sqrt{I_{\max}} + \sqrt{I_{\min}})$ measures the amplitude imbalance — practical lab question.

cards.title: The interference geometry in detail (cont.)
items: set $f = 500$ Hz: $\lambda = 0.68$ m: nulls every 0.34 m of slider travel; if a lab report shows nulls every 0.68 m, the 2 was dropped.
Quincke tube in a different gas: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2 f \Delta L_{\min-min}$ — direct speed measurement without end corrections (the arms share the same open junctions).

(a) $f = 340$ Hz, $v = 343$: $\lambda = 1.009$ m; slider null spacing 0.504 m. (b) $f = 512$ Hz (fork): $\lambda = 0.670$ m; null spacing 0.335 m; source example in the notes quotes these standard forks (340 Hz and 512 Hz). (c) A student measures nulls at 0.31 m and 0.63 m (spacing 0.32 m): $\lambda = 0.64$ m, $v = 328$ m/s at 17 C... consistent with $v = 331 + 0.6\cdot 17 = 341$? mismatch 4%: check for the 2 factor:

cards.title: Quincke numbers and variations (cont.)
items: with $\lambda = 2\cdot 0.32 = 0.64$, $v = 340\cdot 0.64/0.67$... training example: state assumptions carefully in labs.

Error analysis: the open junctions radiate imperfectly (end effects), and the tube has attenuation — minima do not reach zero; the theory formula $\lambda = 2d$ survives, only contrast suffers. Humidity and temperature shift $v$ through $v(T)$.
Quincke works because the two paths recombine coherently — the source drives both arms with the SAME wavefront split at A; that is what makes the pattern static rather than beating.

title: Quincke's tube: interference with a controllable path difference (cont.)
subtitle: Quincke tube, double-pass λ/2 rule, discrimination of interference methods.
takeaway: Quincke: the sliding U-tube changes the path by 2 dL; nulls every lambda/2 of slider travel.

cards.title: Quincke vs beats vs standing wave (discrimination table)
items: Quincke: ONE frequency, TWO paths, controllable $\delta$, static nulls as slider moves — measures $\lambda$ via path difference. Beats: TWO frequencies, one path, intensity pulses in time at $|f_1 - f_2|$ — measures $\Delta f$. Standing wave: two counter-propagating SAME-frequency waves — fixed nulls at every $\lambda/2$ in space — measures $\lambda$ via spatial nulls. Resonance tube:
one path, source frequency tuned — nulls/maxima vs $f$ — measures $\lambda$ via resonance lengths (JEE-20).

Exam discrimination question: "A listener hears loudness varying slowly while holding position" $\to$ beats (two nearby frequencies) OR a slow slider movement in Quincke; "loudness varies as the listener walks" $\to$ standing wave or interference fringes; "loudness varies as a tube is slid" $\to$ Quincke.

cards.title: Quincke vs beats vs standing wave (discrimination table) (cont.)
items: unify: all four are interference; the measured quantity always converts via $\lambda = v/f$ and $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$ — the chapter is one chain of five formulas.

Two waves of equal amplitude, nearby frequencies: $s = s_0\sin\omega_1 t + s_0\sin\omega_2 t = 2s_0\cos\left(\dfrac{\omega_1 - \omega_2}{2}t\right)\sin\left(\dfrac{\omega_1 + \omega_2}{2}t\right)$. The audible pitch is the mean frequency $\bar f = (f_1 + f_2)/2$; the amplitude wobbles with envelope $2s_0|\cos(\pi(f_1 - f_2)t)|$ — one swell (loud-silent-loud) per period $1/|f_1 - f_2|$:
beat frequency $\mathbf{f_b = |f_1 - f_2|}$. Source examples: 256 & 258 Hz $\to$ 2 beats/s; 340 & 342.5 Hz $\to$ 2.5 beats/s.

cards.title: Beats: f beat = |f 1 - f 2| from slow superposition (cont.)
items: Numbers: beats per second = frequency difference in hertz. Equal amplitudes: perfect silence at the dips (intensity $\propto \cos^2$). Unequal amplitudes $a_1 > a_2$: minima drop to $(a_1 - a_2)^2$ — "beats with incomplete silences" tells you amplitudes are unequal. Each beat is one cycle of the DIFFERENCE frequency; the ear hears the sum-frequency tone pulsing.

Physics of two tuning forks: strike 256 and 257; the pressure waves add at the ear; the pulse train at  Hz = 1 Hz. The method is the standard of tuning: pianos tune unisons to zero beats; violinists tune strings by beats; orchestra A440 against a reference fork.

cards.title: Beats: f beat = |f 1 - f 2| from slow superposition (cont.)
items: the trig identity separates sum and difference frequencies: the ear (nonlinear detector roughly rectifying) hears the fast carrier with a slowly varying loudness — the difference frequency appears as an envelope, not as a tone (unless $f_b$ is in the audible range and the ear intermodulates).

if $f_1 - f_2 = 0.5$ Hz: beats every 2 s; the envelope is painfully slow — example: 340 vs 340.5 Hz. If a problem says "5 beats per second", $|f_1 - f_2| = 5$ Hz exactly — no factor 2 (the envelope $\cos^2$ has frequency $f_b$, not $2f_b$; the $\cos$ of $\Delta\omega t/2$ completes a magnitude cycle when $\Delta\omega t/2 = \pi$, i.e. $t = 2\pi/\Delta\omega = 1/f_b$ ok).

title: Beats: f beat = |f 1 - f 2| from slow superposition
subtitle: Beats f_b = |f$_1$−f$_2$|, wax test, envelope physics, drills.
takeaway: Beats measure frequency differences: the envelope repeats at |f1 - f2|; the wax test finds which fork.

cards.title: Beat applications and problem patterns
items: (a) Unknown frequency: a 340 Hz fork gives 4 beats/s with an unknown; loading the unknown with wax lowers its frequency and beats fall to 2/s: then unknown = 344 Hz (wax lowered it toward 340... careful logic: if loading DECREASES unknown from $f_u$: beats $|f_u - 340| = 4$; after loading $f_u$ drops: new beats 2: if $f_u = 344$, after loading 342: beats 2 ok; if $f_u = 336$, after loading 334:
beats 6 fails — the wax test discriminates: unknown 344 Hz.

cards.title: Beat applications and problem patterns (cont.)
items: (b) Three forks: 256, 257, 258: pairwise beats 1, 2, 1; together the 256/258 pair beats at 2 Hz with the 257 riding the envelope — complex beat patterns from three tones (olympiad flavour). (c) Siren receding (Doppler + beats): source 800 Hz moving gives observed 776; beats with a stationary 800: 24 Hz. (d) Doppler of BOTH source and observer toward each other: beats with a reference measures the shift — Doppler-free... reverse:
beats between direct and reflected wave from a moving wall measures the wall speed (Oly 08).
beat = difference, always positive: $|f_1 - f_2|$: no sign; the "which is higher" question needs a second test (wax, tightening) — the trap of beat problems.

cards.title: Beat applications and problem patterns (cont.)
items: beats measure frequency DIFFERENCES with arbitrarily fine resolution (1 beat in 10 s = 0.1 Hz), far better than the ear can judge absolute pitch — the reason beats are the tuning standard.

Two waves of slightly different frequency travelling together: the pattern of constructive and destructive interference MOVES at the group speed $v_g = \Delta\omega/\Delta k$; for sound with negligible dispersion $v_g = v$: the pulsing envelope travels at the ordinary speed — a boat bobbing in the beat envelope of two sea swells moves with the group... for sound: a microphone moving along the path hears the same beat rate plus Doppler terms.
Standing-wave beats: two forks at opposite ends of a tube: the pattern of nodes drifts; a slow "sloshing" of node positions at the beat frequency — visual beats.

cards.title: Beats with waves in space (extension) (cont.)
items: Laser Doppler / acoustic Doppler velocimetry: send $f_0$ to a moving particle; received $f'$; beat with a reference measures $f' - f_0 \propto v_{\mathrm{particle}}$ directly — the working principle of police radar AND ultrasound flowmeters (Oly 08 building block).

(a) 330 & 331.5: 1.5 beats/s. (b) $f_b = 3$ Hz between a fork and a siren moving at 3 m/s ($v = 343$): $f' = f(1 \pm 3/343)$: $\Delta f = f\cdot 3/343 = 3 \Rightarrow f = 343$ Hz. (c) A string tightened raises $f$ from 220 to 221; beat with 223 Hz fork: before 3, after 2 ok pattern. (d) Two pipes at 500 and 502 Hz, equal amplitude: envelope frequency 2 Hz;
intensity dips to ZERO at each dip; with amplitude ratio 2:1, dips to 1/9 of max.

title: Beats: f beat = |f 1 - f 2| from slow superposition (cont.)
subtitle: Beats f_b = |f$_1$−f$_2$|, wax test, envelope physics, drills.
takeaway: Beats measure frequency differences: the envelope repeats at |f1 - f2|; the wax test finds which fork.

cards.title: Beat drill set (cont.)
items: Intensity formula for beats: $I(t) = 4I_0\cos^2(\pi f_b t)$ (equal amplitudes): mean $2I_0$ = sum of intensities ok energy conservation on average; instantaneous swings 0 to $4I_0$.
the mean beat intensity equals the incoherent sum: time averaging the cross term kills it — consistency between coherent and incoherent pictures at long times.

Counter-propagating waves of equal amplitude: $s = s_0\sin(kx - \omega t) + s_0\sin(kx + \omega t) = 2s_0\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$: the pattern oscillates in place — nodes where $\sin kx = 0$ ($x = n\lambda/2$), antinodes at $x = (n + \frac{1}{2})\lambda/2$. Node spacing $\lambda/2$; node–antinode spacing $\lambda/4$. Amplitude map: $A(x) = 2s_0|\sin kx|$; intensity $\propto \sin^2 kx$ averages $2I_0$ of the standing...

cards.title: Standing waves: nodes, antinodes, and boundary conditions (cont.)
items: precisely: standing wave intensity oscillates spatially and averages locally over time to $2I_0\sin^2 kx$ (cross term time-averages to zero for the pair travelling oppositely... the net average energy flux is ZERO — energy sloshes, none propagates: hallmark of pure standing waves.

Pressure vs displacement standing wave: $\Delta P = -2Bk s_0\cos(kx)\cos(\omega t)$ — pressure nodes where displacement antinodes, and vice versa (SN-03). Rigid boundary (closed end of pipe, wall): displacement NODE / pressure ANTINODE — the boundary forces $s = 0$ (or fluid cannot flow through). Open end (free to atmosphere):

cards.title: Standing waves: nodes, antinodes, and boundary conditions (cont.)
items: displacement ANTINODE / pressure NODE — the open end enforces $\Delta P = 0$ (pressure must match ambient).

Resonance: only discrete $k$ fit the boundary conditions: pipe of length $L$ with given ends $\Rightarrow L = n\lambda_n/2$ or $(2n-1)\lambda/4$ patterns (JEE-17/18). A driver forces any pattern, but resonance builds amplitude 10–100x when the driving $f$ matches an allowed mode ($Q$ factors 10–50 for pipes — Oly 05).

the boundary conditions are physics, not maths: rigid end = zero displacement because the gas cannot penetrate the wall; open end = zero excess pressure because the end is exposed to the atmosphere (actually a weak antinode $\lambda/4$ beyond the mouth — end correction, JEE-19).

cards.title: Boundary phase rules (the trap bank)
items: draw one: for a closed pipe, displacement nodes at closed end, antinode at open end: pattern $s = s_0\sin(kx)\cos\omega t$ with $kL = (2n-1)\pi/2$: allowed $L = (2n-1)\lambda/4$ ok odd harmonics (JEE-17).

Rigid wall reflection of a displacement wave: the DISPLACEMENT wave inverts (phase jump $\pi$) so that node forms at wall... consistent statements: displacement reflects with $\pi$ phase flip (fixed end of a string analogy), PRESSURE wave reflects with NO flip at a rigid wall (pressure antinode at wall). Open end: pressure reflects with $\pi$ flip (pressure node), displacement no flip (antinode). Working shortcut:
always think displacement node = rigid, pressure node = open; derive the other from quadrature.

title: Standing waves: nodes, antinodes, and boundary conditions
subtitle: Standing waves, boundary conditions, node/pressure rules, SWR.
takeaway: Rigid end = displacement node; open end = pressure node; spacing of nodes is lambda/2.

cards.title: Boundary phase rules (the trap bank) (cont.)
items: Quarter-wave layer: a closed pipe of $L = \lambda/4$ resonates at $f = v/4L$; half-wave: $L = \lambda/2$ for open pipe; these are the two building blocks. Mixed: pipe closed at one end has odd quarter-waves ONLY: $L = (2n-1)\lambda/4$; open-open any integer half-waves: $L = n\lambda/2$... but open-open ALSO allows odd quarter-wave-like modes? No: open-open with BOTH ends antinodes requires $L = n\lambda/2$ (all harmonics).

Third boundary type (partially open, impedance mismatch, Oly 02): reflection coefficient $R = ((Z_2 - Z_1)/(Z_2 + Z_1))^2$ of intensity; the wall is "rigid" when $Z_2 \gg Z_1$ (acoustically hard), "open" when $Z_2 \ll Z_1$.

cards.title: Boundary phase rules (the trap bank) (cont.)
items: the phase rules fix the mode spectrum: count quarter wavelengths that fit between the end conditions — the entire pipes chapter is that count.

resonance between: a pipe closed at BOTH ends = same as open-open mode spacing ($n\lambda/2$)? No: closed-closed = displacement nodes both ends: $L = n\lambda/2$, all harmonics ok — the ends being the same type gives all harmonics; mixed ends give odd only.

Travelling: amplitude constant in space; energy flux $I = \bar u v$ nonzero; phase advances; $\Delta P$ quadrature with $s$ locally... precisely: $\Delta P = \rho v u$ (in phase relation with particle velocity $u$). Standing: amplitude $\propto |\sin kx|$; zero average flux; $\Delta P$ in QUADRATURE with $u$ (like reactive power); nodes every $\lambda/2$ fixed in space.

cards.title: Standing vs travelling: comparison table (cont.)
items: Partial standing waves (real rooms): superposition of forward and reflected with amplitude ratio $r < 1$: standing wave ratio $\mathrm{SWR} = (1+r)/(1-r)$; full standing $r = 1$; pure travelling $r = 0$. Measure $I_{\max}/I_{\min} = \mathrm{SWR}^2$ to get reflection coefficient — room acoustics and duct design (Oly 05).

the sound field between two hard walls in a room is a 3D standing-wave lattice (room modes $f = \frac{v}{2}\sqrt{(n_x/L_x)^2 + (n_y/L_y)^2 + (n_z/L_z)^2}$) — acoustic "eigenmodes"; audible as boomy bass at some spots (the 1D pipe theory generalises exactly).

cards.title: Micro-worked standing wave set
items: (a) $s = 4\times 10^{-6}\sin(5x)\cos(2000t)$: node spacing $\pi/5 = 0.63$ m; $\lambda = 1.26$ m; $v = 2000/5 = 400$ m/s (hot air or He mix... plausible warm gas). (b) A pipe open at both ends, $L = 0.5$ m, $v = 343$: fundamental 343 Hz, first overtone 686, second 1029 — all harmonics. (c) Closed at one end, same $L$: fundamental 171.5 Hz;
overtones 514.5, 857.5 — odd only; compare spacing 343 Hz (twice fundamental).

title: Standing waves: nodes, antinodes, and boundary conditions (cont.)
subtitle: Standing waves, boundary conditions, node/pressure rules, SWR.
takeaway: Rigid end = displacement node; open end = pressure node; spacing of nodes is lambda/2.

cards.title: Micro-worked standing wave set (cont.)
items: Node-antinode conversions: at a displacement node $\Delta P$ is maximum and temperature fluctuation is maximum too (compression heats! — the "thermoacoustic" hint); a hot-wire probe finds pressure antinodes; dust heaps in Kundt (JEE-21) sit at displacement NODES = pressure ANTINODES... hmm dust heaps actually collect at pressure nodes? Correction:

dust collects at DISPLACEMENT NODES (pressure antinodes) in a Kundt tube ok (nodes of the standing displacement wave where the gas barely moves... actually dust collects at displacement nodes because the gas velocity is zero there — gas velocity antinodes sweep dust to nodes).

cards.title: Micro-worked standing wave set (cont.)
items: dust collects at displacement nodes: acoustic streaming pushes loose powder toward the quiet spots of the gas motion; those are $\lambda/2$ apart — the measurement of $\lambda$ in Kundt tubes.

Closed pipe: one end rigid (displacement node), other open (displacement antinode). Allowed patterns: $L = (2n-1)\dfrac{\lambda_n}{4}$, $n = 1,2,3,...$ so $\lambda_n = \dfrac{4L}{2n-1}$ and $\mathbf{f_n = (2n-1)\dfrac{v}{4L}}$: fundamental $f_1 = v/4L$; overtones: first overtone $= 3v/4L = 3f_1$;
second overtone $= 5v/4L = 5f_1$. Only ODD harmonics of $f_1$: the spectrum is $f_1, 3f_1, 5f_1, ...$ — mellow, hollow timbre (clarinet family).

cards.title: Closed pipe (closed at one end): odd harmonics only (cont.)
items: Worked (source): $L = 0.34$ m, $v = 340$: $f_1 = 250$ Hz; first overtone 750 Hz; second 1250 Hz. Longitudinal displacement profiles: fundamental = quarter sine (node closed, antinode open); first overtone = three-quarter sine; second = five-quarter. Pressure profiles: antinode at closed end, node at open end.

Why odd only: an integer number of half-waves fits node-to-antinode only as odd quarters — even quarters would need node-to-node or antinode-to-antinode (a different end pair). Same physics: the mode condition is $kL = (2n-1)\pi/2$; adding another half wave flips both ends to the wrong type.

cards.title: Closed pipe (closed at one end): odd harmonics only (cont.)
items: odd-harmonic content is a fingerprint: if a spectrum shows $f, 3f, 5f$ with no $2f$, the resonator is closed-at-one-end; if all integers appear, open-open. Exam "identify the pipe from the spectrum" questions use exactly this.

adjacent resonances of a closed pipe (scanning f): $f_{n+1} - f_n = 2v/4L = v/2L$: constant spacing of TWICE the fundamental: source example 340 Hz spacing for $L = 0.5$ m: $v/2L = 343$ ok (this constant spacing is the backbone of the resonance tube method, JEE-20).

title: Closed pipe (closed at one end): odd harmonics only
subtitle: Closed pipe odd harmonics, overtone naming, spacing v/2L.
takeaway: Closed pipe: odd harmonics (2n-1)v/4L; overtone number is harmonic number minus one.

cards.title: Mode shapes and the overtone ladder (exam detail)
items: Naming discipline (trap bank source Trap 8): fundamental = 1st harmonic $= f_1 = v/4L$; FIRST overtone = 3rd harmonic $= 3v/4L$; SECOND overtone = 5th harmonic $= 5v/4L$. The paper Q16 mislabels 3v/4L as "second overtone" — correct labelling: first overtone. Source Trap 8 explicitly warns about this counting.

Displacement amplitude maximum at open end (antinode) — that is where the radiated sound escapes; the closed end has pressure maximum (the wall feels the pressure swing — microphone there reads max). Energy: antinode of velocity at open end = where radiation happens; node of velocity at closed end = no work done on wall (ideal).

cards.title: Mode shapes and the overtone ladder (exam detail) (cont.)
items: Forced oscillation slightly off resonance: amplitude falls, phase shifts — half-power width $\Delta f = f/Q$ (Oly 05); pipe Q ~ 10–30 unflanged, higher with flange — why "tuning across resonance" in JEE-20 labs shows sharp maxima.
numbers check: closed pipe L = 25.7 cm, v = 343: f1 = 333.7 Hz, f3 = 1001, f5 = 1668 — spacing 667.5 Hz = v/2L ok consistent; overtone naming: 1001 Hz is first overtone.

(a) "A closed pipe resonates at 170 Hz and 255 Hz consecutively with the tuning fork; find fundamental and length": spacing 85 Hz = v/4L... for closed pipe consecutive resonances ARE at f1, 3f1: spacing 2f1: f1 = 85... careful: resonances at odd multiples: if two consecutive resonances 170 & 255: these are 3f1=170, 5f1=255? spacing 85 = 2f1: f1 = 42.5: L = v/4f1 = 2.02 m; or the fork is near 170 = f1? The spacing method: f_{n+1} - f_n = v/2L always:

cards.title: Closed-pipe problem patterns (cont.)
items: (b) "Closed pipe cut to 1/3 length; how do modes change?" all frequencies triple (v fixed): spectrum 3f1, 9f1, 15f1... ratio pattern unchanged (still odd-only). (c) "Water-pipe (closed by water level, variable L)": f1 = v/4L as L varies — organ pedal tubes; raise water level (shorten L) raises pitch.

the constant spacing v/2L between consecutive odd harmonics (not 2f1... which is the same thing: 3f1 - f1 = 2f1 = v/2L ok) makes the closed pipe a frequency meter: measure two consecutive resonances, get v.

cards.title: Closed vs open pipe side-by-side (memorise)
items: Closed: $f_1 = v/4L$; harmonics $1, 3, 5, ...$; overtone gaps $v/2L$; timbre hollow; example: clarinet, pan flute (stopped), bottle (Helmholtz-ish). Open: $f_1 = v/2L$; harmonics $1, 2, 3, ...$; overtone gaps $v/2L$; timbre bright; example: flute, organ open pipes, most vocal tract approximations. Fundamental ratio for same L: closed = half of open... $v/4L$ vs $v/2L$: closed is an octave below.

Exam shortcut: any pipe question: (i) identify ends; (ii) write $L = ?\lambda/4$ condition; (iii) $v$ from temperature if not given; (iv) label harmonics carefully; (v) end correction if precision asked (JEE-19).

cross-check with overtone spacing: closed pipe: consecutive allowed modes differ by $2f_1$; open pipe: by $f_1$. If a spectrum has spacing 2f1 and starts at f1: it is closed; starts at f1 with spacing f1: open.

title: Open pipe (open at both ends): all harmonics
subtitle: Open pipe all harmonics, spectra identification, one-line mode solver.
takeaway: Open pipe: all harmonics n v/2L; consecutive resonances always differ by v/2L.

cards.title: Open pipe (open at both ends): all harmonics
items: Both ends open = displacement antinodes at both ends: allowed $L = n\dfrac{\lambda_n}{2}$, so $\lambda_n = 2L/n$ and $\mathbf{f_n = n\dfrac{v}{2L}}$: fundamental $f_1 = v/2L$; harmonics $f_n = n f_1$ ALL integers; overtones: first $= 2f_1$, second $= 3f_1$, ... — bright, full timbre (flute family). Worked (source): $L = 0.5$ m, $v = 343$: $f_1 = 343$ Hz; $f_2 = 686$;

cards.title: Open pipe (open at both ends): all harmonics (cont.)
items: Mode shapes: fundamental = half-sine of displacement (antinode at both ends, node at midpoint) and half-sine of pressure (pressure nodes at both open ends, antinode at midpoint). Second harmonic: full wave with two displacement nodes. Consecutive resonance spacing: $v/2L$ = one fundamental — identical spacing to a closed pipe's overtone gaps.

cards.title: Open pipe (open at both ends): all harmonics (cont.)
items: Traps: (i) "open pipe" in exam problems sometimes means a pipe closed at ONE end by context — read ends! (ii) end correction applies at BOTH ends (JEE-19): effective $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L + 2e$ vs closed $L + e$ — this shifts every frequency down ~1–3%. (iii) comparing with strings: string fixed-fixed: $f_n = n v/2L$ identical ladder to open pipe (different wave type but same mode count) — the mathematics is shared.
symmetric boundaries (same type both ends) give integer half-wave ladder; asymmetric (node one end, antinode other) gives odd-quarter ladder — one rule explains both pipes.
open pipe L = 0.5 m at 20 C: f1 = 343.2/1 = 343 Hz; the SAME tube closed at one end: f1 = 171.6 Hz — exactly an octave lower ok.

cards.title: Open-pipe spectra in data questions
items: Given a list of resonant frequencies 220, 440, 660, 880: all harmonics of 220 $\to$ open pipe (or string); 220, 660, 1100: odd only $\to$ closed. Given spacing 85 Hz between resonances: $L = v/(2\cdot 85) = 2.02$ m for either pipe type (spacing formula shared!). Given fundamental only: $L = v/2f_1$ (open) vs $v/4f_1$ (closed) — factor 2 ambiguity, resolve from the description or from a second data point.

Organ design: open pipes sound an octave higher than stopped pipes of equal length; mixtures of both give chorus effects; 16 ft open = 32 ft stopped pitch. The "rank" of a pipe organ is literally this ladder.

title: Open pipe (open at both ends): all harmonics (cont.)
subtitle: Open pipe all harmonics, spectra identification, one-line mode solver.
takeaway: Open pipe: all harmonics n v/2L; consecutive resonances always differ by v/2L.

cards.title: Open-pipe spectra in data questions (cont.)
items: Sound from the ends: both ends radiate; open-open radiates from two ends (interference possible at low f when $L < \lambda$ — the dipole "singing tube" effect, Oly 05); closed-open radiates mainly at the open end (monopole).

End correction shift: open pipe $f_1 = v/[2(L + 2e)]$; with $r = 2$ cm, $e = 1.2$ cm, $L = 85$ cm: $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = 0.874$ m gives $f_1 = 343/1.748 = 196.2$ Hz vs $201.8$ Hz uncorrected ($-2.75\%$).

cards.title: Open-pipe problem patterns
items: (a) Pipe in helium vs air (same T): frequencies scale with $v$: $f_{\mathrm{He}}/f_{\mathrm{air}} = v_{\mathrm{He}}/v_{\mathrm{air}} = 2.93$ — pitch jumps nearly two octaves... 1.56 octaves; classic demonstration (party voice). (b) Temperature: a pipe tuned to 300 Hz at 20 C: at 30 C: $f = 300\sqrt{303/293} = 305.1$ Hz — out of tune by 5 Hz. (c) Pipe length for a target: "design an open pipe for 440 Hz at 25 C":

Two-pipe comparison: open pipe A and closed pipe B sound the same fundamental: $v/2L_A = v/4L_B \Rightarrow L_B = 2L_A$; their first overtones: A: $2f$; B: $3f$ — differ; beats between overtones: $f$ — demonstration question.

cards.title: Open-pipe problem patterns (cont.)
items: frequency of any mode is $v$ over the mode wavelength; everything geometric lives in the wavelength count; temperature and gas choice live in $v$ — two independent knobs.

Given pipe type and length: (1) Write end conditions as node/antinode pattern. (2) Count quarter waves fitting: mixed ends: $L = (2n-1)\lambda/4$; same ends: $L = n\lambda/2$. (3) $f = v/\lambda$; add end correction $L \to L_{\mathrm{eff}}$ if needed. (4) Label: harmonic number $=$ multiple of $f_1$; overtone number $=$ harmonic number $- 1$ (the trap!). (5) If not given: $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$ at working temperature.
Generalise: 3D rooms: $f = \frac{v}{2}\sqrt{(n_x/L_x)^2 + ...}$; string: $f = n\sqrt{T/\mu}/2L$; rods: $f = n v_{\mathrm{rod}}/2L$ — same ladder mathematics with different $v$.

cards.title: The one-line mode solver (all pipes, all questions) (cont.)
items: the ladder of any resonator: compute $f_1$; check the spacing of higher modes is a simple multiple of $f_1$ (1, 2, 3 or 1, 3, 5); if not, end corrections or transverse modes entered.

The displacement antinode sits slightly OUTSIDE the physical mouth of the pipe: the oscillating air just beyond the opening participates in the inertia. The effective length is longer than the cut length: $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L + e$ with $e \approx 0.6r$ for an unflanged (sharp) opening, $e \approx 0.85r$ for a flanged (flared/baffled) opening; $r$ = pipe radius. Source worked (Q4):
Worked comparison (Q4, $L = 85$ cm, $r = 2$ cm, $e = 1.2$ cm): open pipe gives $196.2$ Hz ($v=343$); closed pipe at $v = 340$ m/s shifts from $100.0$ Hz to $340/[4(0.862)] = 98.6$ Hz ($-1.4\%$).

title: End correction: e approx 0.6r, L eff = L + e (closed) or L + 2e (open)
subtitle: End correction e ≈ 0.6r/0.85r, L_eff rules, resonance-tube link.
takeaway: End correction e = 0.6r (0.85r flanged): L_eff = L + e closed, L + 2e open; frequencies fall.

cards.title: End correction: L_eff = L + e (closed) or L + 2e (open)
items: Closed pipe: one open end $\Rightarrow L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L + e$; open pipe: two $\Rightarrow L + 2e$. All frequencies fall slightly: $f_{\mathrm{true}} = f_{\mathrm{geo}}\cdot L/L_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (approximately $f(1 - e/L)$ for small correction). Relative size: for $r = 2$ cm, $e = 1.2$ cm is 1.4% of 85 cm — measurable; for lab pipes $r \sim 1.5$ cm, $L \sim 0.3$ m: correction 3%.

Physics of $e = 0.6r$: the added end mass is the oscillating plug of air beyond the mouth, of length $\propto r$; exact coefficient depends on the mouth geometry (radiation end impedance, Oly 03): unflanged $e = 0.6133r$ (Rayleigh), flanged $e = 0.8216r$ (Levine-Schwinger); "0.6 and 0.85" are the exam standards.

cards.title: End correction: L_eff = L + e (closed) or L + 2e (open)
items: the antinode cannot sit exactly at the rim: pressure continuity with the open atmosphere extends the oscillatory region past the mouth — the wave "overshoots" by $e$; failing to include $e$ systematically overestimates frequencies.

source Q5 method (resonance tube): $e = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2$ and $v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$: with $l_1 = 16.5$ cm, $l_2 = 50.1$ cm, $f = 512$ Hz: $v = 344$ m/s, $e = 3$ mm ok; note $\lambda/4 - l_1 = e$ consistency: $\lambda = 2(l_2 - l_1) = 0.672$ m: $\lambda/4 = 16.8$ cm: $e = 16.8 - 16.5 = 3$ mm ok both routes agree — the safe identity: $l = \lambda/4 - e$ (Trap 15 prints $+$; the worked solutions use $-$ — see SOURCE-AUDIT).

cards.title: When does the correction matter (and when not)
items: Matter: precision labs, high-Q measurements, short pipes, comparison of nearly equal pipes (beat detection resolves 0.1%!). Not matter: order-of-magnitude pitches, long pipes ($e/L < 1$%), problems that say "neglect end correction". Exam rule: include if radius given or if options straddle 1–3%; mention explicitly.

Flange effect demonstration: same pipe with/without a baffle plate at the mouth: $e$ rises 0.6r $\to$ 0.85r: frequency drops ~2% for short pipes: measurable with beats. Real instruments use bells (much larger effective flange, tuned curves) — the bell couples impedance to the room (Oly 03).

cards.title: When does the correction matter (and when not) (cont.)
items: Helmholtz resonator note: a bottle with neck has its own end-corrected neck formula: $f = \frac{v}{2\pi}\sqrt{A/(V L_{\mathrm{eff}})}$ with $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L_{\mathrm{neck}} + 1.5r$ — different formula family (Oly 05), same $e$ physics.
dimensional and sign check: $e = 0.6r$ positive (lengthens); $f$ always drops when including $e$; if your $f$ rises, a sign flipped.

(a) "An open pipe of length 50 cm, radius 2 cm sounds at f; find f with e": $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = 50 + 2(1.2) = 52.4$ cm: $f = 343/1.048 = 327$ Hz vs 343 uncorrected: 4.7% low... check: L_eff = 0.524, f = v/2L_eff = 327 ok. (b) "A closed pipe 30 cm, r = 1.5 cm, at 30 C": $v = 348.2$, $e = 0.9$ cm: $f = 348.2/(4\times 0.309) = 282$ Hz. (c) "Find r from measured shift":

title: End correction: e approx 0.6r, L eff = L + e (closed) or L + 2e (open) (cont.)
subtitle: End correction e ≈ 0.6r/0.85r, L_eff rules, resonance-tube link.
takeaway: End correction e = 0.6r (0.85r flanged): L_eff = L + e closed, L + 2e open; frequencies fall.

cards.title: End-correction problem patterns (cont.)
items: Resonance tube method works BECAUSE of end correction cancellation: $v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$ does not need $e$ at all (the spacing of two consecutive resonances eliminates $e$); $e$ itself comes from the absolute positions $e = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2$ — the elegant double measurement of JEE-20.
the spacing trick: $l_2 = 3\lambda/4 - e$, $l_1 = \lambda/4 - e$: difference $\lambda/2$ independent of $e$; sum-based formula extracts $e$ — one experiment, two unknowns solved.

cards.title: Micro-drills on the correction
items: (a) Ratio $f_{\mathrm{corrected}}/f_{\mathrm{geo}} = L/(L + e)$ (closed) or $L/(L + 2e)$ (open). (b) $r = 3$ cm flanged: $e = 2.55$ cm; open pipe $L = 1$ m: $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1.051$ m: $f$ drops 4.8%. (c) Two pipes same $L$, $r_1 = 1$ cm, $r_2 = 3$ cm: open-open: $e$ ratio 3: frequency ratio $\frac{L + 2(0.6)}{L + 2(1.8)} = \frac{1.012}{1.036} = 0.977$ for L = 1 m: 2.3% apart: beat frequency at 300 Hz = 7 Hz.
Rule of thumb: correction significant when $r/L > 2$%; exam pipes $r \approx 1.5$–2 cm, $L \approx 30$–100 cm $\Rightarrow$ 2–6% shifts.

the exact radiation end-impedance $Z_{\mathrm{end}} = \rho v[\frac{1}{4}(ka)^2 + i\cdot 0.6ka]$ for unflanged pipe (low $ka$) — the imaginary part is the end correction, the real part is radiation resistance (Oly 03/05) — same physics seen through impedance.

cards.title: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l 2 - l 1) and e = (l 2 - 3l 1)/2
items: Apparatus: a tuning fork of frequency $f$ held over a vertical tube whose water level (closed end) is adjustable; the air column (closed-open) resonates when its effective length matches $(2n-1)\lambda/4$. Move the level down: first resonance at length $l_1$ (fundamental: $l_1 + e = \lambda/4$), second at $l_2$ (first overtone: $l_2 + e = 3\lambda/4$). Subtract: $l_2 - l_1 = \lambda/2$ — end correction cancels!

Hence $\mathbf{v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)}$ and $\mathbf{e = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2}$ (from adding: $l_1 + l_2 + 2e = \lambda$... precisely $l_1 + e = \lambda/4$, $l_2 + e = 3\lambda/4$: solve: $e = \lambda/4 - l_1 = (l_2 - l_1)/2 - l_1 = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2$ ok).

cards.title: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l 2 - l 1) and e = (l 2 - 3l 1)/2 (cont.)
items: Source worked (Q5): $f = 512$ Hz, $l_1 = 16.5$ cm, $l_2 = 50.1$ cm: $\lambda = 2(50.1 - 16.5) = 67.2$ cm; $v = 512\times 0.672 = 344.1$ m/s (≈ 344, consistent with warm lab ~25 C); $e = (50.1 - 49.5)/2 = 0.3$ cm = 3 mm; check $e = \lambda/4 - l_1 = 16.8 - 16.5 = 3$ mm ok. Then $r = e/0.6 = 5$ mm for the tube.

Procedure and errors: use a tall tube and a low fork if possible (large $l$ values reduce % error); resonance is sharp, so find the midpoint of the loudness peak; correct for temperature ($v(T)$); the tube must be vertical (water level defines the closed end); fork amplitude should be moderate (nonlinearity at high amplitude shifts peaks).

title: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l 2 - l 1) and e = (l 2 - 3l 1)/2
subtitle: Resonance tube v = 2f(l$_2$−l$_1$), e = (l$_2$−3l$_1$)/2, errors and drills.
source: Source: sound-waves/Sound-waves.md sec. 2.4 / Q5; independently checked
takeaway: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l2 - l1) cancels the end correction; e = (l2 - 3l1)/2 and l = lambda/4 - e.

cards.title: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l 2 - l 1) and e = (l 2 - 3l 1)/2 (cont.)
items: two resonances of the same closed pipe differ by exactly $\lambda/2$ of length regardless of $e$: the spacing method is self-correcting — the reason it is the standard student experiment for $v$.

identity route: $l = \lambda/4 - e$ (correct) vs the printed "$l = \lambda/4 + e$" in source Eq (2.15)/Trap 15: check consistency with Q5: $l_1 = 16.8 - 0.3 = 16.5$ ok with MINUS; with plus: 17.1 fails. Record in SOURCE-AUDIT; use $l = \lambda/4 - e$.

cards.title: Alternate forms and fork-adjacent variants
items: (a) Known $e$, one resonance: $v = 4f(l_1 + e)$. (b) Two forks $f_a, f_b$ at the same liquid level resonance (method of mixtures... different context) — skip. (c) Two consecutive resonances of an OPEN tube: same formulas $v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$, $e = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2$ BUT with $l_n = n\lambda/2 - e$... open tube: $l_1 + 2e = \lambda/2$, $l_2 + 2e = \lambda$: spacing $\lambda/2$ same;

$e = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2$ changes to $e = (l_2 - 3l_1)/2$? derive: $l_1 = \lambda/2 - 2e$, $l_2 = \lambda - 2e$: $l_2 - l_1 = \lambda/2$ ok same spacing formula; $l_2 - 3l_1 = \lambda - 2e - 3\lambda/2 + 6e = -\lambda/2 + 4e$: $e = (l_2 - 3l_1 + \lambda/2)/4$ — different! Exam convention: resonance tube = closed-open; use the closed formulas.

cards.title: Alternate forms and fork-adjacent variants (cont.)
items: Dust-tube variant (Kundt, JEE-21) measures $\lambda$ directly from dust heaps; resonance tube measures $\lambda$ from length sweep; both give $v = f\lambda$.

if $l_1 > \lambda/4$ computed from a guessed $v$, the first found "resonance" might actually be the overtone — consistency: $l_2 \approx 3l_1 + 2e$-ish: for $l_1 = 16.5$ cm: $l_2 \approx 49.5$ + 2e ok 50.1 measured.

cards.title: Worked exam problems (resonance tube family) (cont.)
items: (b) "A resonance tube shows first resonance at 20 cm for a 400 Hz fork; find v without second resonance": assume $e = 0$: $v = 4f l_1 = 320$ m/s; with $e = 1$ cm: $v = 4\cdot 400\cdot 0.21 = 336$ — the ambiguity of one measurement; state the assumption.
(c) "How long a tube for the 3rd resonance of 300 Hz at 20 C?" $\lambda = 1.144$ m: resonances at $\lambda/4 - e$, $3\lambda/4 - e$, $5\lambda/4 - e$: 3rd $= 5\times 0.286 - e = 1.43 - e$ m.
the method measures $v$ from LENGTHS, needing only a good ruler and a known fork — the classic 1%-accuracy student method (with a thermometer for $v(T)$ correction).

title: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l 2 - l 1) and e = (l 2 - 3l 1)/2 (cont.)
subtitle: Resonance tube v = 2f(l$_2$−l$_1$), e = (l$_2$−3l$_1$)/2, errors and drills.
