takeaway: Resonance tube: v = 2f(l2 - l1) cancels the end correction; e = (l2 - 3l1)/2 and l = lambda/4 - e.

cards.title: Error analysis and exam "find the mistake" questions
items: Systematic: (i) neglecting $e$ in one-resonance method: error $e/L_1$ up to 5%. (ii) temperature drift during the lab: $v$ moves 0.6 m/s/K. (iii) tube not exactly uniform: resonance peak broadens. (iv) fork frequency off by heating from hands: 0.1%. (v) loudness judgment bias: read the peak midpoint.

Mistake-finding format: "A student reports $v = 300$ m/s from $l_1 = 16.5$, $l_2 = 50.1$, $f = 512$." — check: $2f(l_2 - l_1) = 344$; 300 is wrong (maybe used $l_2 - l_1$ in cm as m: 33.6... or dropped the 2: $f(l_2 - l_1) = 172$... wrong arithmetic). Diagnosis drill: recompute the chain $\lambda = 2\Delta l$, $v = f\lambda$.

cards.title: Error analysis and exam "find the mistake" questions (cont.)
items: using a microphone + oscilloscope instead of the ear: resonance shown as amplitude vs length curve — peak positions give $l_1, l_2$ more precisely (lab modernisation of the same physics).

Apparatus: a long glass tube with a little cork dust (lycopodium) powder, gas-filled; a rod clamped at its middle, stroked lengthwise, drives the tube at the rod fundamental via a disc at one end. The acoustic standing wave in the gas is dusted into visible heaps:

powder collects at DISPLACEMENT NODES of the gas (where the gas barely moves — acoustic streaming sweeps it there), spaced $\lambda_{\mathrm{gas}}/2$ apart. Read $d = \lambda_{\mathrm{gas}}/2$ directly with a ruler.

cards.title: Kundt's tube: measure v gas from dust-heap spacing (cont.)
items: Clamped-centre Kundt rod: node at midpoint, antinodes at free ends $\Rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{rod}} = 2L_{\mathrm{rod}}$, $f = v_{\mathrm{rod}}/(2L_{\mathrm{rod}})$. Matching gas heap spacing $d = \lambda_{\mathrm{gas}}/2$ gives $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = v_{\mathrm{rod}}\,d/L_{\mathrm{rod}}$ (e.g. $5000 \times 0.08 / 1.0 = 400$ m/s).

with $d = \lambda/2$ and matching frequency: $f = v_{\mathrm{rod}}/(2L_{\mathrm{rod}}) = 5000/2 = 2500$ Hz; $\lambda_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2d = 0.16$ m; $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2500\times 0.16 = 400$ m/s ok (source chain: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = v_{\mathrm{rod}}\cdot d/L_{\mathrm{rod}}$ — consistent with $f = v_{\mathrm{rod}}/2L_{\mathrm{rod}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2d$).

cards.title: Kundt's tube: measure v gas from dust-heap spacing (cont.)
items: Full formula chain: $f = \dfrac{v_{\mathrm{rod}}}{2L_{\mathrm{rod}}} = \dfrac{v_{\mathrm{gas}}}{2d}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = v_{\mathrm{rod}}\dfrac{d}{L_{\mathrm{rod}}}$. Measure $d$ (heap spacing), know $L_{\mathrm{rod}}$ and $v_{\mathrm{rod}}$ (or measure $v_{\mathrm{rod}}$ separately): get $v_{\mathrm{gas}}$. The method is elegant because the same $f$ drives both media — no fork calibration needed.

dust heaps at nodes: the oscillating gas velocity is zero at displacement nodes; radiation pressure / streaming pushes loose powder toward velocity minima — visualising the invisible wave. The heap spacing is HALF a wavelength — the classic factor-2 trap.

subtitle: Kundt tube, dust heaps at nodes λ/2, v_gas = v_rod·d/L_rod.

takeaway: Kundt: dust heaps sit lambda/2 apart at displacement nodes; v_gas = v_rod d/L_rod.

cards.title: Kundt's tube: measure v gas from dust-heap spacing (cont.)
items: source numbers once more: $v_{\mathrm{rod}} = 5\times 10^{3}$ m/s (steel-ish, L = 1 m): $f = 2.5$ kHz; $d = 8$ cm: $\lambda = 16$ cm; $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2.5\times 10^{3}\times 0.16 = 400$ m/s ok (hot air: $v = 331\sqrt{T/273} = 400 \Rightarrow T = 398$ K = 125 C — plausibly warm gas in the tube).

Rod clamped at middle: boundary = node at middle, free ends = antinodes: fundamental: $\lambda_{\mathrm{rod}} = 2L_{\mathrm{rod}}$ (half-wave with antinode-antinode: the clamped middle is the node: pattern: antinode-node-antinode over the rod = one full... wait: free-free rod with central node: the half-rod (L/2) is node-to-antinode = quarter wave: $\lambda/4 = L/2$: $\lambda = 2L$ ok). So $f = v_{\mathrm{rod}}/\lambda = v_{\mathrm{rod}}/(2L_{\mathrm{rod}})$ ok. Rubbing lengthwise excites longitudinal modes.

cards.title: The rod modes in detail (factor-of-2 discipline) (cont.)
items: Alternative: rod clamped at END: $\lambda = 4L$: $f = v/4L$ — half as loud/low; exam variants specify the clamping. Any of these can drive the tube: just use the actual $f$ in $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = f\lambda_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2fd$.

Precision: heap spacing measurement error 2 mm on 80 mm: 2.5%; rod length error 0.5%; temperature: gas speed known $\pm 0.3$% — total few-% method. Edge effects: the disc end reflects imperfectly; heaps fade near the ends.

dimensional: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = v_{\mathrm{rod}} d/L_{\mathrm{rod}}$: m/s = m/s × m/m ok; extreme: $d = L_{\mathrm{rod}}$: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = v_{\mathrm{rod}}$: the heap spacing equals rod half-wavelength... $\lambda_{\mathrm{gas}} = 2d = 2L$: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = f\cdot 2L = v_{\mathrm{rod}}$ ok consistent.

cards.title: Kundt problems and modern readings
items: (a) Rod of aluminium $v = 5100$, $L = 0.5$ m clamped middle: $f = 5.1$ kHz; heaps 2.5 cm: $\lambda = 5$ cm: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = 5100\times 0.025/0.5 = 255$ m/s (cold heavy gas? $T$: 255 = $331\sqrt{T/273}$: $T = 164$ K — a cold CO2-ish experiment; or wrong clamp assumption!). (b) "Dust heaps 4 cm apart in hydrogen at 0 C ($v = 1260$): find f": $f = v/2d = 1575$ Hz.

Modern reading: the Kundt tube is the acoustical analogue of the Melde experiment; dust visualisation = node mapping; the same apparatus measures gas composition via $v_{\mathrm{gas}}$ (from $M_{\mathrm{eff}}$, JEE-09) and even $\gamma$ (with two gases).

cards.title: Kundt problems and modern readings (cont.)
items: acoustic streaming from the standing wave drives steady gas circulation in cells of size $\lambda/2$ — the powder ALSO traces the streaming cells; both effects give the same spacing.

Kundt: directly visualises $\lambda/2$ (dust heaps), needs rod + tube + powder, measures $v_{\mathrm{gas}}$ via rod frequency; resonance tube: finds resonance LENGTHS of a fixed fork, computes $\lambda = 2(l_2 - l_1)$; both give $v$; both have factor-2 traps (heap spacing $= \lambda/2$; length spacing $= \lambda/2$).

Quick exam signal words: "dust / powder / heaps" $\to$ Kundt; "water level / liquid / loudness maxima as length changes" $\to$ resonance tube; "two paths / sliding U-tube" $\to$ Quincke; "two forks / pulsing loudness" $\to$ beats; "moving source or observer" $\to$ Doppler.

cards.title: Kundt vs resonance tube (discrimination) (cont.)
items: after any $v$ computation, compare with $v(T)$ anchors: air 331–343; if Kundt gives 400, gas is warm (~125 C) or He-mixed; if 1300, it is H2; sanity first, algebra second.

Source moves toward a stationary observer at speed $u_s$ along the line joining them. Each successive crest is emitted closer to the observer: the wavelength ahead compresses to $\lambda' = \lambda - u_s T = (v - u_s)/f$; the observer measures $f' = v/\lambda' = f\dfrac{v}{v - u_s}$ (toward). Receding: $\lambda$ stretches:

cards.title: Doppler effect 1: moving source, stationary observer (cont.)
items: $\mathbf{f' = f\dfrac{v}{v \mp u_s}}$ with minus for approach, plus for recession. Source example: $f = 400$ Hz, $u_s = 35$ m/s, $v = 343$: approach $f' = 400\cdot 343/308 = 445$ Hz; recede: $400\cdot 343/378 = 363$ Hz.

Key physics: the SOURCE motion changes the WAVELENGTH (crowded wavefronts ahead); the observer is passive. If $u_s \to v$: $f' \to \infty$ (source keeping pace with its own crests — pile-up at the shock boundary, JEE-28 Mach cone). If $u_s > v$: the formula flips sign meaning (observer in the "silent" region behind the cone before the shock arrives; overtaken events arrive in reverse order — outside syllabus but the qualitative breakdown is fair).

cards.title: Doppler effect 1: moving source, stationary observer (cont.)
items: The ratio form: $f'/f = v/(v \mp u_s)$: pure geometry of wavefront spacing. For $u_s \ll v$: $f' \approx f(1 \pm u_s/v)$ — the fractional shift equals $u_s/v$ — this linear form drives most precision applications (radar guns, ultrasound flow, Oly 08).

wavelength compression is kinematics of emitted crests: in one period $T = 1/f$ the source moves $u_s T$ while the crest ahead moves $vT$; the gap between consecutive crests in the direction of motion is $(v - u_s)T$ — that IS the observed $\lambda$; $f' = v/\lambda'$ follows.
limits: $u_s = 0$: $f' = f$ ok; approach always $f' > f$; recede $f' < f$; speed of sound is that of the MEDIUM, not of the source — wind (JEE-25) modifies $v$ itself, separately.

cards.title: Sign discipline for moving source (the classic trap)
items: Source approaching: $f' = f\dfrac{v}{v - u_s}$ — denominator SHRINKS, frequency rises. Source receding: $f' = f\dfrac{v}{v + u_s}$ — denominator grows, frequency falls. Mnemonic: "approach = subtract in the denominator (for source speed);

add for observer speed when approaching" — but mixed cases slip; the robust method is always: (1) write $\lambda'$ for source motion or $v_{\mathrm{rel}}$ for observer motion; (2) $f' = v_{\mathrm{rel}}/\lambda'$; (3) specialise. Oly-06 gives the sign-free formula.

title: Doppler effect 1: moving source, stationary observer
subtitle: Doppler moving source, λ compression, asymmetry with observer motion.
takeaway: Moving source compresses wavelength: f = f0 v/(v - u_s) toward, v/(v + u_s) away.

cards.title: Sign discipline for moving source (the classic trap) (cont.)
items: Worked source-vs-observer asymmetry ($f = 1000$ Hz, speed $u = 30$ m/s, $v = 340$ m/s): (i) source approaching stationary observer: $f' = 1000\times 340/(340 - 30) = 1096.8$ Hz (receding: $918.9$ Hz).

"A train approaches a station at 30 m/s sounding 1000 Hz; v = 340" — (a) platform hears 1096.8 Hz; (b) passenger in train hears own horn: 1000 Hz (no relative motion); (c) reflected echo back to train: double Doppler 1193.5 Hz; approx 1176 with 2u/v. The 1088.2 = moving OBSERVER receding at 30: $1000\times 310/340 = 911.8$?? Compute: $1000\times(340-30)/340 = 911.8$.

cards.title: Sign discipline for moving source (the classic trap) (cont.)
items: (ii) Observer approaching stationary source at $30$ m/s: $f' = 1000\times(340 + 30)/340 = 1088.2$ Hz (receding: $911.8$ Hz). Moving source shifts $8.6$ Hz higher at $u/v = 0.088$ because $(1 - u/v)^{-1} > 1 + u/v$.

same 30 m/s gives different shifts depending on WHO moves — 1096.8 (source moves) vs 1088.2 (observer moves). Second-order difference: $f u_s^2/(v(v-u_s)) \approx 8.6$ Hz ok the source asymmetry term.

cards.title: Sign discipline for moving source (the classic trap) (cont.)
items: asymmetry magnitude: $\Delta = f u^2/(v(v-u)) = 1000\times 900/(340\times 310) = 8.5$ Hz ok matches 1096.8 − 1088.2 = 8.6 Hz — the pair of formulas differ at second order in $u/v$; first order identical.

source motion distorts the wave geometry (a nonlinear function $v/(v-u)$), observer motion only changes the crest-collection rate (linear $1 \pm u/v$) — that asymmetry is real and measurable (the "Doppler of sound vs light" exam discussion: light in vacuum is symmetric: $f' \approx f(1 \pm u/c)$ both ways at first order).

cards.title: Moving-source problem patterns
items: (a) Ambulance 800 Hz at 25 m/s ($v = 343$): approach 862.2 Hz; recede 748.9 Hz; the pitch DROP heard as it passes: $\Delta f = 113$ Hz — the glissando scale question. (b) Two trains approaching each other at 20 m/s each, horn 500 Hz: source motion 20 + observer 20: $f' = 500\times 363/323 = 562$ Hz (both effects stack). (c) Source circling (tangential):
at closest approach $u_s$ perpendicular: no first-order shift — the frequency slides from high to low through the pass: "siren of a passing car" waveform.
Blunt instrument vs formula: for $u/v = 0.1$: exact $1/0.9 = 1.111$; linear $1.1$: 1% error; exams: use exact unless told to approximate.

title: Doppler effect 1: moving source, stationary observer (cont.)
subtitle: Doppler moving source, λ compression, asymmetry with observer motion.
takeaway: Moving source compresses wavelength: f = f0 v/(v - u_s) toward, v/(v + u_s) away.

cards.title: Moving-source problem patterns (cont.)
items: the pitch glide of a passing siren has a characteristic "swoosh": $f'(t) = f v/(v - u_s\cos\theta(t))$... the full 2D form (JEE-26): $f' = f\dfrac{v}{v - u_s\cos\theta}$: smooth slide through $f$ at the perpendicular instant.

(a) $f = 320$ Hz, $u_s = 40$, $v = 340$: approach: $320\times 340/300 = 362.7$; recede: $320\times 340/380 = 286.3$. (b) "Source moving at $v/2$: factor 2 rise approaching": $f\cdot 340/170 = 2f$ ok dramatic demo.
(c) "How fast must a source move to shift 440 to 450 Hz?" $u_s = v(1 - f/f') = 340(1 - 440/450) = 7.6$ m/s approaching (solve $450 = 440\cdot 340/(340 - u)$).

cards.title: Numbers drill (moving source) (cont.)
items: Consistency: the shift observed in a round trip (source + reflector + observer) doubles the effect (JEE-27) — police radar uses exactly the double shift.
the exact formula is a pure kinematic ratio; every number above comes from $v/(v \mp u)$ — nothing else to memorise once the sign convention is fixed.

Source at rest emits $f$ with wavelength $\lambda = v/f$ (unchanged). Observer moving toward the source at $u_o$ meets crests faster: crest-collection rate $f' = \dfrac{v + u_o}{\lambda} = f\dfrac{v + u_o}{v}$ (toward); receding: $f' = f\dfrac{v - u_o}{v}$. Boxed family:

cards.title: Doppler effect 2: moving observer, stationary source (cont.)
items: $\mathbf{f' = f\dfrac{v \pm u_o}{v}}$ — plus for approach. Example: $f = 500$ Hz, observer 30 m/s toward, $v = 343$: $f' = 500\times 373/343 = 543.7$ Hz; away: 456.3 Hz.

Physical picture: the observer "scoops" wavefronts; the relative speed of crest encounter is $v \pm u_o$; wavelength in the medium untouched. Contrast with moving source (JEE-22): that changes $\lambda$; this changes encounter rate. At first order both give $\Delta f = f u/v$; at second order they differ (8.6 Hz at 1000 Hz, 30 m/s — the 1096.8 vs 1088.2 pair).

cards.title: Doppler effect 2: moving observer, stationary source (cont.)
items: Motion along an angle (2D, JEE-26): only the radial component counts: $f' = f\dfrac{v + u_o\cos\theta_o}{v}$; a passing car: observer walking across the street hears the shift only through the line-of-sight component.

the medium carries the wave pattern at $v$; the observer adds their own velocity to the encounter speed — Galilean composition for the observer side (wave speed in medium frame is fixed; observer velocity simply adds).

title: Doppler effect 2: moving observer, stationary source
subtitle: Doppler moving observer, combined formula, sign conventions.
takeaway: Moving observer sweeps crests faster: f = f0 (v + u_o)/v; source and observer formulas differ at second order.

cards.title: Doppler effect 2: moving observer, stationary source (cont.)
items: extremes: $u_o = v$ toward: $f' = 2f$ (double rate — observer surfing crest-to-crest... at $u_o = v$ the observer keeps pace with one crest... hmm encounter rate $2v/\lambda$: yes $2f$); $u_o = v$ away: $f' = 0$ (never meets a crest: staying exactly with the wave); $u_o > v$ away: formula gives negative $f'$ — meaning the observer passes crests in reverse order (sign of overtaking).

Both moving along the line joining source and observer (positive speeds toward each other): $\mathbf{f' = f\dfrac{v + u_o}{v - u_s}}$ — observer approach ADDS to $v$; source approach SUBTRACTS from $v$. Then: both approaching: $f' = f(v + u_o)/(v - u_s)$ (biggest shift); both receding: $f' = f(v - u_o)/(v + u_s)$; mixed:

cards.title: Combined formula and sign convention (working standard) (cont.)
items: substitute signs accordingly. This is the standard textbook convention (positive toward); the exam-safe procedure: sketch, mark who runs toward whom, write the box formula with your OWN sign bookkeeping, then evaluate.

Source-style worked (combined): source 1000 Hz at 30 m/s toward observer approaching at 20 m/s, $v = 340$: $f' = 1000\times 360/310 = 1161.3$ Hz — compare paper Q36 answer 1161 ok (double motion stacks, nonlinear in $u_s$).

Convention traps: (i) some texts write $f' = f(v \mp u_o)/(v \pm u_s)$ with opposite sign convention — ALWAYS re-derive quickly for the case at hand instead of recalling a sign pattern; (ii) motion at an angle: use radial components (JEE-26); (iii) wind: replace $v$ by $v + w$ in the right places (JEE-25).

cards.title: Combined formula and sign convention (working standard) (cont.)
items: the combined formula is just $f' = \dfrac{\text{encounter speed of crests}}{\text{spacing of crests}} = \dfrac{v + u_o}{(v - u_s)/f}$: numerator from observer kinematics, denominator from source kinematics — two independent effects multiply.

validate the box on special cases: $u_s = 0$ $\to$ observer formula ok; $u_o = 0$ $\to$ source formula ok; both zero $\to$ $f' = f$ ok; both approaching at $u$ small: $f' \approx f(1 + 2u/v)$? expand: $(1+u/v)(1+u/v) \approx 1 + 2u/v$ — double first-order shift ok.

cards.title: Observer-motion problem patterns
items: (a) Listener in a car approaching a 600 Hz source at 20 m/s ($v = 343$): $f' = 600\times 363/343 = 634.9$ Hz. (b) "A bat flying toward a wall at 5 m/s, emitting 40 kHz, $v = 340$": double Doppler (JEE-27): $f' = 40000\times 345/335 = 41.2$ kHz... the reflected echo: two shifts: wall as moving... actually bat = moving source AND moving observer:
$f'' = f\frac{v + u}{v - u} = 40000\times 345/335 = 41.2$ kHz received. (c) Observer in train hearing another train: relative speeds along the line.
Beat-vs-Doppler discrimination: Doppler changes pitch (heard tone shifts); beats change loudness of TWO tones. A shifted tone BEAT against a reference measures the shift (Oly 08).

title: Doppler effect 2: moving observer, stationary source (cont.)
subtitle: Doppler moving observer, combined formula, sign conventions.
takeaway: Moving observer sweeps crests faster: f = f0 (v + u_o)/v; source and observer formulas differ at second order.

cards.title: Observer-motion problem patterns (cont.)
items: symmetry check: source moving at $u$ toward stationary observer vs observer moving at $u$ toward stationary source: the two answers differ by the second-order term only ($\approx f u^2/v^2$ relative) — first-order symmetric, second-order not; light in vacuum is exactly symmetric (SR) — sound is NOT (medium picks a frame): favourite conceptual contrast question.

(a) $f = 340$ Hz, $u_o = 34$ m/s toward, $v = 340$: $f' = 374$ Hz ($\Delta = 34$ Hz $= f\cdot u/v$ ok linear). (b) Combined: $u_s = 25$ toward, $u_o = 15$ toward, $f = 400$, $v = 343$: $f' = 400\times 358/318 = 450.3$ Hz. (c) "Police radar 10 GHz, car 30 m/s": double Doppler $\Delta f = 2f u/c = 2000$ Hz... radar uses EM waves (speed c):

cards.title: Numbers drill (moving observer / combined) (cont.)
items: $\Delta f = 2\cdot 10^{10}\times 30/3\times 10^{8} = 2000$ Hz — the same formula with $v = c$ (radar: double shift always, source and observer co-located).
Reverse: "A stationary source 800 Hz; measured 824; observer speed?" $u_o = v(f'/f - 1) = 340\times 0.03 = 10.2$ m/s toward.

linear-shift shortcut $\Delta f = f u/v$ is exact for observer motion and first-order for source motion — precision problems must state which effect they use; the shortcut errs by $u^2/v^2$ for sources.

cards.title: Doppler master class: conventions, vectors, and the full 1D family
items: All 1D cases from one bookkeeping: measure speeds positive toward the other party. $f' = f\dfrac{v + u_o}{v - u_s}$. Then: (1) source toward, observer still: $f(v)/(v-u_s)$ ok JEE-22; (2) observer toward, source still: $f(v+u_o)/v$ ok JEE-23; (3) both toward: $f(v+u_o)/(v-u_s)$; (4) source toward, observer away:

$f(v-u_o)/(v-u_s)$ — INDETERMINATE sign of shift: depends on magnitudes (e.g. $u_o = u_s = u$: $f' = f(v-u)/(v-u) = f$ — "the patrol car following at equal speed hears exactly f" ok worked source example).

cards.title: Doppler master class: 1D sign conventions (cont.)
items: Equal-speed chase: source leading away at $u$ while observer chases behind at $u$: $f' = f\dfrac{v + u}{v + u} = f$ — zero Doppler shift because separation stays constant.

if source flees and observer chases: $f' = f\frac{v + u_o}{v + u_s} = f$ when $u_o = u_s = u$ ok (observer toward formula: +u_o; source fleeing: +u_s in denominator): $f(v+u)/(v+u) = f$ ok — no shift for lock-step motion.

title: Doppler master class: conventions, vectors, and the full 1D family
subtitle: Doppler conventions, equal-speed chase, reverse estimation, trap bank.
takeaway: One bookkeeping: f = f0 (v + u_o)/(v - u_s) with signs set by toward/away; lock-step motion gives no shift.

cards.title: Doppler master class: conventions, vectors, and the full 1D family (.
items: Sign-gymnastics summary table: toward: $+u_o$ top, $-u_s$ bottom; away: $-u_o$ top, $+u_s$ bottom. Radical simplification (source §2.12): define speeds ALGEBRAICALLY along the line from source to observer: $f' = f\dfrac{v - v_o}{v - v_s}$ with $v_o, v_s$ positive along the direction from source to observer: approaching pair: $v_o$ negative...
the clean version is the vector form (Oly 06): $f' = f\dfrac{c - \vec v_o\cdot\hat r}{c - \vec v_s\cdot\hat r}$.

cards.title: Doppler master class: conventions, vectors, and the full 1D family (.
items: one formula with signed velocities beats four memorised cases: define $\hat r$ from source toward observer; project both velocities on $\hat r$; the ratio $\dfrac{v - v_{o,r}}{v - v_{s,r}}$ handles every geometry including 2D and wind (with $v$ the medium-frame speed).

test the master formula on all four line cases with $u = 30$, $f = 1000$, $v = 340$: (1) 1096.8 (2) 1088.2 (3) $1000\times 370/310 = 1193.5$ (4) $1000\times 310/310 = 1000$ ok — the four-cell answer grid.

cards.title: Common problem shells (with their answers)
items: (a) Car horn while circling a roundabout: at the tangent point $u_{s,r} = 0$: instantaneous $f' = f$; before: high, after: low — the classic swoop. (b) Source and observer on perpendicular paths: only radial components count (JEE-26). (c) Train platform scenario: train passes platform at $u$ sounding $f$: platform hears $f v/(v - u)$ then $f v/(v + u)$; the CHANGE as the engine passes:
$\Delta f = f v\left(\frac{1}{v-u} - \frac{1}{v+u}\right) = f\frac{2uv}{v^2 - u^2}\approx 2fu/v$ for small $u$.

cards.title: Common problem shells (with their answers) (cont.)
items: Factorising problem statements: "A moves toward B at x, B moves toward A at y" $\to$ both toward: $f\frac{v+y}{v-x}$. "A moves away from B at x while B chases at y": $f\frac{v+y}{v+x}$... wait: A = source fleeing: $+x$ in denominator; B = observer chasing (toward source): $+y$ on top: $f(v+y)/(v+x)$ ok. When $y = x$: no shift ok.
the swoop-down (siren) is the integral of the instantaneous shift as the radial velocity component sweeps through zero: the slide is smooth and the midpoint (closest approach) is exactly $f$.

title: Doppler master class: conventions, vectors, and the full 1D family (cont.)
subtitle: Doppler conventions, equal-speed chase, reverse estimation, trap bank.
takeaway: One bookkeeping: f = f0 (v + u_o)/(v - u_s) with signs set by toward/away; lock-step motion gives no shift.

cards.title: Speed-estimation from shift (reverse problems)
items: Pass-by speed formula: if a horn drops from $f_+ = 460$ Hz (approach) to $f_- = 386$ Hz (recede) at $v = 343$ m/s, $u = v\dfrac{f_+ - f_-}{f_+ + f_-} = 343\times\dfrac{74}{846} = 30.0$ m/s and $f_{\mathrm{true}} = \dfrac{2 f_+ f_-}{f_+ + f_-} = 419.8$ Hz.

$f_+ f_- = f^2 v^2/(v^2 - u^2)$: $460\times 400 = 420^2\cdot\frac{343^2}{343^2 - u^2}$: solve $u = 343\sqrt{1 - 420^2/(460\cdot 400)} = 343\sqrt{1 - 0.957} = 71$?? inconsistent — as a training note: when data over-determine (two shifts + known f), CHECK self-consistency;

cards.title: Speed-estimation from shift (reverse problems) (cont.)
items: mismatch means the "true" f is wrong or wind is present.

Method: measure both shifts: $u = v\frac{f_+ - f_-}{f_+ + f_-}$ (exact for source motion? derive: $f_+ = fv/(v-u)$, $f_- = fv/(v+u)$: ratio: $f_+/f_- = (v+u)/(v-u)$: solve $u = v\frac{f_+ - f_-}{f_+ + f_-}$ ok exact) — the "measure speed from two pitch readings" formula; no need to know $f$!
with $f_+ = 460$, $f_- = 400$: $u = 343\times 60/860 = 23.9$ m/s; then $f = f_+(v-u)/v = 460\times 319/343 = 427.7$ Hz — the internal-$f$ estimate; consistency restored.

cards.title: Conceptual traps (Doppler family)
items: (i) "Doppler works because the source speed changes the wave speed" — FALSE: wave speed is set by the medium; source motion changes wavelength. (ii) "Observer moving toward at $u$ hears $f(v)/(v-u)$" — FALSE: that is the SOURCE formula; observer: $f(v+u)/v$. (iii) "Wind changes the pitch" — only if it has a component along the line and differs for the two directions (JEE-25);

a following wind on both legs cancels in a round trip; stationary source and observer with wind $w$: $f' = f\frac{v+w}{v+w} = f$ — NO shift for uniform wind (source §2.10) — wind shifts only the travel TIME, not the frequency, when both parties are at rest in the medium... correct statement:

cards.title: Conceptual traps (Doppler family) (cont.)
items: uniform wind cannot Doppler-shift sound between two fixed points (it advects the whole pattern).

Speeds are measured RELATIVE TO THE MEDIUM (air), not the ground, in the classical formulas — subtle: "source moves at 30 m/s in a 10 m/s tailwind": $u_s$ in the formula is the speed relative to AIR (20 m/s if tailwind... if the wind moves the air frame: source speed in the air frame = 30 − 10 = 20). Exam convention usually ignores wind for $u$ and sets $v_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (JEE-25); be explicit.
classical Doppler needs the medium: $v$ is the medium-frame wave speed; wind shifts the whole pattern by Galilean transformation; the invariant is $f'$ for co-moving pairs.

title: Wind and Doppler: replace v by v + w directionally
subtitle: Wind: v_eff = v+w convention, no shift for fixed parties, round-trip cancellation.
takeaway: Uniform wind never shifts frequency between fixed parties; it changes travel times only.

cards.title: Wind and Doppler: replace v by v + w directionally
items: Uniform wind of ground speed $+w$ blowing from source S toward observer O advects the medium: sound travels at ground speed $v + w$ downwind (S $\to$ O) and $v - w$ upwind (O $\to$ S).
With ground speeds $u_s$ (S moving toward O) and $u_o$ (O moving toward S), the exact ground-frame Doppler law is $f' = f\dfrac{(v + w) + u_o}{(v + w) - u_s}$.

cards.title: Galilean air-frame equivalence proof
items: In the moving air rest frame, S moves toward O at $u_{s,\mathrm{air}} = u_s - w$, while O moves INTO the oncoming wind (toward S) at $u_{o,\mathrm{air}} = u_o + w$.

Substituting $(u_{s,\mathrm{air}}, u_{o,\mathrm{air}})$ into the still-air formula gives $f' = f\dfrac{v + (u_o + w)}{v - (u_s - w)} = f\dfrac{(v + w) + u_o}{(v + w) - u_s}$: both frames agree identically.

cards.title: Why steady wind never shifts fixed parties
items: When both S and O are fixed on the ground ($u_s = u_o = 0$), S emits crests every $T = 1/f$ while each crest drifts at $v + w$, stretching wavelength to $\lambda = (v + w)/f$.
Crests arrive at O with speed $v + w$ and spacing $\lambda$, so $f' = \dfrac{v + w}{(v + w)/f} = f$: uniform wind changes travel time only, never pitch.

cards.title: Sign trap & upwind rule
items: Classic sign error: writing $u_{o,\mathrm{air}} = u_o - w$ forgets that a stationary observer faces a headwind of $+w$ toward the upstream source.
If wind $w$ blows FROM observer O TOWARD source S (against sound propagation), reverse $w \to -w$: $f' = f\dfrac{(v - w) + u_o}{(v - w) - u_s}$.

title: Wind and Doppler: replace v by v + w directionally (cont.)
subtitle: Wind: v_eff = v+w convention, no shift for fixed parties, round-trip cancellation.
takeaway: Uniform wind never shifts frequency between fixed parties; it changes travel times only.

cards.title: Wind and Doppler: replace v by v + w directionally (cont.)
items: $f' = f\frac{v + w}{v + w \mp u_s}$ style with w adding to v on both — that yields no shift for $u_s = u_o = 0$ ok. Adopt the source convention: $f' = f\dfrac{(v+w) + u_o}{(v+w) - u_s}$ with u positive toward — consistent with their worked wind example (see next card).

Source worked wind case: "source moving toward observer at $u_s$ with wind from behind source (w helping both)": $f' = f\frac{v + w}{v + w - u_s}$... e.g. $f = 500$, $u_s = 30$, $w = 20$, $v = 343$: $f' = 500\times 363/333 = 545.0$ Hz (vs $500\times 343/313 = 547.9$ Hz with no wind): wind REDUCES the shift here (the source chases a drifting pattern less effectively).

cards.title: Wind and Doppler: replace v by v + w directionally (cont.)
items: Round-trip (echo) with wind (JEE-27): out-and-back times differ; echo frequency shifts asymmetrically; classic formulas involve $v + w$ outbound and $v - w$ inbound (for motion along wind).

wind adds a Galilean drift to the pattern: the exam-safe prescription is "add w to the wave speed toward each observer, and measure all speeds relative to the ground, consistently" — mixing frames is the standard trap; the source convention does exactly this.

limits of the adopted formula: $w = 0$ recovers JEE-22/23 ok; $u_s = u_o = 0$ gives $f' = f$ ok (source convention); strong following wind with receding source: $f' = f\frac{v+w}{v+w+u_s}$: shift shrinks ok plausible.

cards.title: Travel time with wind (the more common exam use)
items: Wind affects TIME OF FLIGHT always (even when frequency unchanged): one-way trip along wind: $t = L/(v + w)$; against: $L/(v - w)$. Round trip along wind direction (sound out and back... e.g. source at A, reflector at B downwind): $t = \frac{L}{v+w} + \frac{L}{v-w} = \frac{2Lv}{v^2 - w^2}$ ≈ $\frac{L}{v}(1 + w^2/v^2)$ for the round trip... expand:

$2L v/(v^2 - w^2) = (2L/v)(1/(1 - w^2/v^2))$ — the WIND CANCELLS at first order in a round trip along the wind line ok famous result: measuring sound speed by echo along wind is insensitive to small wind at first order.

cards.title: Travel time with wind (the more common exam use) (cont.)
items: Cross-wind: effective speed $\sqrt{v^2 - w^2}$ for the transverse legs; general: add vectorially: ground-frame sound velocity $\vec v_s = \vec v + \vec w$; travel time along any path solves the vector problem (triangles of velocity — exam hard questions).

Echo in wind (Q12): out leg runs downwind at $v+w$, return leg upwind at $v-w$. For fixed source & fixed wall, $f'' = f$ (zero shift on both legs); for a wall approaching at $u_w$, $f'' = f\dfrac{v+w+u_w}{v+w}\cdot\dfrac{v-w}{v-w-u_w}$.

title: Wind and Doppler: replace v by v + w directionally (cont.)
subtitle: Wind: v_eff = v+w convention, no shift for fixed parties, round-trip cancellation.
takeaway: Uniform wind never shifts frequency between fixed parties; it changes travel times only.

cards.title: Travel time with wind (the more common exam use) (cont.)
items: round-trip time expansion: $t = \frac{2Lv}{v^2 - w^2}$: at $w = 0.1v$: $t = \frac{2L}{v}\cdot 1.01$: 1% second-order effect ok: first-order cancellation — worth memorising for rapid problems.

(a) "Sound from a lightning 3 km downwind takes how long with w = 10 m/s?" $t = 3000/(343+10) = 8.50$ s vs 8.75 s still air: 0.25 s — timing precision question. (b) "A train horn in a 20 m/s wind, train 30 m/s toward stationary observer": source speed relative to air = 10 m/s (wind helps source): $f' = f\frac{v+w}{v+w-30}$?? Under the source convention $f' = f\frac{343+20}{343+20-30} = f\times 1.09$;

cards.title: Wind problem patterns (cont.)
items: under air-frame convention: $u_s' = 10$: $f' = f\frac{343 + 0 - 20\cdot 0}{343 - 10}$-ish — the two conventions give ~5% different answers at these speeds — exam papers adopt one; state yours. (Source convention is consistent and standard in Indian exam texts: "speed of sound relative to ground is v + w; use v_eff everywhere.")
Uniform wind between fixed parties: NO frequency shift (source §2.10) but travel time changes — the dichotomy that examiners love to test.
frequency shift needs relative radial motion of the wave pattern phase; uniform wind translates the pattern without compressing it; only the travel duration registers the drift.

cards.title: Wind formula quick card
items: Adopted convention (source): $f' = f\dfrac{v_{\mathrm{eff}} + u_o}{v_{\mathrm{eff}} - u_s}$ with $v_{\mathrm{eff}} = v + w$ (w positive when wind blows from source toward observer), all $u$ positive toward each other. Travel time legs: use $v_{\mathrm{eff}}$ along each direction of travel (against wind: $v - w$). Echo round trip along wind: $t = 2Lv/(v^2 - w^2)$.

Air-frame alternative (Oly 06 vector form): measure $u_s, u_o$ relative to the air; $f' = f\frac{v + u_{o,\mathrm{air}}}{v - u_{s,\mathrm{air}}}$; both conventions agree on fixed parties (no shift) and on pure wave-speed problems; they differ on "who moves with the wind" cases — for exams, pick one and say so.

cards.title: Wind formula quick card (cont.)
items: consistency triple: (1) $u = 0$: no shift; (2) round-trip first-order wind cancellation; (3) $w = -u$ (source outrunning following wind at its own speed): effective still air: shift as in still air with $u_s = u - w$-ish ok.

Source moves on a straight line past a stationary observer at closest distance $b$ (impact parameter), speed $u_s$, emitting $f$. Line-of-sight direction $\hat r$ from source to observer; radial component of source speed: $v_{s,r} = u_s\cos\theta$ where $\theta$ is angle between source velocity and line of sight. Observed (source §2.12 2D form):

title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide
subtitle: 2D Doppler projections, closest-approach glide, slope magnitude f u_s^2/(v b).
takeaway: 2D Doppler uses radial projections; the glide slope at closest approach is f u^2/(v b).

cards.title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide (con.
items: $\mathbf{f' = f\dfrac{v}{v - u_s\cos\theta(t)}}$ with $\cos\theta(t) = \dfrac{u_s t}{\sqrt{b^2 + u_s^2 t^2}}$ for a flyby (source at $(u_s t, b)$-style geometry, $t = 0$ at closest approach).

The pitch glide: far before: $\cos\theta \to 1$... wait geometry: as the source approaches along its line, the angle between its velocity and the line TO the observer: initially 0 (head-on): $f' = fv/(v - u_s)$ maximum; at closest approach $\theta = 90°$: $\cos\theta = 0$: $f' = f$ exact; after: $\cos\theta < 0$: $f' = fv/(v + u_s|\cos\theta|)$ minimum far away $fv/(v+u_s)$.

cards.title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide (con.
items: The swoop is symmetric in geometry but NOT in frequency (the $v/(v-u)$ vs $v/(v+u)$ asymmetry — glide through f at the midpoint).

Source worked (glide slope): $df'/dt$ at closest approach: differentiate: at $t = 0$: $\cos\theta \approx u_s t/b$: $f' \approx f(1 + u_s^2 t/(vb))$: $\left.\dfrac{df'}{dt}\right|_{0} = \dfrac{f u_s^2}{v b}$ magnitude — source prints $\frac{f v_s^2}{vb}$... with numbers f = 1000, $u_s = 20$, $v = 340$, $b = 100$ m:
$1000\cdot 400/(340\cdot 100) = 11.8$ Hz/s. Source prints exactly the derivative $df^{\prime}/dt|_0 = -f v_s^2/(v b)$ — correct in sign and magnitude;

cards.title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide (con.
items: the surrounding text of Eq (4.2) is sign-confused (its cos-theta-about-1-while-approaching remark contradicts its own $\cos	heta = v_s^2 t/\sqrt{b^2+v_s^2t^2}$, negative on the approaching side) — record in SOURCE-AUDIT; the derivative itself needs no fix. Our worked numbers: magnitude 11.8 Hz/s at $f = 1000$, $u_s = 20$ m/s, $b = 100$ m.

the glide slope is pure geometry: only the line-of-sight component of velocity compresses wavefronts; at closest approach the radial velocity is zero and its rate of change is maximal ($u_s^2/b$) — that is the slope.

cards.title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide (con.
items: limits: $b \to 0$ (head-on pass-through... direct hit): $df'/dt \to \infty$ (pitch flips discontinuously — the 1D jump); $b \to \infty$: slope $\to 0$ (barely any glide — distant flyby barely shifts).

Setup: a light plane flies past at $u_s = 20$ m/s emitting 1000 Hz; closest approach $b = 100$ m; $v = 340$ m/s. Glide-slope magnitude at the pass: $|df^{\prime}/dt|_0 = f u_s^2/(v b) = 1000\cdot 400/(340\cdot 100) = 11.8$ Hz/s. Source prints exactly this formula $df^{\prime}/dt|_0 = -f v_s^2/(v b)$ with the correct negative sign;

its surrounding remark about $\cos\theta \approx 1$ while approaching is sign-confused against its own $\cos\theta = v_s^2 t/\sqrt{b^2+v_s^2t^2}$ (record in SOURCE-AUDIT) — the derivative itself is right.

title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide (cont.)
subtitle: 2D Doppler projections, closest-approach glide, slope magnitude f u_s^2/(v b).
takeaway: 2D Doppler uses radial projections; the glide slope at closest approach is f u^2/(v b).

cards.title: Closest-approach numbers (the glide example, worked) (cont.)
items: Instantaneous picture over the pass: at $t = -5$ s: $\cos\theta = -100/\sqrt{100^2 + 100^2} = -0.707$... using $\cos\theta = u_s t/\sqrt{b^2 + u_s^2 t^2} = -0.707$: $f^{\prime} = 1000\cdot 340/(340 + 14.1) = 960.1$ Hz (approaching side is the HIGH side with the standard sign: flip the sign convention so before = high:
$f^{\prime} = 1043.2$ Hz at $t = -5$ s, 960.1 Hz at $t = +5$ s): the glide spans about 83 Hz within $\pm 5$ s; average slope $\sim 8$ Hz/s vs peak 11.8 Hz/s.

cards.title: Closest-approach numbers (the glide example, worked) (cont.)
items: Ranging by slope: knowing $f$ and $u_s$, measuring the pitch slope at the pass gives $b = f u_s^2/(v |slope|)$ — acoustic impact-parameter estimation (the Oly-08 McAfee-style method in elementary form). Detecting slope requires resolving ~10 Hz/s over a second: a stopwatch-and-ear estimate or a spectrogram.

at the pass the radial velocity is zero but its rate of change is maximal: $du_r/dt = u_s^2/b$; the shift $\Delta f = f u_r/v$ then slides at $f u_s^2/(vb)$ — the slope measures how fast the geometry turns over, not the speed itself.

cards.title: Closest-approach numbers (the glide example, worked) (cont.)
items: limits: $b \to 0$ gives an unbounded slope (the 1D pitch jump); $b \to \infty$ gives zero slope (a distant flyby barely glides); the slope scales as $f$: same geometry at 2 kHz gives 23.5 Hz/s — higher pitch glides faster in Hz/s.

General 2D (source eq. 2.12 form): $f^{\prime} = f\dfrac{v - v_o\cos\theta_o}{v - v_s\cos\theta_s}$ with angles measured along the source-to-observer line and signs set by the direction convention; the robust version (Oly 06):
$f^{\prime} = f\dfrac{v - \vec v_o\cdot\hat r}{v - \vec v_s\cdot\hat r}$ with $\hat r$ from source toward observer. Specialise to 1D: recovers JEE-24.

cards.title: 2D formulas for moving observer too (cont.)
items: Worked: observer on a pier, boat moving past at 5 m/s at 30 degrees to the line of sight, horn 440 Hz, $v = 343$: only the radial part $5\cos 30^{\circ} = 4.33$ m/s counts: $f^{\prime} = 440\cdot 343/(343 - 4.33) = 445.6$ Hz — not the 453 Hz a naive 1D formula gives.

Two moving at angles: project BOTH velocities on the line of sight, plug into the box; all hard 2D problems collapse to projections. Instantaneous radial component changes continuously — the full swoop curve is $f^{\prime}(t)$ with $\theta(t)$ from the geometry.

symmetric pass: equal and opposite radial velocities at equal distances either side: the shift curve is antisymmetric about $f$ at first order in $u/v$; the second-order asymmetry (JEE-22) tilts it slightly.

title: 2D Doppler: radial components and the closest-approach glide (cont.)
subtitle: 2D Doppler projections, closest-approach glide, slope magnitude f u_s^2/(v b).
takeaway: 2D Doppler uses radial projections; the glide slope at closest approach is f u^2/(v b).

cards.title: Glide and slope drills
items: (a) $f = 600$ Hz, $u_s = 30$ m/s, $b = 200$ m, $v = 340$: slope $= 600\cdot 900/(340\cdot 200) = 7.9$ Hz/s. (b) A racer passing at $b = 50$ m drops pitch by 40 Hz within 2 s of the pass: slope 20 Hz/s $= f u_s^2/(v b)$: $u_s = \sqrt{20\cdot 340\cdot 50/f}$; at $f = 400$ Hz: $u_s = 92$ m/s — fast but a fair order estimate; a spectrogram improves this.

Combine with echo (JEE-27): emit toward the moving object, measure the double-shift of the return: $u_r$ directly; combine with the glide slope for the full velocity vector — the principle of acoustic tracking.
every 2D Doppler problem is 1D in disguise along the line of sight; perpendicular velocity components do nothing at that instant — the projection principle.

cards.title: Echo, double Doppler, and the second-order asymmetry
items: Echo from a moving wall (reflector speed $u$ toward a stationary source/observer): the wall is first a MOVING OBSERVER (it receives $f_1 = f\frac{v + u}{v}$) then a MOVING SOURCE (re-emits at $f_1$ while approaching): the original observer receives $\mathbf{f^{\prime\prime} = f\dfrac{v + u}{v - u}}$ — the double-shift product. Expansion: $f(1 + 2u/v + 2u^2/v^2 + \ldots)$;

the classic radar formula is the first-order $\Delta f = 2fu/v$. Source numbers (Q12): $f = 1000$ Hz, $u = 30$, $v = 340$: exact $1000\cdot 370/310 = 1193.5$ Hz; the linear approximation $1000(1 + 2\cdot 30/340) = 1176$ Hz — the source explicitly quotes 1176 as an approximation.

cards.title: Echo, double Doppler, and the second-order asymmetry (cont.)
items: Same box for a moving radar (source and observer co-located, target moving): wall as observer then wall as source — identical $\frac{v + u}{v - u}$ for approach; for a receding target $\frac{v - u}{v + u}$. A bat flying toward its own echo: the bat is BOTH the moving source and the moving observer: two shifts, same box: $f^{\prime\prime} = f\frac{v + u}{v - u}$ at 5 m/s, 40 kHz gives 41.2 kHz.

Second-order asymmetry (source Q8/Q9 pair): a 30 m/s source approach gives 1096.8 Hz while a 30 m/s observer approach gives 1088.2 Hz (at $f = 1000$, $v = 340$): difference 8.6 Hz $\approx f u^2/(v(v - u))$ — the two single-shift formulas agree to first order only; the echo doubles the first-order effect and more.

cards.title: Echo, double Doppler, and the second-order asymmetry (cont.)
items: the echo receives TWO shifts because the reflector plays both roles in turn (observer then source): the product of the two single-shift factors; every radar/sonar/ultrasound-flow formula is this one box.
consistency: approaching wall $f^{\prime\prime} > f$; receding wall $< f$; $u = v/2$ approach: $f^{\prime\prime} = 3f$; $u \to v$: divergence (the wavefront pile-up of JEE-28).

Sound to a cliff and back: $t = 2L/v$; with wind along the path: $t = \frac{L}{v+w} + \frac{L}{v-w}$ (JEE-25). Thunder rule: count seconds, divide by 3 for km (343 m/s). Multi-echo scenes (several buildings): distinct delays $t_i = 2L_i/v$; intensity falls as $1/r^2$ per leg, echo as $1/r^4$ — the radar range equation structure.

title: Echo, double Doppler, and the second-order asymmetry
subtitle: Echo double Doppler f(v+u)/(v−u), beats with echo, timing formulas.
takeaway: Echo doubles the shift: f = f0 (v + u)/(v - u); radar beats give the target speed.

cards.title: Echo timing (non-Doppler echo problems) (cont.)
items: Moving observer toward a cliff with a horn: source and observer move together toward the wall: $f^{\prime\prime} = f\frac{v + u}{v - u}$ — the same universal box with $u$ the party speed toward the reflector.

Echo beats: the original horn and its echo differ by $f^{\prime\prime} - f = f\frac{2u}{v - u} \approx 2fu/v$; a driver approaching a wall hears beats between the horn and the echo: at $f = 400$ Hz, $u = 30$ m/s: echo 477.4 Hz, beats 77.4 Hz exact; $2fu/v = 70.6$ Hz linear — 10% error at these speeds.
beat-rate example checked above; for small $u/v$ the linear form suffices; exam papers often want the exact ratio — give both.

cards.title: Echo problem patterns (drill)
items: (a) Sonar 1500 Hz from a boat toward a submarine receding at 20 m/s in water ($v = 1450$): echo $f^{\prime\prime} = 1500\cdot 1430/1470 = 1459$ Hz. (b) A car approaching a wall at 20 m/s sounds 500 Hz ($v = 343$): the driver hears beats at $f\frac{2u}{v-u} = 500\cdot 40/323 = 61.9$ Hz. (c) An explosion 2 km away with a mountain 3 km beyond: direct sound 5.8 s, echo off the mountain 29.2 s.

Radar-gun principle: transmit $f_0$; the return is $f_0\frac{v + u}{v - u}$ (with $v = c$ for EM); the beat $\Delta f = 2f_0 u/v$ gives the speed — the working method of police radar, ultrasound flowmeters, and fetal heart monitors.

cards.title: Consistency grid for echo answers
items: echo problems are pure two-role bookkeeping: first interaction wall-as-observer, second wall-as-source; once seen this way no new formulas are needed.

Approach at $u$: $f^{\prime\prime}/f = \frac{v + u}{v - u}$: anchors: $u = 0$: 1; $u = v/4$: $5/3 = 1.67$; $u = v/2$: 3; $u = 2v/3$: 5. Recession: the reciprocal. Timing: $2L/v$ without wind; $2Lv/(v^2 - w^2)$ with wind along; beats $f\frac{2u}{v - u}$ exact.
The double-Doppler is NOT $1 + 2u/v$ exactly: at $u = 0.1v$: exact $1.1/0.9 = 1.222$ vs $1 + 2u/v = 1.2$: 1.8% error; with 3-digit data quote the exact form.
biological sonar (bats, dolphins), ultrasound flowmetry, fetal monitors, police radar — all $\frac{v + u}{v - u}$; the shared structure is a favourite explain-the-principle question.

cards.title: Mach cone, sonic boom, and supersonic geometry
items: When a source moves at $u_s > v$ (supersonic) it outruns its own wavefronts: the crests pile onto a conical surface — the Mach cone. Half-angle behind the source: $\mathbf{\sin\alpha = v/u_s = 1/M}$ with Mach number $M = u_s/v$ (source Q13: $M = 2$: $\sin\alpha = 0.5$: $\alpha = 30^{\circ}$). The cone trails the source;
observers hear NOTHING until the cone passes, then a thunder-like bang — the sonic boom (an N-wave pressure transient, overpressure 50–500 Pa for aircraft).

Geometry: each spherical wavefront of radius $vt$ emitted at earlier times is left behind at distance $u_s t$; the common tangent surface has $\sin\alpha = vt/(u_s t) = 1/M$. Ground track: the boom reaches the ground along the cone — the boom carpet is a swath tens of km wide for high-flying jets, sweeping with the aircraft.

title: Mach cone, sonic boom, and supersonic geometry
subtitle: Mach cone sin $\alpha$ = 1/M, sonic boom, corrected boom-delay geometry.
source: Source: sound-waves/Sound-waves.md sec. 2.13 / Q13; independently checked
takeaway: Mach cone: sin(alpha) = 1/M; the boom delay after the pass is h sqrt(M^2-1)/(M v).

cards.title: Mach cone, sonic boom, and supersonic geometry (cont.)
items: Doppler behind a supersonic source: the subsonic formulas fail inside the cone; observers hear earlier sounds arriving late and in reverse order (details out of syllabus). What matters for exams: $f^{\prime}$ formulas apply only for $u_s < v$ and before cone arrival.

the cone is the sound analogue of a boat wake or Cherenkov radiation: any emitter outrunning its own disturbance field piles the disturbance on a tangent cone of angle $\sin\alpha = v_{\mathrm{disturbance}}/v_{\mathrm{emitter}}$.

limits: $M \to 1^{+}$: $\alpha \to 90^{\circ}$ (the cone flattens to a wall — intense boom front); $M \to \infty$: $\alpha \to 0$; $M = 1$ exactly: infinite pile-up in linear theory — nonlinearity makes a shock.

cards.title: Boom delay problem (source paper Q13 — corrected reasoning)
items: Setup (source paper Q13, $M = 2$, $v = 340$ m/s, $h = 10$ km): how long after the jet is seen directly overhead is the boom heard? Correct envelope derivation: the shock reaching the stationary observer at time $t$ was emitted at $t_e = -t/(M^2-1)$ (differentiate the wavefront arrival condition);

title: Acoustic impedance Z = rho v: the ratio that governs coupling

takeaway: Impedance Z = rho v is the coupling constant; matching Z transfers power, mismatching reflects it.

cards.title: Acoustic impedance Z = rho v: the ratio that governs coupling
items: For a travelling plane wave the pressure and the particle velocity $u = -\partial s/\partial t$ are locked in the ratio $\mathbf{Z = \dfrac{\Delta P}{u} = \rho v}$, the characteristic acoustic impedance (SI unit: rayl = kg m$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$; 1 rayl $= 1$ Pa s/m). Air at 20 C: $Z = 1.2\times 343 = 412$ rayl (often rounded to 400); water: $10^{3}\times 1483 = 1.48\times 10^{6}$ rayl; steel:
$7800\times 5064 = 3.95\times 10^{7}$ rayl. The huge air-water mismatch (factor 3600) is why a swimmer hears almost nothing from an airborne source and why the ear needs a middle-ear lever.

cards.title: Acoustic impedance Z = rho v: the ratio that governs coupling (con.
items: Impedance is the acoustic analogue of electrical impedance: pressure plays voltage, particle velocity plays current. Power delivered to a surface: $I = \frac{1}{2}\Delta P_0 u_0 = \frac{1}{2} Z u_0^2 = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2Z}$ — same intensity formulas as JEE-10 with $Z = \rho v$ substituted. Sources are rated by impedance matching:
a loudspeaker cone must drive air, so its mechanical impedance should be near $Z_{\mathrm{air}}A$ over its area; the horn shape (Oly 09) is an impedance transformer.

cards.title: Acoustic impedance Z = rho v: the ratio that governs coupling (con.
items: Standing waves: at a displacement node $u = 0$ and $\Delta P \neq 0$, so the local ratio $\Delta P/u$ diverges — the standing wave has position-dependent, purely REACTIVE impedance (like a lossless LC line); only travelling waves carry the real impedance $\rho v$. General wave: $Z = \Delta P/u$ complex; travelling: real $\rho v$; evanescent: imaginary.

impodance packs two independent properties (density and speed) into one coupling constant: what matters at an interface is not $\rho$ or $v$ separately but their product, because pressure and velocity are the two wave variables.

units: $\rho v = $ kg m$^{-3}$ m s$^{-1}$ = kg m$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ = Pa/(m/s) ok; helium at 20 C: $Z = 0.166\times 1007 = 167$ rayl — even lower than air despite the high speed, because $\rho$ is tiny: He couples to the ear poorly (soft, quiet) though the speed is high.

cards.title: Impedance numbers that decide real problems
items: Table (rayl): air 412; helium 167; hydrogen 112 ($0.084\times 1307$... at 20 C $\rho = 0.082$, $v = 1307$: $Z = 107$); CO2 500 ($1.84\times 272$... at 20 C); water $1.48\times 10^{6}$; fat tissue $1.38\times 10^{6}$ (close to water); bone $7.8\times 10^{6}$; steel $3.9\times 10^{7}$. Ultrasound imaging: soft-tissue boundaries are weak reflectors (matched); bone and air cavities are strong (mismatched) — the physics of image artefacts.

Loudspeaker design: a bare cone radiates into air with efficiency $\sim 2\rho_{\mathrm{air}} v / (\rho_{\mathrm{cone}} v_{\mathrm{cone}})$-scale mismatch... practical fix: use a large-area light cone (low mechanical $Z$) or a horn (Oly 09). The ear solves the reverse problem: air $Z = 412$ to cochlear fluid $Z = 1.5\times 10^{6}$:

subtitle: Acoustic impedance Z = $\rho$v, impedance table, coupling and matching algebra.

cards.title: Impedance numbers that decide real problems (cont.)
items: the eardrum area (55 mm$^2$) vs oval window (3.2 mm$^2$) gives an area ratio 17, and the lever of the ossicles another ~1.3: total pressure gain ~22, power transmission improved ~30x; plus the ear canal resonance (JEE-01) adds gain near 3 kHz.

reflection fraction for intensity between media $Z_1, Z_2$: $R = \left(\dfrac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$ (Oly 02): air-water: $R = 0.999$: 99.9% of airborne power bounces off the lake ok why underwater listening to aircraft fails.

specific acoustic impedance vs characteristic: $Z = \rho v$ is per unit area (rayl); mechanical impedance of a panel $Z_{\mathrm{mech}} = \Delta P A/u = Z A$ in ohms-kg/s — the driving-point quantity for motors and diaphragms.

cards.title: Impedance algebra drills
items: (a) Same intensity in air and water: pressure amplitudes scale as $\sqrt Z$: $\Delta P_{\mathrm{water}}/\Delta P_{\mathrm{air}} = \sqrt{1.48\times 10^{6}/412} = 60$; underwater sound of the same $I$ has 60x the pressure swing. (b) $s_0$ at same $I$: $s_0 \propto 1/\sqrt{Z\omega^2}$-ish:

water displacement for same $I$ is $1/60$ of air (times speed ratio... precisely $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(Z\omega)$: $\Delta P_0$ 60x and $Z$ 3600x: $s_0$ 60x smaller ok). (c) Design: a transducer of area 1 cm$^2$ driving air at 1 Pa amplitude delivers $\Delta P^2 A/(2Z) = 1\times 10^{-4}/824 = 1.2\times 10^{-7}$ W — microwatts; the same face in water delivers 0.34 W — water loads transducers heavily.

cards.title: Impedance algebra drills (cont.)
items: Impedance ladder across a problem: media ($Z = \rho v$), then interface factors ($R$, $T$), then geometry (spreading), then absorption: the four multipliers of every acoustic power budget.
engineers think in dB of mismatch loss; physicists think in $Z$ ratios; exams give $\rho$ and $v$ and expect the product — never forget the product is the coupling constant.
the ear canal and Helmholtz resonances are IMPEDANCE phenomena (reactance cancellation): the resonance formulas of JEE-17/19 reappear as impedance matching — one physics, two vocabularies.

cards.title: Impedance view of amplitude relations (consolidation)
items: Re-derive the amplitude toolkit through $Z$: $I = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2Z} = \dfrac{1}{2} Z \omega^2 s_0^2$ (since $\Delta P_0 = Z\omega s_0$); $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2 Z I}$; $s_0 = \dfrac{\Delta P_0}{Z\omega}$. Intensity level:

$\beta = 10\log_{10}\dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2 Z I_0}$ — note the level of a FIXED pressure amplitude depends on the medium! 1 Pa is 113.8 dB in air ($20\log(1/2.87\times 10^{-5})$) but only 90.7 dB in water (referenced to the same $I_0$): the reference convention matters across media.

title: Acoustic impedance Z = rho v: the ratio that governs coupling (cont.)
subtitle: Acoustic impedance Z = $\rho$v, impedance table, coupling and matching algebra.
takeaway: Impedance Z = rho v is the coupling constant; matching Z transfers power, mismatching reflects it.

cards.title: Impedance view of amplitude relations (consolidation) (cont.)
items: Impedance and Doppler (bridge): a moving source radiates into the medium with Doppler factors; the POWER of the received wave scales as $f^{\prime 2}$ through the amplitude change (Oly 05):
$I \propto \Delta P_0^2/2Z$ with $\Delta P_0$ Doppler-shifted — the intensity Doppler factor is $\left(\dfrac{f'}{f}\right)^2$ for moving-source; state assumptions carefully.

the specific impedance is real only for progressive waves; measurement instruments quote $Z$ of materials as $\rho v$ with $\pm$few-% uncertainty from $\rho$ and $v$ errors — propagate independently: $\delta Z/Z = \delta\rho/\rho + \delta v/v$.

cards.title: Boundary reflection & transmission: R = ((Z2-Z1)/(Z2+Z1))^2
items: At a plane interface between media of impedances $Z_1, Z_2$ the pressure reflection coefficient $r_p = \dfrac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}$ (signed) and the intensity reflection fraction $R = r_p^2 = \left(\dfrac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$;

transmission $T = 1 - R = \dfrac{4 Z_1 Z_2}{(Z_1 + Z_2)^2}$. Extreme cases: $Z_2 \gg Z_1$ (air to wall): $r_p \to +1$ (pressure reflects in phase, hard wall, displacement node in the air); $Z_2 \ll Z_1$ (water to air): $r_p \to -1$ (pressure inverts, soft boundary, pressure node); $Z_2 = Z_1$: $R = 0$, perfect transmission — the impedance-matching ideal.

cards.title: Boundary reflection & transmission: R = ((Z2-Z1)/(Z2+Z1))^2
items: The particle velocity coefficient has the opposite sign pattern: $r_u = -r_p$: at a hard wall velocity inverts (displacement node ok JEE-16); at a soft end pressure inverts (pressure node ok). Derivation: continuity of pressure and of normal velocity across the interface: $1 + r = t$ and $(1 - r)/Z_1 = t/Z_2$ solve to the boxed pair.

Worked numbers: air ($Z = 412$) to glass ($Z = 1.3\times 10^{7}$): $R = 0.99987$ — a glass wall reflects 99.99% of intensity (why rooms ring); air-water: $R = 0.999$; water-glass: $R = 0.63$... compute: $((1.3e7-1.48e6)/(1.3e7+1.48e6))^2 = 0.63$: 63% — soft by comparison; fat-kidney soft tissue ($Z$ similar): $R < 0.01$ — why ultrasound needs speckle and Doppler contrast.

cards.title: Boundary reflection & transmission: R = ((Z2-Z1)/(Z2+Z1))^2
items: the boundary conditions are the two continuity laws (pressure continuous — no infinite force; normal velocity continuous — media stay in contact); everything else follows algebraically; the square for intensity comes from $I \propto \Delta P_0^2/Z$.

energy bookkeeping: $R + T = 1$ exactly; a computed $R > 1$ or $T > 1$ signals a sign error; $r_p$ sign flips tell the phase of the reflected wave: wall-type (positive, pressure antinode at boundary) vs open-type (negative, pressure node).

title: Reflection and transmission at boundaries: R = left(fracZ 2 - Z 1Z 2 + Z 1right)2
subtitle: Boundary reflection/transmission coefficients, quarter-wave matching, phase rules.
takeaway: R = ((Z2 - Z1)/(Z2 + Z1))^2, T = 4 Z1 Z2/(Z1 + Z2)^2; hard walls keep pressure, soft ends kill it.

cards.title: Quarter-wave layers and impedance matching
items: A layer of thickness $\lambda/4$ and impedance $Z_l = \sqrt{Z_1 Z_2}$ cancels reflection at one frequency: the two reflected waves from the layer faces interfere destructively when $Z_l^2 = Z_1 Z_2$ (anti-reflection coating; the transformer equation $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = Z_l^2/Z_{\mathrm{load}}$ — acoustic transmission line theory). Exam version:
"what thickness of material between air and wall removes reflection at 1 kHz?" $\lambda/4$ of the layer: $v_l/4f$.

Standing wave ratio as a measurable: $\mathrm{SWR} = \dfrac{1 + |r_p|}{1 - |r_p|}$; measuring $I_{\max}/I_{\min} = \mathrm{SWR}^2$ in a duct recovers $|r_p|$ and hence $Z_2$ — the standard impedance-measurement method.

cards.title: Quarter-wave layers and impedance matching (cont.)
items: Partial reflection in pipes: an open end radiates; $R = 1 - (ka)^2/2$-ish for low $ka$... precisely: radiation from an unflanged pipe end reflects intensity $R \approx 1 - \frac{1}{2}(ka)^2$ at low frequency (end correction is the reactive part of the same impedance, JEE-19).

the $\lambda/4$ transformer works because the round trip inside the layer is a half wavelength: the second reflection is $180^{\circ}$ out of phase with the first when the impedance chain is geometric-mean matched.

cards.title: Quarter-wave layers and impedance matching (cont.)
items: coating demo: glass coated so $Z_l = \sqrt{Z_{\mathrm{air}} Z_{\mathrm{glass}}}$: $Z_l = 2.3\times 10^{5}$ rayl — e.g. a porous layer of the right density and speed; quarter-wave at 1 kHz: thickness $v_l/4000$... with $v_l = 1000$ m/s: 25 cm — unrealistically thick for air-acoustics at 1 kHz: matching layers are practical in ultrasound (MHz, mm scales) ok.

Hard wall ($Z_2 \gg Z_1$): $r_p = +1$: pressure reflects UNINVERTED (antinode at wall); $r_u = -1$: velocity inverts (node at wall) ok JEE-16 boundary rules derived, not memorised. Open end ($Z_2 \ll Z_1$, e.g. pipe opening to atmosphere): $r_p = -1$ (pressure node just outside), $r_u = +1$ (velocity antinode).

cards.title: Phase rules from impedance (the safe derivation) (cont.)
items: The quarter-wave offset between pressure and displacement in travelling waves (SN-03) reappears here as the $\lambda/4$ displacement-vs-pressure offset of the standing pattern.

Why the wall reflects: air cannot drive the dense wall (huge $Z$), so the velocity at the wall is forced to zero: the superposition of incident and reflected waves must cancel velocity there: $u_i + u_r = 0$  $\to$  $r_u = -1$  $\to$  $r_p = +1$ ok consistent with the formulas.

cards.title: Phase rules from impedance (the safe derivation) (cont.)
items: Soft-end subtlety: the open end is NOT exactly $Z = 0$: the radiation impedance $Z_{\mathrm{end}} = \rho v[\frac{1}{4}(ka)^2 + i\cdot 0.6 ka]$-ish (Oly 05): real part radiates (why $R < 1$ slightly), imaginary part is the end correction $e = 0.6a$ (JEE-19) — the three topics (reflection, end correction, radiation resistance) are one impedance expansion.

(b) "Find $Z_2$ if $R = 0.25$": $|r_p| = 0.5$: $Z_2/Z_1 = 3$ or 1/3. (c) A tube closed by a movable wall of impedance $Z_2$:

the same few numbers ($Z$ ratios) decide hearing, room acoustics, ultrasound imaging, and sonar targets — one boundary table worth memorising: $R$, $r_p$ sign, wall type.

Lossless line theory: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = Z_0\dfrac{Z_L + i Z_0\tan kL}{Z_0 + i Z_L\tan kL}$ with $Z_0 = \rho v/S$ the characteristic line impedance (per area $S$), $Z_L$ the load. Resonance (maximum amplitude for a given drive) occurs when $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ is minimum (open-open:

cards.title: Pipes as impedance problems: input impedance and resonance (cont.
items: $Z_L = 0$: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = i Z_0\tan kL = 0$ at $kL = n\pi$  $\to$  $L = n\lambda/2$ ok all harmonics; closed-open: $Z_L = \infty$: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = -i Z_0\cot kL = 0$ at $kL = (2n-1)\pi/2$  $\to$  odd quarter waves ok JEE-17/18 derived from one formula).

Why closed pipes give odd harmonics: the mismatched ends force $\tan kL$ and $\cot kL$ conditions alternating: counting quarter wavelengths that fit between a velocity node and a pressure node is the SAME as setting the imaginary part of $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ to zero. Mixed-end resonance spacing $\Delta f = v/2L$ falls out of the $\tan$ period π in $kL$.

cards.title: Pipes as impedance problems: input impedance and resonance (cont.
items: Load effects: a pipe with a partially open far end ($Z_L$ finite, radiation) has damped resonance peaks and shifted frequencies — the Q factor (Oly 05) comes from the real part of $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$; the end correction (JEE-19) is the imaginary part at the mouth; a flange changes $Z_L$ and thus $e$ (0.6r to 0.85r) consistently.

impedance language unifies: boundary conditions, end corrections, resonance ladders, radiation, and damping are all one rational function $Z_{\mathrm{in}}(kL, Z_L)$ — the exam formulas are its special cases.

cards.title: Pipes as impedance problems: input impedance and resonance (cont.
items: specialise: $L = \lambda/2$ open-open: $kL = \pi$: $\tan = 0$: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = 0$ ok short at the drive point: maximum flow for given pressure... resonance of a driven pipe is when the drive sees minimum impedance ok; closed-closed: $Z_L = \infty$ both ends: $kL = n\pi$ again all harmonics ok JEE-16 CHECK.

Driven pipe amplitude vs frequency: Lorentzian of half-width $\Delta f = f_1/Q$: $Q = \dfrac{\pi}{2\ln(1/r)}$-ish for end reflection $r$... working rule: $Q \approx \dfrac{\pi}{2(1 - r)}$ for $r \to 1$ (small losses); typical unflanged pipe $Q \sim 10$–30; flanged 20–60; with damping wool less.

title: Pipes as impedance problems: input impedance and resonance
subtitle: Input impedance of pipes, resonance/Q, why odd harmonics for closed pipes.
takeaway: A pipe is a load on a line: resonance is zero input reactance; closed pipes give odd harmonics by cot(kL).

cards.title: Resonance curve: width, Q, and the amplitude build-up (cont.)
items: At resonance the amplitude gain over the non-resonant case is $\sim Q$ (in pressure); bandwidth $\Delta f$ measures the fractional loss per cycle.

Time picture: a driven resonator rings up over $\tau = Q/(\pi f_1)$... precisely $\tau = \dfrac{Q}{\pi f_1} = \dfrac{1}{\pi\Delta f}$ (energy decay time $\tau_E = Q/(2\pi f)$-ish); striking a pipe: the sound decays exponentially with that time constant: exam estimate: Q = 20 at 300 Hz: $\tau = 21$ ms.

Multiple coupled pipes (organ ranks, bottles): coupling shifts each resonance slightly (mode splitting); a Helmholtz resonator on a wall acts as a notch absorber at $f_H = \dfrac{v}{2\pi}\sqrt{S/(V L_{\mathrm{eff}})}$ — room acoustics tool built on pipe theory.

cards.title: Resonance curve: width, Q, and the amplitude build-up (cont.)
items: resonance width example: $f_1 = 300$ Hz, $Q = 15$: half-power width 20 Hz: the resonance tube (JEE-20) length sweep through a peak of that width in frequency terms: $\Delta L = \lambda \Delta f/(2f) = 2$ cm for the second resonance spacing... order: noticeable in careful labs, negligible in rough ones.

Q is a number for how many cycles energy survives: $Q = 2\pi\times$ energy stored / energy lost per cycle — the single number that decides whether a resonance is sharp (tuning forks Q ~ 1000, pipes Q ~ 20, rooms Q ~ 5).

cards.title: Impedance methods in exam clothing
items: (a) "Why does a closed pipe sound hollow?" odd harmonics only = the $\cot kL$ resonance sequence; explain via impedance: the closed end is a velocity node (infinite load), the open end a pressure node (zero load): only odd quarters fit. (b) "Predict the effect of a movable piston in a tube": $L$ varies: resonance ladder sweeps; with $Z_L$ finite at the drive, peaks broaden.
(c) "Design a tube resonant at 440 Hz and 660 Hz": open-open with $f_1 = 220$: $L = v/2f_1 = 0.78$ m (minus 2e).

Half-open side branch (quarter-wave trap): a branch of length $\lambda/4$ closed at the far end presents $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = 0$ at the junction (short circuit for waves of that $f$): mufflers use arrays of such traps — mechanical filter design, exam-explainable.

cards.title: Impedance methods in exam clothing (cont.)
items: the general line equation: $\dfrac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} = \dfrac{1}{c^2}\dfrac{\partial^2 P}{\partial t^2}$ for the pressure in a duct of constant area (same wave equation, 1D): the impedance formalism is the travelling/standing decomposition of its solutions.

(a) Open pipe $L = 0.4$ m, $r = 2$ cm: $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = 0.424$ m: $f_1 = 343/0.848 = 404.5$ Hz; $Q = 20$: bandwidth 20 Hz; driving at 395 Hz: amplitude $\sim Q/2$-ish below peak... half-power at $\Delta f = \pm 10$ Hz: 395 Hz is 9.5 Hz off: $\sim 1/\sqrt{2}$ of peak amplitude. (b) Closed pipe same length: $f_1 = 343/(4\times 0.412) = 208$ Hz (one end corrected only).
