items: End-loaded pipe: with $Z_L = Z_0/2$ (e.g. a partially open damper): resonance shifts between the open and closed ladders; solving $\tan kL = Z_0/Z_L$... the transcendental decides: exam problems state "closed" or "open" only.
the impedance method gives answers without redrawing node pictures: write $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$, set the reactance to zero, read the ladder — faster and safer under time pressure.

A harmonic wave at a point is a rotating phasor of length $a$ and phase $\phi$: $s = a\cos(\omega t - \phi) \leftrightarrow a e^{i\phi}$. Sum of many same-frequency waves = phasor polygon: $A = \left|\sum_k a_k e^{i\phi_k}\right|$; phase $\arg\left(\sum\right)$. Two phasors:

cards.title: Phasors: superposition of harmonic waves as vector addition (cont.)
items: $A = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + 2a_1a_2\cos\Delta\phi}$ (the JEE-13 formula, now a picture); equal amplitudes: $A = 2a\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$ bisecting the angle.

Why phasors work: the wave equation is linear and time-harmonic; the time factor $e^{-i\omega t}$ cancels in all ratios and sums; only spatial phases matter. Interference problems become geometry: equal spacing $\delta = \lambda/N$ between $N$ sources closes the polygon (partial cancellation); symmetric arrangements give closed polygons (silence: e.g.
3 sources at the vertices of an equilateral triangle seen from the centre: phases 0, 120, 240: sum zero).

cards.title: Phasors: superposition of harmonic waves as vector addition (cont.)
items: Beats revisited: two phasors of nearby frequency rotate at slightly different rates: the resultant length oscillates at the difference rate — the beat envelope IS the rotating-vector picture (JEE-15); the phasor tip traces an epicycloid.

complex exponentials turn differentiation into multiplication ($\partial_t \to -i\omega$): the wave equation becomes algebraic; every resonance, impedance, and interference formula of this chapter is a statement about complex sums.

three-source check: $a, a, a$ with phases 0, 120°, 240°: sum = 0 ok (used in three-phase cancellation and in $N$-slit minima conditions $\delta = \lambda/N$ multiples... precisely minima of $N$-source interference when $N\delta/\lambda$ is a non-multiple-of-N integer).

cards.title: Phasor clinic: worked sums
items: (a) $a_1 = 3$, $a_2 = 4$, $\Delta\phi = 90^{\circ}$: $A = 5$; phase $\tan^{-1}(4/3) = 53.1^{\circ}$ from phasor 1. (b) $N = 4$ equal phasors with successive phase $\delta = 60^{\circ}$: closed-chain geometry: $A = a\dfrac{\sin(N\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)} = a\dfrac{\sin 120^{\circ}}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = 1.73 a$ — the array-factor formula (same as $N$-slit optics).
(c) Two waves of amplitude ratio 3:1 in antiphase: $A = 2a$; the "zero" of interference is incomplete (contrast $\mathcal{V} = 2\cdot3/(9+1) = 0.6$).

title: Phasors: superposition of harmonic waves as vector addition
subtitle: Phasor addition, array factor sin(N$\psi$/2)/sin($\psi$/2), quadrature as rotation.
takeaway: Phasors turn interference into vector sums; the array factor sin(N psi/2)/sin(psi/2) covers N sources.

cards.title: Phasor clinic: worked sums (cont.)
items: Array factor: $A(\theta) = a_0\dfrac{\sin(N\psi/2)}{\sin(\psi/2)}$ with $\psi = kd\cos\theta + \beta$ the progressive phase — loudspeaker arrays and diffraction gratings in one formula; principal maxima at $\psi = 2\pi m$.
Power of the picture: instead of trig identities, DRAW: equal-length chords, inscribed polygon, radius $R = a/2\sin(\psi/2)$-ish; the sum is the closing chord — Euclidean geometry replaces algebra.

array-factor sanity: $\psi = 0$: $A = Na$ ok (the $\sin/\sin$ limit); $\psi = 2\pi/N$: $A = 0$? $\sin(N\cdot\pi/N) = \sin\pi = 0$ ok first minimum; for $N = 2$: $A = 2a\cos(\psi/2)$ ok beats/interference formula recovered.

cards.title: Phasors for standing waves and quadrature energy
items: Standing wave as two counter-rotating phasors (equal $\omega$, opposite direction): at a node they cancel always (antiparallel); at an antinode they add. The pressure-displacement quadrature (SN-03) is a $90^{\circ}$ phasor offset: energy shuttles between the two quadrature components, total constant for a standing wave.

Energy in phasor language: for $s = a\cos(\omega t - \phi)$, $u = \partial_t s = a\omega\sin(\omega t - \phi)$ — velocity phasor leads displacement by $90^{\circ}$; the impedance $Z = \Delta P/u$ is the ratio of two phasors; reactive impedance = $90^{\circ}$ offset (stored energy), real = in-phase (radiated power).
Power factor of a source: a driver in phase with the velocity radiates max power (real $Z$); $90^{\circ}$ out of phase it stores (near-field reactance) — antenna and loudspeaker design language.

cards.title: Phasors for standing waves and quadrature energy (cont.)
items: the phasor at $90^{\circ}$ is the mathematical seat of the quadrature physics: every "X leads Y by 90°" statement in this chapter is a phasor sentence.

round trip: $\Delta P = -B\partial s/\partial x$ is a spatial derivative = $90^{\circ}$ phase rotation for sinusoids: pressure phasor = displacement phasor rotated by $-90^{\circ}$ and scaled by $Bk = Z\omega$ ok consistent with $\Delta P_0 = Z\omega s_0$.

(a) Two speakers driven in phase, listener at path difference $3\lambda/4$: $\Delta\phi = 270^{\circ}$: amplitude $2a|\cos 135^{\circ}| = 0.71\cdot 2a$... $\sqrt{2} a$ of the sum-free... precisely $2a\cos(135^{\circ}) = -\sqrt{2} a$: amplitude $\sqrt{2}a$: intensity 2x one source. (b) Three equal sources, phases 0, 90°, 180°: $A = a|1 + i - 1| = a$:

cards.title: Phasor drill set (cont.)
items: intensity = one source. (c) Balanced bridge of four speakers in a square, driven alternately in phase/antiphase: at the centre all pairs cancel — architectural silence.
General N: geometric series $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} a e^{ik\psi} = a\dfrac{1 - e^{iN\psi}}{1 - e^{i\psi}}$ — derive the array factor in one line; the phase-only version drives phased-array sonar.

phasors extend to noise and pulses by Fourier decomposition: any waveform = phasor sum; linear systems act on each phasor independently with a transfer function $H(\omega)$ — the door to signal processing.

title: Energy flux, radiation resistance, and the Q of resonance
subtitle: Radiation resistance, near/far field, Q = $\omega$E/P, ring-down and bandwidth.
takeaway: Q = omega E / P_loss ties ring-down, bandwidth and gain; small sources are poor radiators.

cards.title: Energy flux, radiation resistance, and the Q of resonance
items: Time-averaged intensity of a travelling wave: $I = \bar u v = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2 Z}$ with $Z = \rho v$ (Oly 01). For a general (possibly reactive) field the instantaneous flux $\Pi = \Delta P \cdot u$ oscillates; only its average transports. A driven resonator near resonance stores energy $\mathcal{E}$ and loses power $P_{\mathrm{loss}} = \omega \mathcal{E}/Q$;

quality factor $Q = \dfrac{\omega\mathcal{E}}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}} = 2\pi\dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{\text{loss per cycle}}$; ring-down time $\tau = Q/\omega$ (amplitude) — the number that separates tuning forks ($Q \sim 10^{3}$) from rooms ($Q \sim 5$).

cards.title: Energy flux, radiation resistance, and the Q of resonance (cont.)
items: Radiation resistance: a vibrating surface of area $S$ and velocity amplitude $u_0$ radiates $P = \frac{1}{2}R_r S u_0^2$ with $R_r \approx Z_{\mathrm{air}}$ for a large baffle ($R_r = Z$ per unit area) but $R_r \propto (ka)^2 Z$ for a small piston ($ka < 1$): small sources are BAD radiators — the reason a bare vibrating rod is quiet and a loudspeaker cone is big. Multipole order: monopole (pulsating sphere) radiates best at low $ka$;

Near field vs far field: within $r < \lambda/2\pi$ the reactive component dominates ($\Delta P \perp u$): energy sloshes, no net flux; beyond, the travelling wave $\Delta P = Zu$ carries $I \propto 1/r^2$. Microphone placement and speaker measurements must sit in the far field.

cards.title: Energy flux, radiation resistance, and the Q of resonance (cont.)
items: Q is the single number connecting ring-down, bandwidth, and amplitude build-up: $\Delta f = f/Q$, $\tau = Q/(2\pi f)$-ish in time units, and peak gain $\propto Q$ for a given drive — one concept, three exam formulas.

consistency: $Q = 2\pi\mathcal{E}/W_{\mathrm{cycle}}$; $\Delta f = f_1/Q$; $\tau_{\mathrm{amp}} = Q/(\pi f_1)$... at $Q = 20$, $f = 300$ Hz: $\tau = 21$ ms and $\Delta f = 15$ Hz: a struck pipe fades in ~3 ringing times ≈ 60 ms ok audible clap-coloration.

Pulsating sphere radius $a$, $ka < 1$: $R_r = \rho c (ka)^2/4$ per area... source power $P = 2\pi a^2 u_0^2 \rho c (ka)^2/4$... exam form: $P = \dfrac{\rho c k^2 u_0^2}{4\pi}\,V^2$-type scaling with volume velocity $Q_v = u_0 S$; a 5 cm speaker at 1 kHz ($ka = 0.9$): roughly $R_r \sim Z/2$: efficient;

cards.title: Radiation from real sources (monopole, dipole, baffles) (cont.)
items: the same at 100 Hz ($ka = 0.09$): $R_r \sim Z/250$: wimpy bass — why woofers are large and ported.

Baffle and enclosure effects: an unbaffled driver short-circuits front-to-back at low $ka$ (dipole cancellation, 6 dB/octave rolloff); a box or horn restores monopole radiation; the infinite baffle gives $R_r = Z$ per area (pressure doubling at the panel).

Biological speakers: the human voice ~1 cm$^2$ glottis at 100–300 Hz: $ka < 0.1$: extremely inefficient (~0.01% of metabolic power): the mouth and vocal tract resonance (formants) do the impedance matching; birds sing 2–8 kHz where $ka \sim 1$: efficient little radiators.

title: Energy flux, radiation resistance, and the Q of resonance (cont.)
subtitle: Radiation resistance, near/far field, Q = $\omega$E/P, ring-down and bandwidth.
takeaway: Q = omega E / P_loss ties ring-down, bandwidth and gain; small sources are poor radiators.

cards.title: Radiation from real sources (monopole, dipole, baffles) (cont.)
items: power scaling: $P \propto u_0^2 f^2$ at low $ka$ for a fixed source: doubling frequency from 100 to 200 Hz multiplies radiated power by 4 at the same diaphragm speed ok why tweeters are easy and woofers hard.

(a) A 0.5 W source at 340 Hz in air: $I = P/(4\pi r^2)$: at 5 m: $1.6\times 10^{-3}$ W/m$^2$ = 92 dB; $\Delta P_0 = \sqrt{2ZI} = 1.14$ Pa; $s_0 = \Delta P_0/(Z\omega) = 1.3\mu$m. (b) "How much power to hold 1 Pa at 1 kHz over 1 m$^2$?" $P = \Delta P_0^2 S/(2Z) = 1.2$ W — modest; for 100 Pa (pain) 12 kW over 1 m$^2$ — concert-scale.

cards.title: Energy-budget problems (cont.)
items: (c) A fork of Q = 500, $f = 256$ Hz struck to 1 mm amplitude: stored energy $\mathcal{E} \sim \frac{1}{2}m_{\mathrm{eff}}\omega^2 x^2$: for $m_{\mathrm{eff}} = 20$ g: $1.3\times 10^{-3}$ J; loss per cycle $\mathcal{E}\cdot 2\pi/Q = 16\,\mu$J; ring-down $\tau = Q/(\pi f) = 0.62$ s.
Acoustic vs perceived: equal-loudness (Fletcher-Munson): physical $I$ must rise at low $f$ to match perceived loudness — power budget of hi-fi at 40 Hz is 10–20 dB more than at 1 kHz.

energy methods shortcut amplitude problems: instead of solving the wave equation, balance $P_{\mathrm{source}} = \oint I\,dA + d\mathcal{E}/dt + P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ — the acoustic version of the work-energy theorem.

cards.title: Q and resonance in the exam frame
items: (a) "A closed pipe Q = 12 at f1 = 200 Hz is driven: amplitude at resonance vs 10 Hz off": ratio $\approx Q\Delta f/f$-ish: at $\delta = 10$ Hz = half-width: amplitude $1/\sqrt{2}$ of peak. (b) "Two pipes of equal f1 but Q = 10 and 40: which is louder at resonance, which more selective?" same peak if loss-limited... high-Q rings louder after excitation and narrower in sweep.

(c) "Estimate the Q of a room from reverberation": $Q = \pi f T_{60}/6.9$... standard: $T_{60} = 0.161 V/A$ (Sabine): Q from bandwidth of a mode: $Q = f T_{60}/2.2$-ish: at 100 Hz, $T_{60} = 0.5$ s: $Q = 23$.

cards.title: Q and resonance in the exam frame (cont.)
items: Traps: (i) $\tau = Q/\omega$ vs $Q/(\pi f)$: factor conventions — state which amplitude time you use; (ii) Q is defined for ENERGY; amplitude decays twice as slowly... amplitude time $\tau_A = 2\tau_E$: exam convention varies: give both. (iii) Nonlinear large-amplitude acoustics drops Q (shock losses).

the resonator as a mechanical RLC: mass = acoustic inertance $\rho L/S$, compliance = $V/(\rho c^2)$, resistance = radiation + viscous: $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ of Oly 03 is the acoustic RLC impedance — identical mathematics.

title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case
subtitle: Vector Doppler f' = f(c − v_o·r)/(c − v_s·r), projections replace cases.
takeaway: f = f0 (c - v_o.r)/(c - v_s.r): one vector formula replaces the entire case library.

cards.title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case
items: Let $\hat{\mathbf r}$ point from source to observer at the emission event; let $\mathbf v_s, \mathbf v_o$ be the velocities of source and observer relative to the medium; $c$ the sound speed in the medium. Then the received frequency is $\mathbf{f' = f\dfrac{c - \mathbf v_o\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{c - \mathbf v_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}}$ — no signs to memorise: projections carry the signs. Check 1D: source approaching ($\mathbf v_s$ along $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ toward observer...

observer at larger $r$: $\mathbf v_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf r} = +u_s$... hmm careful: $\hat{\mathbf r}$ from source to observer: source moving toward observer means $\mathbf v_s$ has positive projection on $\hat{\mathbf r}$: denominator $c - u_s$ ok the approach rise; observer approaching means $\mathbf v_o$ points AGAINST $\hat{\mathbf r}$: $\mathbf v_o\cdot\hat{\mathbf r} = -u_o$: numerator $c + u_o$ ok exactly JEE-24.

cards.title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case (cont.)
items: Wind: replace $c\hat{\mathbf r}$-type bookkeeping by the medium velocity $\mathbf w$: sound velocity in ground frame $\mathbf c = c\hat{\mathbf r} + \mathbf w$; the clean invariant form measures $\mathbf v_s, \mathbf v_o$ RELATIVE TO THE MEDIUM and $c$ in the medium: $f' = f\dfrac{c - (\mathbf v_o - \mathbf w)\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{c - (\mathbf v_s - \mathbf w)\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}$... the robust recipe:

transform to the medium frame (subtract $\mathbf w$ from every ground velocity), apply the box, transform back (frequency is frame-invariant in classical acoustics for the observer present... the RECEIVED frequency is what the observer measures in their own frame: do all algebra in the medium frame then quote f').

cards.title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case (cont.)
items: Derivation: in the medium frame the wavefronts have spacing $\lambda' = \dfrac{c - \mathbf v_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{f}$ (source compresses along $\hat{\mathbf r}$) and the observer sweeps them at rate $\dfrac{c - \mathbf v_o\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{\lambda'}$: quotient = the box. Nothing else.
the dot products are the entire content of the 2D, angled, wind, and echo cases: every hard Doppler problem reduces to drawing $\hat{\mathbf r}$ and projecting — the box replaces a case library.

cards.title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case (cont.)
items: specialise all cases: observer at rest: numerator $c$; source at rest: denominator $c$; both at rest in wind: ratio $(c - \mathbf w\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})/(c - \mathbf w\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}) = 1$ ok no shift in uniform wind (JEE-25 convention); tangential source ($\mathbf v_s \perp \hat{\mathbf r}$): $f' = f$ at that instant ok glide midpoint.

(a) Source on the x-axis at $(vt, b)$ moving +x at $u$; observer at origin: $\hat{\mathbf r} = \dfrac{(-vt, -b)}{\sqrt{v^2t^2 + b^2}}$... set $u t$ for source position: $\hat{\mathbf r} = \dfrac{(-ut, -b)}{\sqrt{u^2t^2 + b^2}}$;

title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case (cont.)
subtitle: Vector Doppler f' = f(c − v_o·r)/(c − v_s·r), projections replace cases.
takeaway: f = f0 (c - v_o.r)/(c - v_s.r): one vector formula replaces the entire case library.

cards.title: Vector clinic: worked projections (cont.)
items: $\mathbf v_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf r} = \dfrac{-u^2 t}{\sqrt{u^2 t^2 + b^2}} = -u\cos\theta(t)$: $f' = f\dfrac{c}{c + u\cos\theta}$... check sign convention: approaching ($t < 0$): $\cos\theta < 0$: denominator $< c$:
$f' > f$ ok matches glide picture (with $\theta$ measured from the velocity direction).

(b) Observer moving at angle: pedestrian walking at 2 m/s at $60^{\circ}$ to the line from a 800 Hz siren 50 m away, $u_s = 30$ m/s: project both; the pedestrian term is $2\cos 60 = 1$ m/s: $f' = 800\dfrac{343 - 1}{343 - 30\cos\theta}$ — geometry first, numbers last.

cards.title: Vector clinic: worked projections (cont.)
items: (c) Echo as two applications of the box: target = intermediate observer/source; compose: $f'' = f\dfrac{c - \mathbf v_T\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{c - \mathbf v_T\cdot(-\hat{\mathbf r})}$-ish for monostatic... yields $\dfrac{c + u}{c - u}$ for approach ok JEE-27.

frame sanity: the medium frame is singled out by the physics (sound needs a medium); the formula is NOT Lorentz-invariant — the contrast with light (relativistic Doppler: $f' = f\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}$ approach... $\frac{1}{\gamma(1\mp\beta)}$ factors) is a favourite exam discussion.

cards.title: Where the case library hides inside the box
items: Case reduction: (i) 1D: projections $\pm u$; (ii) 2D: $u\cos\theta$ instantaneous; (iii) wind: shift to medium frame; (iv) moving reflector: two box applications; (v) accelerating: integrate projections over emission events (Oly 07); (vi) source passing: $\theta(t)$ from the geometry — the glide (Oly 08). The "four cases" of JEE-24 are four projection patterns of one sentence.

Second-order asymmetry explained: the box is exact; expanding $f' = f\dfrac{c + u_o}{c - u_s}$: the $u_s$ denominator is a geometric series while the $u_o$ numerator is finite — the asymmetry is built into the kinematics of wavefront emission vs collection.

cards.title: Where the case library hides inside the box (cont.)
items: Applications: acoustic Doppler velocimetry (measure $\mathbf v_o\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}$ of particles), anemometry (wind from $\mathbf w\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}$ via two beams), bat sonar (dual use of box + echo), fetal Doppler (blood-cell reflectors).
the vector box makes reasoning CHECKABLE: after any case analysis, re-derive with projections; agreement validates the sign work — the antidote to sign errors.

(a) $f = 500$ Hz source at $u_s = 40$ m/s at $30^{\circ}$ to the line of sight, receding side: $f' = 500\dfrac{343}{343 + 40\cos 30^{\circ}} = 500\cdot\dfrac{343}{377.6} = 454$ Hz. (b) Both moving toward each other at $u = 20$ each, 1D: $f' = 500\cdot\dfrac{363}{323} = 562$ Hz.

title: Sign-free Doppler: one vector formula for every case (cont.)
subtitle: Vector Doppler f' = f(c − v_o·r)/(c − v_s·r), projections replace cases.
takeaway: f = f0 (c - v_o.r)/(c - v_s.r): one vector formula replaces the entire case library.

cards.title: Box drills (answers in one line each) (cont.)
items: (c) Wind 15 m/s along the line, both at rest in ground: $f' = f$ (no shift), travel time downwind $L/(c+w)$ ok both parts of JEE-25 from one formula.
Reverse use: measure $f'$ from two positions to get the velocity projections; two beams at known angles solve for the 2D velocity vector — the Doppler ultrasound vector flow meter.

relativistic check: for light in vacuum the medium-frame concept dies; the invariant formula is $f' = f\gamma(1 - \beta\cos\theta)$ — same projection structure, different dynamics: a satisfying comparison answer.

cards.title: Accelerated motion: integrating the instantaneous shift
items: For a source with arbitrary velocity $\mathbf v_s(t)$ the observer hears $f'(t_e) = f\dfrac{c}{c - \mathbf v_s(t_e)\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}(t_e)}$ evaluated at the EMISSION time $t_e$: what is heard at time $t$ was emitted at $t_e = t - R(t_e)/c$ (implicit!) — retarded-time bookkeeping. Constant velocity: closed form (JEE-26 glide); constant acceleration along the line:
$f'(t_e) = f\dfrac{c}{c - a t_e}$: frequency diverges as the source approaches speed $c$... for $a t_e \to c$; reached at finite time: sonic boom geometry (JEE-28).

cards.title: Accelerated motion: integrating the instantaneous shift (cont.)
items: The glide-slope example as an integral: closest approach at $t = 0$, speed $u$, impact $b$: $f'(t) = f\dfrac{c}{c - u^2 t/\sqrt{b^2 + u^2 t^2}}$ (Oly 06 projections): linearising near $t = 0$: $f' \approx f\left(1 + \dfrac{u^2 t}{c b}\right)$:
slope $\dfrac{df'}{dt}|_0 = \dfrac{f u^2}{c b}$ downward after the pass ok the JEE-26 formula as the first term of the exact expansion.

cards.title: Accelerated motion: integrating the instantaneous shift (cont.)
items: Slowly accelerating radial motion: quasi-static shift $f'(t) \approx f(1 + v_r(t)/c)$: the frequency curve is the RADIAL VELOCITY curve scaled by $f/c$ — acoustic velocimetry: measuring $f'(t)$ reads $v_r(t)$ directly (differencing successive spectra).

the retarded-time structure is why accelerating-source problems are implicit: the emission point itself moves; solvable cases are (i) slow variation (quasi-static), (ii) constant velocity (closed form), (iii) special geometries (circular motion: Bessel sidebands).

title: Accelerated motion: integrating the instantaneous shift
subtitle: Glide from the vector box, slope fu²/(cb), retarded-time thinking.
takeaway: Accelerated motion: integrate the instantaneous shift at emission time; the glide is the first lesson.

cards.title: Accelerated motion: integrating the instantaneous shift (cont.)
items: circular motion check: source circling at radius $R$, angular rate $\Omega$: $v_r = u\cos(\Omega t)$-ish: $f' = f\left(1 + \dfrac{u}{c}\cos\Omega t\right)$ first order: PURE frequency modulation with sidebands $f \pm \Omega/2\pi$ — the ambulance-on-a-roundabout FM signal.

Setup recap: straight path, impact $b$, speed $u$, stationary observer, emission continuous. $\cos\theta(t) = \dfrac{ut}{\sqrt{b^2 + u^2t^2}}$ (sign per convention); $f'(t) = f\dfrac{c}{c - u\cos\theta(t)}$; values: $t = 0$: $f' = f$; $t \to \pm\infty$:

cards.title: Glide geometry: the exact curve and its slope (cont.)
items: $f\dfrac{c}{c \mp u}$; slope at 0: $\mp\dfrac{f u^2}{c b}$ (decreasing through the pass). Characteristic width: the glide occupies $\Delta t \sim b/u$ (the time to swing $\theta$ by a radian).

Spectrogram picture: a hyperbolic-like chirp symmetric in time but NOT in frequency (approach side higher by the $c/(c-u)$ vs $c/(c+u)$ asymmetry); a bat or porpoise hears the whole swoop and uses the slope for ranging (Oly 08).

Numbers (corrected source example): $f = 1000$ Hz, $u = 20$ m/s, $b = 100$ m, $c = 340$: slope 11.8 Hz/s; $f'(\pm 5$ s$) = 1043.2/960.1$ Hz; asymmetry at equal times: $83.1$ Hz total swing: the integral of the slope over the pass.

cards.title: Glide geometry: the exact curve and its slope (cont.)
items: consistency of slope and swing: average slope over $\pm 5$ s $\approx 83/10 = 8.3$ Hz/s vs peak 11.8 — smooth rolloff ok; far-field asymptotes reproduce the 1D pair 1043.5/960.5 Hz within 0.5 Hz at $\pm 5$ s... hmm far asymptotes are $1000\cdot 340/320 = 1062.5$ and $1000\cdot 340/360 = 944.4$: the pass values are closer to $f$ than the asymptotes ok correct shape.

(a) A car accelerating from rest toward a listener at $a = 2$ m/s$^2$: $v_r = at$: $f' = f(1 + at/c)$-ish until significant: at $t = 10$ s, $v = 20$ m/s: $f' = 1.06 f$: the pitch RISES continuously (unlike constant-velocity pass which glides down after). (b) A dropped source: $v_r = g t$ toward a listener below: same linear chirp downward in observed... source falling AWAY from an observer above:

cards.title: Accelerated-source problem patterns (cont.)
items: $f' = f(1 - gt/c)$: a falling whistle chirps down at $g f/c = 28.7$ Hz/s for $f = 1000$.

Retarded-time example: source at distance $d$ moving away at $u$ emitted at $t = 0$: received at $t = d/c$; the NEXT wavefront is received at $t = (d + u/f)/c$-ish: spacing stretched by $(c + u)/c$ ok the receding factor derived from scratch.

rotating and vibrating sources: turbine blades, sirens, ultrasound transducers: the spectrum is a set of sidebands $f \pm n f_{\mathrm{rot}}$ — Bessel-function amplitudes; the exam-accessible part is the first-order FM picture.

title: Accelerated motion: integrating the instantaneous shift (cont.)
subtitle: Glide from the vector box, slope fu²/(cb), retarded-time thinking.
takeaway: Accelerated motion: integrate the instantaneous shift at emission time; the glide is the first lesson.

cards.title: Slope-and-swing drills
items: (a) $f = 600$ Hz, $u = 25$ m/s, $b = 150$ m: slope $= 600\cdot 625/(340\cdot 150) = 7.35$ Hz/s. (b) "The observed pitch of a passing cycle horn (500 Hz) falls 60 Hz within 3 s of the pass: estimate $u^2/b$": slope 20 Hz/s $= f u^2/(c b)$: $u^2/b = 20\cdot 340/500 = 13.6$ m/s$^2$-ish units: with $u = 25$: $b = 46$ m. (c) Bat closing on an insect: both glide AND radial approach:
total slope = glide term + $f a/c$ from acceleration.

What can go wrong: near-field ($b \lesssim \lambda$) wave geometry breaks the ray picture; supersonic $u > c$ invalidates the subsonic formula entirely (JEE-28); turbulent air adds scintillation (amplitude noise), not frequency shift.

cards.title: Slope-and-swing drills (cont.)
items: the glide is the acoustic fingerprint of the geometry: slope gives $u^2/b$ (one equation, two unknowns — need the swing width $b/u$ or a second measurement to separate $u$ and $b$ — the structure of exam problems.

If the emission frequency $f$ and the source speed $u$ are known, one second of spectrogram near closest approach gives $b = \dfrac{f u^2}{c |slope|}$ (from Oly 07). If instead $b$ is known (e.g. flyby altitude), the slope gives $u$:

cards.title: Ranging from frequency slope: the acoustic McAfee method (cont.)
items: $u = \sqrt{\dfrac{c\,b\,|slope|}{f}}$. With BOTH slope and swing width $\Delta t \sim b/u$: the pair determines $u$ and $b$ independently: $u = |slope|\,c\,\Delta t/f$-ish... precisely combine $S = f u^2/(c b)$ and $W = b/u$: $u = \sqrt{S c W/f}$... derive: $S W = f u^2/(c b)\cdot b/u = f u/c$:
$u = \dfrac{S W c}{f}$ ok and $b = u W$.

cards.title: Ranging from frequency slope: the acoustic McAfee method (cont.)
items: Echo version (radar/sonar McAfee): measure the beat $\Delta f = 2 f u/c$ between direct and echo (JEE-27): $u = \dfrac{\Delta f\,c}{2f}$ directly; combine with the echo delay $\tau = 2R/c$ for range; the pair ($\Delta f$, $\tau$) gives ($u$, $R$) of the target — the full tracking state at one instant.

Accuracy: frequency slope measurable to ~1% from a clean spectrogram: $b$ to ~2%; the method needs no timing sync — pure frequency metrology: robust to amplitude noise; fails when $u$ is unknown along with $b$ (add a second pass or beam).
the slope method converts a TIME-domain difficult problem (nanosecond timing) into a FREQUENCY-domain easy one (Hz over seconds) — the deep reason Doppler ranging works.

title: Ranging from frequency slope: the acoustic McAfee method
subtitle: Ranging via slope u²/b, echo beats, two-beam tracking, method table.
takeaway: Frequency slope gives u^2/b; echo beats give u; two measurements give the full state.

cards.title: Ranging from frequency slope: the acoustic McAfee method (cont.)
items: units: $[f u^2/(c\,slope)] = $ Hz m$^2$s$^{-2}$ / (m s$^{-1}$ Hz s$^{-1}$) = m ok; numbers: $f = 1000$, $u = 20$, $c = 340$, slope 11.8: $b = 100$ m ok recovers the geometry.

Two beams at angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ to the target line: measure radial speeds $u\cos\theta_i$... solve: $u = \dfrac{v_{r1} - v_{r2}}{\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2}$-style elimination; three beams give the full 3D velocity vector — Doppler sodar and ultrasound vector flow imaging.
Track differentiation: successive ($u$, $R$) estimates give acceleration $a = du/dt$; the glide trajectory then fits ($b$, $u$, $a$) — the standard manoeuvring-target model.

cards.title: Two-beam and multi-beam Doppler tracking (cont.)
items: GPS-free ground speed: doppler log on ships (beam to the seabed), air data from pitot + acoustic cross-check; police lidar/radar: EM version of the same math ($c \to 3\times 10^{8}$, double shift always).
double-beam example: $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ beams, measured $v_r = 43.3$ and 0 m/s (one beam along the motion): $u = 50$ m/s ok cross-check $50\cos 30 = 43.3$ ok.

(a) "A jet of known speed 250 m/s at unknown altitude passes; the 400 Hz tone glides at 300 Hz/s through the closest point: find altitude": $b = f u^2/(c S) = 400\cdot 62500/(340\cdot 300) = 245$ m — absurdly low for a jet: sanity-check rejects the numbers (maybe $S$ read wrong from the spectrogram) — the discipline of orders of magnitude.

cards.title: Slope-method problem patterns (cont.)
items: (b) "A drone hovers at 40 m emitting 2 kHz; a cyclist approaches at 8 m/s: beat with the echo": $\Delta f = 2 f u_r/c$ with radial 8 m/s: 94 Hz beats — drone speed sensors use exactly this (acoustic flow sensors). (c) Bat 1: measure slope of the insect pass at $b = 2$ m, $u = 4$ m/s, 40 kHz: slope $= 40000\cdot 16/(340\cdot 2) = 941$ Hz/s — bats chirp-sweep over ~2 kHz in ms, resolvable.
combining slope + swing + echo delay separates $u$, $b$, $R$ — the exam trinity of ranging unknowns and their three equations.

cards.title: Method comparison table (which tool for which question)
items: Echo delay: gives RANGE $R = c\tau/2$ directly; needs timing. Doppler beat: gives RADIAL SPEED $\Delta f = 2fu/c$; needs clean spectrum. Glide slope: gives $u^2/b$; needs a pass geometry. Echo delay + beat: state $(u, R)$ ok. Slope + swing: state $(u, b)$ ok. Two beams: vector velocity ok. Time-of-flight + speed of sound thermometer: $c$ from $T$ (JEE-08).

Error budget: frequency measurements are precise ($10^{-4}$ easily) but $c$ depends on $T$ ($\pm 0.2$% per K) and wind ($\pm w/c$): for precision ranging, measure $T$ and $w$ or use two-way symmetric methods that cancel wind to first order (JEE-25).

title: Ranging from frequency slope: the acoustic McAfee method (cont.)
subtitle: Ranging via slope u²/b, echo beats, two-beam tracking, method table.
takeaway: Frequency slope gives u^2/b; echo beats give u; two measurements give the full state.

cards.title: Method comparison table (which tool for which question) (cont.)
items: the same toolkit works from bat sonar to medical Doppler to police radar; changing $c$ and $f$ scales the numbers, never the structure — the closing argument for learning the vector box.

For a duct of slowly varying cross-section $A(x)$ with negligible reflection (smooth taper, $|dA/dx| \ll kA$), conservation of time-averaged acoustic power gives $I(x) A(x) = $ const. Since $I = \dfrac{\Delta P_0^2}{2Z}$ and $I = \frac{1}{2} Z \omega^2 s_0^2$ in the same medium:

pressure amplitude $\Delta P_0 \propto A^{-1/2}$, displacement amplitude $s_0 \propto A^{-1/2}$, intensity $I \propto A^{-1}$ — a horn concentrates SOUND PRESSURE as $1/\sqrt{A}$ from throat to mouth.

cards.title: Slowly varying ducts and horns: I(x) A(x) = constant (WKB) (cont.)
items: WKB validity: the reflection coefficient per taper step is $R \sim \left(\dfrac{d\ln Z_c}{2k\,dx}\right)^2$-ish with $Z_c = \rho c/A$ the local characteristic impedance... practical rule: $R$ negligible when the area changes by much less than a factor 2 per wavelength; abrupt changes reflect (JEE-16 boundary theory).

Exponential horn: $A(x) = A_0 e^{mx}$: the horn equation has wave solutions with local wavenumber $k_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{k^2 - (m/2)^2}$: below cutoff $k < m/2$: EVANESCENT (horn stops passing — the horn cutoff frequency); the flare constant $m$ sets the cutoff $f_c = \dfrac{mc}{4\pi}$-ish... standard: $f_c = \dfrac{mc}{4\pi}$ for exponential:

cards.title: Slowly varying ducts and horns: I(x) A(x) = constant (WKB) (cont.)
items: low-frequency horns must flare gently (large mouth) — why trumpets end in big bells.

power conservation is the entire WKB content: the wave equation in a slowly varying duct with the ansatz $\Delta P = \mathcal{A}(x) e^{i\int k dx}$ gives $\mathcal{A}\sqrt{Z_c}$-type invariants; the exam physics is the $A(x) I(x) = $ const line.

convergence example: throat 1 cm$^2$ to mouth 100 cm$^2$: $I$ drops 100x (20 dB) but $\Delta P_0$ RISES 10x: horns trade intensity for pressure at the throat — exactly what a driver needs (impedance matching, Oly 01: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} \sim Z/A$-ish).

cards.title: Horns as impedance transformers (why they work)
items: A driver of area $S_d$ couples to air poorly (Oly 05 radiation resistance); a horn raises the throat loading: $Z_{\mathrm{throat}} \approx \rho c/A_{\mathrm{mouth}}\cdot$ (geometric gain): the mouth impedance $\rho c$ scaled by area ratio: efficiency up to ~50% vs a few % for a bare cone. The same mathematics as the middle ear (Oly 01) and the megaphone of antiquity.

Cutoff and directivity: below $f_c$ the horn is a poor radiator (evanescent throat); above, the mouth radiates a beam of angle $\theta \sim \sin^{-1}(\lambda/(\pi d))$-ish for mouth size $d$: megaphones beam high frequencies — the shouter hears their own voice differently than listeners do.
Mufflers and ducts: the reverse design — expansions and side branches reflect (Oly 03 traps); a smooth diffuser recovers pressure (wind tunnels, exhausts).

title: Slowly varying ducts and horns: I(x) A(x) = constant (WKB)
subtitle: WKB duct I·A = const, amplitude $\propto$ A^(−1/2), horn cutoff and matching.
takeaway: Slowly varying ducts carry I A = constant: amplitudes fall as A^(-1/2); horns match impedance.

cards.title: Horns as impedance transformers (why they work) (cont.)
items: numbers: exponential horn $m = 5$ m$^{-1}$: $f_c = 5\cdot 343/(4\pi) = 136$ Hz: audible bass passes; $m = 50$: $f_c = 1.36$ kHz: a trumpet-ish cutoff ok plausible instrument numbers.

(a) A duct halves its area: $I$ doubles, $\Delta P_0$ rises $\sqrt{2}$: the speed of the air in the throat rises as $u \propto I/\Delta P \propto 1/\sqrt A$... $u = \Delta P/Z$ stays? $\Delta P_0 \propto A^{-1/2}$, $u_0 = \Delta P_0/Z \propto A^{-1/2}$: velocity rises as the duct narrows ok (like a river through a constriction).

cards.title: WKB drill set (cont.)
items: (b) "Design a horn to halve the pressure amplitude of a 1 Pa source at the mouth": expand area 4x.

Horn equation quick form: $\dfrac{1}{A}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(A\dfrac{dP}{dx}\right) + k^2 P = 0$: WKB solution $P \propto \dfrac{e^{\pm ikx}}{\sqrt{A}}$ ok recovering the amplitude law; exact for cones and exponentials in terms of Bessel/Hankel functions.
shallow-water waves obey the same $I A = $ const rule (energy conservation); the "water hose narrowing" and tidal-bore funnelling are WKB in geophysics.

cards.title: When WKB fails (scope guards)
items: (i) Area jumps: full reflection analysis (Oly 02/03). (ii) $A \to 0$ (a closed end): WKB diverges; the boundary layer solution takes over (JEE-17). (iii) $dA/dx \sim kA$: significant reflection; (iv) losses (viscous boundary layers: $\alpha \propto \sqrt{f}/a$ in narrow tubes) break power conservation: horns must stay wide vs the viscous skin depth.

Helmholtz resonator limit: when the duct is shorter than $\lambda/4$, the lumped-parameter RLC model replaces WKB entirely — asymptotic methods need their validity conditions stated (the exam phrase: "slowly varying compared with $\lambda$").

cards.title: Elasticity of solids: three speeds from three moduli (cont.)
items: Derivation sketch: Newton 2nd law + Hooke tensor law $\sigma_{ij} = \lambda\,\mathrm{tr}(\epsilon)\delta_{ij} + 2G\epsilon_{ij}$ (Lamé $\lambda$, $G$): plane longitudinal wave: $\rho\ddot{u} = (\lambda + 2G)\nabla^2 u$: $v_P = \sqrt{(\lambda + 2G)/\rho} = \sqrt{(K + 4G/3)/\rho}$ since $K = \lambda + 2G/3$; transverse: $\rho\ddot{u}_\perp = G\nabla^2 u_\perp$: $v_S = \sqrt{G/\rho}$ ok.

Numbers: steel ($K = 160$, $G = 79$ GPa, $\rho = 7800$): $v_P = 5830$, $v_S = 3180$, $v_{\mathrm{rod}} = 5060$ m/s. Granite: $v_P \approx 5200$, $v_S \approx 3000$. Glass ($G = 30$ GPa): $v_S = 2130$. Rubber ($G \approx 1$ MPa, $\rho = 1100$): $v_S = 30$ m/s — slow and lossy.

cards.title: Elasticity of solids: three speeds from three moduli (cont.)
items: three combinations of two elastic constants + density: the rod speed is a boundary-conditioned mixture; the bulk pair is the intrinsic content of the elasticity tensor; Poisson ratio interpolates.

cards.title: Waves in rods: which boundary, which ladder (cont.)
items: Kundt tube (JEE-21) is the rod-speed measurement in reverse: $v_{\mathrm{rod}}$ known gives $v_{\mathrm{gas}}$; with a gas of known speed the rod speed comes out: the two-medium frequency match $f = v_{\mathrm{rod}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{rod}} = v_{\mathrm{gas}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{gas}}$.

Damping: metals ring (low internal friction, Q ~ $10^{3}$–$10^{4}$ for rods); lead and rubber damp (high loss tangent): struck rods of different metals have characteristic ring times — an exam qualitative question.
steel rod 1 m clamped mid: $f = 5060/2 = 2530$ Hz; in Kundt with dust heaps 6.5 cm apart: $v_{\mathrm{gas}} = 5060\times 0.065 = 329$ m/s (cold air ok plausible lab).

items: Composite rods: series springs: effective compliance adds: $1/Y_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sum L_i/(Y_i L)$-ish: wave speed in layered rods uses transfer matrices (outside syllabus; the 1D spring model is in).

dispersion in real solids: $v(\omega)$ bends near lattice resonances (Brillouin); ultrasound velocity metrology uses $v_P$, $v_S$ to get $K$, $G$, $\nu$ non-destructively — the engineering reading of this card.

cards.title: Numbers drill (three speeds)
items: Seismic locate: P-S time difference $\Delta t = d(1/v_S - 1/v_P)$: $d = \dfrac{\Delta t}{1/v_S - 1/v_P}$: for $\Delta t = 10$ s in granite: $d = 10/(3.29 - 1.90)\times 10^{-4}$... units: $d = \Delta t / (1/3040 - 1/5250) = 10/(3.29\times 10^{-4} - 1.90\times 10^{-4}) = 72$ km ok standard method.

cards.title: Numbers drill (three speeds) (cont.)
items: the pair (arrival times of P and S) plus one speed model locates events in three dimensions — the seismology version of echo + beat (Oly 08): two measurements, two unknowns.

Full supersonic toolkit: cone half-angle $\sin\alpha = 1/M$; observer at height $h$ below the flight line: boom delay after closest pass $t = \dfrac{h\sqrt{M^2-1}}{M v}$ (envelope derivation of JEE-28); emission point of the heard boom at $t_e = -t/(M^2-1)$ (BEFORE the pass);
the jet position at hearing is $x = h\sqrt{M^2-1}$ past the closest point. The three quantities answer three different questions — always identify which is asked.

cards.title: Mach geometry clinic: cones, delays, and emission points (cont.)
items: Boom carpet: the shock surface intersects the ground along a swath of width $w = h\cot\alpha\cdot 2$-ish for the full cone crossing... the ground trace: at any instant the cone-ground intersection is a line moving at $M v$; observers under the flight path receive the boom once; those off the track receive it at slant geometry; the overpressure decays slowly with altitude ($\propto h^{-3/4}$-ish empirically).

N-wave structure: the boom is a compression-rarefaction doublet of duration $\tau \sim \dfrac{\ell}{v}\cdot$ (aircraft length factor): Concorde: 0.1–0.3 s at 100–200 Pa; the spectrum of an N-wave is flat to $f \sim 1/\tau$ then falls: characteristic boom "crack".

cards.title: Angles and triangles: the clinic worksheet
items: Step 1: compute $c(T)$ (JEE-08). Step 2: $M = u/c$; $\alpha = \sin^{-1}(1/M)$. Step 3: draw the cone BEHIND the source; the observer is inside after the sweep. Step 5: check limits ($M = 1$: degenerate; $M \to \infty$: delay $\to h/v$).
Two observers: different delays from different $h$ and lateral offsets: the difference in arrival times LOCATES the flight line — inverse boom mapping (used to track supersonic tests).
Sonic boom from manoeuvres: turns pile shocks (focused superbooms); the clinic covers straight-and-level only.

cards.title: Clinic drills (cont.)

focused booms from turns can double overpressure (Whitham theory); "superboom" events over Oklahoma City (1960s tests) seeded the modern low-boom research (X-59) — history with the clinic math.

Mach number $M = u/c$; Mach angle $\alpha = \sin^{-1}(1/M)$; N-wave: two-shock signature; overpressure $\Delta P$: 50–500 Pa typical; carpet: ground swath; boom delay: closest-approach to hearing; superboom: focused enhancement; cutoff Mach: $M = 1$ exactly (infinite linear pile-up).

cards.title: Sonic-boom terminology card (cont.)
items: Regulation: supersonic flight over land banned for civil (US 1973 FAA rule) because of boom annoyance; Concorde flew supersonic only over water; X-59 targets 75 Pa "thump" to reopen the question.
precise vocabulary earns the method marks: examiners look for "cone", "shock", "delay from closest approach", and the $\sin\alpha = 1/M$ relation in any boom answer.

Kit formula set (air unless stated): $c = 331.3\sqrt{T/273}$ m/s; $Z = \rho c \approx 412$ rayl at 20 C; $\lambda = c/f$; $\Delta P_0 = Z\omega s_0$; $I = \Delta P_0^2/(2Z)$; $\beta = 10\log(I/10^{-12})$ dB; point source $I = P/(4\pi r^2)$; beats $|f_1 - f_2|$; Doppler $\frac{c + u_o}{c - u_s}$; echo $\frac{c+u}{c-u}$; pipes $v/4L$, $v/2L$; $e = 0.6r$; $Q = \omega\mathcal{E}/P_{\mathrm{loss}}$.

cards.title: Estimate-first discipline (the Fermi habit)
items: Before writing equations: estimate the answer in rounded numbers (factor-of-3 accuracy); then compute exactly; the two must agree within the rounded uncertainty — if not, a unit or a factor of $2\pi$ is wrong. Worked: "level 2 m from a 0.5 W siren": estimate $I \sim 0.5/50 \sim 0.01$ W/m$^2$: $\beta \sim 100$ dB; exact: 92 dB — same ballpark; the estimate catches the "$P/4\pi r^2$ vs $P/r^2$" family of slips immediately.

Unit traps the kit prevents: dB without a reference; $\lambda$ in cm vs m in $v = f\lambda$; temperature in Celsius inside $\sqrt{T}$; $M$ in g/mol inside $RT/M$; intensity vs pressure amplitude factors of 2; peak vs RMS $\sqrt{2}$.
